News.title: Terrifying moment plane cabin ceiling falls onto screaming passengers during chaotic landing after losing tyre
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment pieces of plane ceiling collapse and crash onto screaming passengers as it comes in to land.

The Boeing 737 flight across Iran was forced to make an impromptu landing when the aircraft interior started falling apart mid-air.



Horrifying footage shows the entire plane cabin violently trembling – before large chunks of aircraft casing begin to plummet down onto flyers.

Women can be heard screaming as one man appears to repeatedly call out to Allah in desperation.



Other flyers can be seen gripping their seats in fear or trying to hold back the ripped-off pieces of plane lining.

At one point the person filming is struck and the camera dramatically view tilts to the floor – where one can see a large square of plane casing.

According to local reports, the harrowing mid-air breakdown unfolded at around 5:40pm on Tuesday.

The Sepehran Airlines plane had burst a tyre shortly after take off, reported the outlet SimplyFlying.

The pilot declared a state of emergency – and immediately triggered an emergency landing.

The average Sepehran Airline plane is over three decades old, according to their fleet data, with the oldest still flying at 37 years.



The Boeing 737 had been headed for the western city of Kermanshah when it experienced a “mechanical failure”.

But the precise problem with the plane has not been made public.

Miraculously, nobody was injured in the terrifying incident.



All passengers and crew were evacuated safely, according to authorities.

Mashhad Airport temporarily shut down the runway for examination.

Iran Civil Aviation Organization has launched a probe into the incident.

It comes just weeks after another Sepehran Airlines Boeing 737-500 accident in Mashhad.

The plane, carrying 127 passengers, reportedly veered off the runway before its nose landing gear collapsed.



No injuries were reported.

News.title: Furious Brit tourist and partner who fled hotel inferno offered just £87 in compensation between them
News.content:
A BRITISH tourist and his partner who fled a hotel inferno have been offered just £87 in compensation between them.

Josh Robbins and Shelby A’Court took an all-inclusive Tui package trip to a £1,800-a-week complex in Croatia.



Yet they had to flee for their lives as flames closed in at the Gava Waterman Milna Resort on the island of Brac.

The couple said they and dozens of others were left to fend for themselves by staff.



They ran to a nearby dock and got away thanks to locals who turned up in a flotilla of boats.

Mortgage adviser Josh, 26, from Dorset, said: “We thought we were going to die.

“We want all our money back and compensation for what we went through but we’re being told it was an ‘act of God’ and we should claim insurance.

“Tui have now offered £87 — or a little more if we accept a voucher.

“I asked them to email the offer.

“I’ll send it to my legal adviser.”



The hotel denied claims guests were abandoned, insisting reception staff aided the evacuation.

Tui was asked to comment.

News.title: Cost of foreign holidays to soar by £100s thanks to Net Zero just days after PM approved UK ‘tourist tax’
News.content:
MEETING Net Zero ­targets could put hundreds of pounds on the price of holiday flights, experts warn.

Jetting to Benidorm on the Costa Blanca would be £150 more by 2050 — and a plane to New York £400 more expensive.



It comes as Labour mayors plan a tax of up to five per cent on overnight stays here.

The flight price hike warnings comes after the Climate Change Committee (CCC), which advises the Government, says the industry should pay for pollution-cutting measures, which will probably be passed on to passengers.



Tim Alderslade, of industry body Airlines UK, said it could “price ordinary people out of the joys of travel”.

CCC chair Nigel Topping, however, said the “polluter pays principle must apply”.



He added: “If aviation is to grow, it must take responsibility for the emissions it creates.”

The CCC said the expansion of Heathrow cannot proceed unless the aviation sector cuts emissions.

To do so, it said, firms must invest in more efficient planes and green fuels.

The Department for Transport said it was investing £219million in sustainable aviation fuel production and £43million in cleaner technologies to back greener aviation.



It said expansion could boost the economy by £40billion and support 60,000 local jobs.

It added: “We will carefully consider the CCC’s advice.”

The Government aims to hit Net Zero by 2050.

News.title: Shock moment driving instructor ploughs into cycling grandma sending her flying & seriously injuring her
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a driving instructor ploughs into a cycling grandma leaving her with devastating injuries.

Rebecca Tanton was sent flying when she was struck by a car travelling 55mph in Lincolnshire two years ago.



Horror footage shows the moment Jon Dick smashes his Ford Puma into the mother-of-three on Manby Road on October 7, 2024.

In one rear view clip, she is seen flying through the air as she is launched from the bike before she crashes to the tarmac.



She is then seen sprawled on the side of the road as a car behind is forced to swerve out of the way.

Dashcam footage then shows Mr Dick in the driver’s seat as the car jolts after hitting Ms Tanton before he slows to a stop, realising what had happened.



Ms Tanton told the Daily Mail her “life is changed completely” adding: “I am simply existing in constant pain, while Jon Dick is still walking around freely – and he has shown no remorse whatsoever.”

“From the moment Jon Dick carelessly drove his car into me, he took away my freedom, independence and love of life,” she added.



She claimed that the driving instructor had never apologised for the incident that left her fighting for her life.

Ms Tanton said she remembered “very little of the aftermath”.

She suffered catastrophic injuries and was raced to hospital for an emergency blood transfusion.

Her pelvis and the bones on the right hand side of her body were left completely shattered by the crash.

The grandmother also suffered a horror facial injury and underwent emergency plastic surgery that evening to stop her haemorrhaging blood.



Over the course of the following weeks, Ms Tanton recovered in ICU where she had seven metal plates screwed into her bones.

When her wounds started to heal, she contracted sepsis as a result of the plates.

An emergency operation to stem the infection resulted in an accidentally torn bladder and was forced to wear a catheter for three months.

And as she recovered, she was forced to make funeral arrangements for her 33-year-old son who tragically passed away from brain cancer.

She said the funeral for the beloved marine pilot had to be postponed until she was in a stable condition, adding she was “barely able to walk” due to her injuries.



Before the crash, Ms Tanton was an avid cyclist riding 40 miles a day while she also enjoyed horse-riding and swimming.

Now, Ms Tanton faces the constant threat of her sepsis returning due to the metal plates fused to her bones.

If it does return, doctors say she has a one-in-three chance of survival.

In December 2025, Jon Dick was found guilty of causing serious injury by careless driving and was handed a suspended prison sentence and two-year driving ban.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In her victim statement she said it had been a “living nightmare” for her and her family.



The Sun has contacted Mr Dick for comment.

News.title: Britain on ‘energy cliff’ after woke Net Zero drive left us exposed to Russia and China, ex-MI6 chief warns
News.content:
BRITAIN is on the edge of an “energy cliff” after prioritising woke Net Zero policies over taking on Russia and China, ex-MI6 chief Sir Richard Dearlove will warned.

The spymaster will tonight blast ministers in a landmark speech after accusing the Government of handing Beijing the tools to turn Britain’s lights out.



Sir Richard, who ran MI6 from 1999 to 2004, will deliver his warning in a lecture to the Global Warming Policy Foundation in London.

He will say: “We have as a nation negligently wandered close to a cliff edge and the adversaries I have described stand ready to help us over it.”



Sir Richard claims ministers have spent too long focusing on climate change and eco policies.

He will say the country’s biggest threat is not global warming but Vladimir Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China.

Both are willing to use Britain’s reliance on foreign equipment and undersea cables as weapons, he added.

He said the Kremlin’s GRU spy agency has spent decades building the capability to sever cables, pipelines and electricity interconnectors.

Sir Richard is to say: “We are not the victims of a conspiracy to make us vulnerable. We have quite casually done this to ourselves.

“Such peacetime dependencies give China strategic leverage.



“Water, sewage, gas networks, rail and underground transport, traffic lights and communication are all mains-connected.

“We have very little industry left to protect and we cannot rebuild non-existent industries which lie in foreign jurisdictions beyond our reach.”

And, taking aim at Ed Miliband, he adds: “Does the Foreign Secretary, the arch prophet of net zero, have any grasp of the country’s predicament?

“His present focus on new West Bank Israeli settlements suggests that his attention is elsewhere.”



He will go on: “To hear the Prime Minister state in Parliament that ‘national security can’t come at the expense of social security’ leaves me in a state of pessimism and extreme concern.

“The first responsibility of government is the safety of the nation.

“However successive governments have forgotten this, and Britain is now caught in an energy trap of its own making.

“The task is urgent. The government should have this amongst its very top priorities.

“Stated simply, we need an energy policy which moves us back a safe distance from the cliff edge.”



Professor Gwythian Prins, of the London School of Economics, said: “As a former head of MI6, Sir Richard’s warnings are of chilling importance.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“No-one can now pretend that our enemies China, Russia and Iran are not using our self-harming delusion with ‘net zero’ to attack the core of national security by Active Measures.”

News.title: Labour U-turn as ministers vow pensioners won’t be hit by tax when state pension tops £13,000
News.content:
LABOUR was yesterday forced to promise the elderly will not be hammered by a “granny tax”.

Chancellor John Healey is drawing up Budget plans to ensure pensioners are not punished when the triple-lock pushes the annual state pension above £13,000 next year.



Tax becomes payable at the current threshold of £12,570.

But if a pensioner has no other income they will not be penalised.



Retirees with other money sources will still pay tax.

New figures showed the state pension is likely to go up by 3.9 per cent next year, the same rate as wages.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds initially refused to rule out the retirees paying tax on the state pension next year.

But pensions Minister Torsten Bell said pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the “administrative burden” of paying small amounts of tax this Parliament.

One Andy Burnham ally, economist Andy Haldane, told LBC that money markets “now suspect that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.



Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith hit out, saying: “Pensioners will spend their last years filling tax returns or on the phone to HMRC.

“Labour will tax everything – from your holiday to Granny’s pension.”

The government faces huge fiscal pressures from high borrowing costs, the Iran war fall-out and welfare costs, such as the state pension rise under the triple lock mechanism.

News.title: Locals furious as motors from ‘dangerous’ car dealership spill out into street blocking roads and causing ‘gridlock’
News.content:
LOCALS have been left furious after a “dangerous” car dealership started using surrounding roads to park its stock.

Residents in Watford, Hertfordshire, say the actions of staff at a Jaecoo and Omoda dealership is causing “gridlock”.



The dealership has received more than 130 enforcement visits in the last month, with claims the motors are blocking pavements and taking up spaces.

But the local council is struggling to take action as some of the cars are unregistered or have no number plates, making it a police matter.



Models including the Jaecoo 7 SUV, which retails from around £30,000, could be seen parked on the street and pavement without number plates.

Neighbour Elsie Humphries, 87, said she wanted to give staff at the dealership “one where the sun don’t shine” because of their behaviour.

She said: “They’re on the pavement where people walk down, so they have to go out into the road to come.

“They say if they haven’t got a number on the front they can put a car where they want.”



Annie Secunda, 83, said her retirement housing community’s local bus stop has been blocked by the dealership’s cars, meaning buses are forced to stop in the middle of the road.

She said: “I’ve got nothing against the cars, I’ve got nothing against the people – but it’s just the inconsideration that they show for everybody else.

“Elderly people have to walk around in the road to get on the bus.”

Nearby resident Glody, 30, said new deliveries of cars were arriving “every day”.

He said: “It’s pretty dangerous – the roads around this area are pretty narrow, and if cars are taking up the footpath, people have to walk in to the road.



“At the end of summer they started to deliver more vehicles, I’ve started seeing a lot more vehicles outside, even on the footpaths.

“It seems like it’s just come out of nowhere. It’s a big problem. They seem like they own the place.”

Peter Taylor, elected Mayor of Watford, said: “Local residents are understandably annoyed that this business is flouting parking restrictions around the dealership.



“The council has increased the number of patrols to try get them to change their behaviour.

“In the last month there have been over 130 visits and we will continue to serve Penalty Charge Notices to vehicles parked illegally where they have registration plates.

“We have visited the dealership and made them aware of our serious concerns.

“We are also working with the Police and Hertfordshire Highways to see what more can be done to stop unregistered vehicles being parked where they shouldn’t be, as this falls outside of our parking enforcement team’s jurisdiction.”

Endeavour Automotive Group, which operates the dealership, said: “We are aware of concerns regarding vehicle parking and deliveries at our Omoda & Jaecoo location on Lower High Street, Watford, and we take these matters seriously.



“As vehicle volumes increase at certain times of the year, we recognise the impact that parking can have on local residents, pedestrians and surrounding public spaces.

“We are continuing to review the matters raised with our site management team, including vehicle delivery arrangements, parking, and the way any concerns from residents have been handled.

“To help address the issue, we have secured additional compound space – three compounds in total – to ease pressure on the site and provide further vehicle storage capacity.

“This is aimed at reducing the need for vehicles to be parked on surrounding roads, while also helping to remove cars from grass verges and keep pedestrian pathways clear and accessible.

“Here at Endeavour Automotive, we are continuing to work with our teams and logistical partners to ensure vehicles are stored responsibly and in accordance with local parking regulations.



“We also expect all colleagues to deal with residents and members of the public in a respectful and professional manner at all times.

“We remain committed to being a good neighbour within the community and will continue to review our operations to help reduce any disruption to local residents, pedestrians and visitors.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Hertfordshire Constabulary spokesperson said: “We appreciate the frustration this situation is causing for residents and understand the concerns around accessibility, road safety and disruption in the area.

“We are actively working with Watford Borough Council, the dealership and other partners to resolve these issues being experienced by the local community.”

News.title: The only way out of the giant mess Britain’s economy is in is for Labour to crackdown on skivers
News.content:
Sicknote UK

THE Welfare Party’s creation of a world where work is increasingly optional is crushing hopes of a return to prosperity.

Yesterday’s unemployment and benefit figures were dismal.

Britain’s sickness benefits bill has ballooned to a record 7.6million claims — including 4.1million on disability PIPs and 3.5million on the health element of Universal Credit.



Shockingly, that is up by ONE MILLION in just a year.



A FIFTH of all working-age adults have now disappeared from the jobs market altogether.

Meanwhile, more than 200,000 jobs have been lost since Labour took power.

Private sector wages are rising at just 2.9 per cent. But in the public sector — where the Government has spent billions on pay bribes to striking doctors, teachers and train drivers — wage increases are DOUBLE at six per cent.

Labour’s addiction to State power means that pay gap will only get wider and the cost to a shrinking number of taxpayers even higher.

Does anyone in Government understand the massive economic problems the country now faces?

Yesterday, allies of Chancellor John Healey desperately briefed he didn’t know how bad things were until arriving in the Treasury. Really?

With debt and welfare spiralling out of control and growth near zero, Britain has been facing a slow-motion economic car crash for well over a year.



The only way out of the giant mess is for Healey to crack down on the skivers’ benefits jamboree.

He then needs to show he is committed to freeing up the strivers by cutting taxes and putting more money back in their pockets.

So far, there’s been precious little sign that Labour has the stomach for the fight needed to deliver either.

Lou blow

SIR Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves’ answer to the crippled public finances was to target business.

But driving up National Insurance on employers and making the minimum wage unaffordable only ended up pricing a million young people out of jobs.



Yesterday, First Minister Lou Haigh unveiled another genius plan.

This time it’s to saddle firms with another costly headache by bringing in new laws which will allow all staff greater flexible working.

That includes the right to demand more working from home. Bosses will be compelled to waste time holding meetings over any requests — and come up with reasons for refusing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It won’t do anything to boost growth or productivity, one of the Government’s main aims. In fact, it might well have the opposite effect.

But it’s not a bad return for the union chiefs who pushed for ever more onerous workers’ rights in return for donating millions to Labour.

News.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
News.content:
OpenAI boss Sam Altman thinks people should have more faith in his company and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about all the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

The fervor over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.

By Tuesday, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.

"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".

News.title: Letby doctor says inquiry 'grim reading' and he wishes 'we had been brave enough to follow suspicions'
News.content:
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading".

Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit.

He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.

"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC.

"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."

The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday.

In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital".

The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns.

Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned.

"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that."

News.title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
News.content:
The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank, aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity."

Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister.

He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine.

He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions.

"Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine â but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine."

It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

News.title: Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84%
News.content:
The number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog has risen by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over rising bills.

The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were.

Water customers in England and Wales have been hit with steep price hikes in recent years. The regulator Ofwat has also allowed firms to put up bills by 36% between 2025 and 2030.

Water UK, which represents firms, said it understood that higher bills was never welcome, but the money was needed "to fund vital upgrades".

The total number of complaints to the watchdog rose to 15,115 in 2025-26, from 8,235 in the previous year.

Meanwhile, complaints made by households directly to water companies, which is required before complaining to the CCW, rose by 56% to 321,347.

The top three subjects of complaints to the CCW were measured billing, affordability and billing admin.

Mike Keil, the chief executive of the CCW, said the figures "reflect just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector".

He said customers are "impatient to see the benefits" of higher bills.

"Companies need to be clear and open with their customers about how they are investing people's money to deliver real improvements."

The CCW assessed each water company's performance on the number of complaints it received for every 10,000 households it serves, and the amount of effort customers have to put in to get their complaint resolved.

Thames Water and South West Water rated "poor" for both performance measures.

David Bird, retail director at Thames, apologised to customers who "have not received the service they should expect".

"We know bill clarity has been a particular source of frustration, which is why we have launched a programme to redesign them, so they are easier to understand," he said.

Bills for the average Thames customer rose by 31% in 2024, but were a lot smaller this year at 3.4%.

South West Water said: "We know there is more to do to improve our customers' experience. We are taking action by reducing repeat contacts, resolving issues when people contact us for the first time, and ensuring they receive clear, timely communication."

Portsmouth Water and Bristol Water were the only companies to score "good" in both metrics, retaining their position at the top of the rankings as the sector's best performers.

Last month, Ofwat approved bill increases for 13 companies to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Five of those companies â Thames, Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Wessex Water and South East Water â were already permitted to hike bills in 2024.

A spokesperson for industry body Water UK said: "We understand increasing bills is never welcome, but the money is needed to fund vital upgrades to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas.

The spokesperson said that 94% of complaints are "being dealt with at the earliest possible stage without the need for further involvement from the consumer body".

"The industry remains committed to improving communication with customers and showing clearly how their money is being used to deliver the improvements they expect," the spokesperson added.

News.title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog
News.content:
A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.

One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.

Meta had already removed the offending ads. But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".

"We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.

"Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm."

The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.

It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform.

The ASA said the law had changed during its investigations and that ads identified in future would be considered in light of both the law and its own rules.

Where ads are identified as illegal, it said it may notify platforms and law enforcement.

News.title: Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers
News.content:
Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved without changes to current climate policies, the government's advisers have said.

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) , externalsaid expansion can still go ahead but only if the aviation industry funds cleaner fuels and pays for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air.

Making the industry pay could push up the cost of flying with a return trip to Alicante costing around Â£150 more by 2050, and a return to New York up Â£400 in today's prices, it said.

Once built, the expanded airport would produce more carbon dioxide than any other single sector of the economy by 2050. Heathrow said expansion and climate goals were "not a choice" and it would deliver both.

"Our advice today is clear - Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK's Net Zero target," said Nigel Topping, the CCC chair.

"Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today."

The CCC report cannot block a new runway but it wants the government to pass legislation pushing responsibility for the long-term clean-up of aviation onto the industry.

The government would "carefully consider" the advice alongside other responses to its consultation according to the Department for Transport (DfT).

The government has an ongoing consultation which aims to judge any expansion against four tests - economy, climate, air quality and noise.

It does not approve a runway - that will come in a Commons vote expected later this year.

The Â£33bn project would raise Heathrow's capacity to 150 million passengers a year - up from 85 million.

A DfT spokesperson said any expansion would need to align with the country's climate targets, but added it "could deliver around Â£40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs".

News.title: Magazine returned to US library after 132 years overdue
News.content:
A 19th century magazine borrowed from a library in New Hampshire 132 years ago has finally been returned.

Concord Public Library said the overdue September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine was returned last week after the library announced a freeze on fines.

The magazine was 48,220 days overdue and would have incurred a $12,055 (Â£8,950) fine.

The patron who returned the magazine, John, said it had been "hanging around" his house for decades, but he had no idea how it ended up in his home.

He decided to return the magazine after reading about the library's fine freeze in the local newspaper.

"We've witnessed many happy faces since announcing our fine freeze," Concord Public Library wrote on Facebook. , external

"Of course, we expected long overdue books to be returned, but certainly not something from the late 19th century!"

Concord Public Library declared a year-long amnesty on overdue fines from 1 September 2026, with plans to evaluate the effects of a "fine-free library".

"Understandably, it won't be placed back in circulation, but perhaps it deserves a spot in the Concord Room," the post on social media said, referring to a section of the library dedicated to local history.

"Thankfully, he won't have to pay the $12,055 fine for being 48,220 days overdue."

News.title: Prolific shoplifters behind more than 28,000 offences, BBC finds
News.content:
At the height of his offending, Jeff Ashman estimates he walked out of shops with goods worth Â£400 to Â£500 on a daily basis.

"It's mind-boggling," he said, describing how much he had stolen from stores in Hastings to fuel his addiction to heroin and crack cocaine.

"I know the misery and grief and despair that I have caused these people for a long period of time."

Shoplifting is now firmly in the past for Ashman, but prolific shoplifters like him continue to plague communities across England.

We asked police about the 10 suspects their forces had most often linked to shoplifting offences between 2020-21 and 2025-26.

It revealed 28,415 recorded offences had been linked to just 270 suspects by the 27 forces who shared data with us.

It is an average of 105 offences per person - and those are just the occasions where a theft was formally reported to police and officers identified a suspect.

The suspects identified include one in Sussex who had been linked to 247 shoplifting offences, the equivalent of a reported crime every 10 days.

Policing minister Sarah Jones said shoplifting was a "pernicious crime that for too long has gone unpunished".

She said: "They need to know that they are going to be punished for what they have done."

News.title: Search launched for boy, 3, missing at playground
News.content:
Emergency services and members of the public are searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing at a playground.

Noah Woods was with a relative at the small park at Merriam Close in Brantham, but "became separated" from them as they left at about 15:00 BST, Suffolk Police said.

The toddler, who is partially deaf, autistic and non-verbal, was reported to have run down a nearby alleyway towards a newbuild housing estate.

"We ask local residents to please check their outbuildings, gardens and sheds, and report any sightings to police on 999," Supt Pete Partridge said.

A helicopter has been pictured flying over the scene, which is near the estuary of the River Stour and close to the Essex border.

Police described Noah as white, with curly ginger hair, and said he would not respond to his name being called.

News.title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
News.content:
An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said.

The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected.

An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told.

The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Those affected are being notified directly, the department said.

News.title: 'One in, one out' scheme costs £56,000 per person returned to France, home secretary says
News.content:
The government's "one in, one out" scheme to send migrants who cross the Channel back to France costs on average Â£56,000 per person, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said.

That is higher than the Home Office's estimated average cost for enforced migrant returns of Â£48,800.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

Mahmood told MPs the policy had been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved were still "relatively small".

She said the total number deported under the scheme since it began in August 2025 was around 1,400.

Asked by the Conservative MP Robbie Moore whether she thought the scheme had been a success, Mahmood said: "On its own terms, can you prove the concept that such a deal is viable, that you can get returns off and up and running - yes.

"It's not been without its challenges, obviously. The numbers are still relatively small.

"What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system."

She said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme.

News.title: British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
News.content:
Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement.

The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (Â£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators.

Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm.

A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance.

"I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying.

Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities.

The UK Foreign Office told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

News.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
News.content:
MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the Â£100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

When the government set out its plans to cap foreign donations in March and July, it did not mention the idea of an enhanced residency test for political donors.

Asked repeatedly by reporters whether the idea of tightening residency rules had only been discussed after Delo and Harborne's most recent donations to Reform, the prime minister's official spokesman would not give a timeframe.

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost Â£43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

News.title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
News.content:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"That is bringing results.

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

UK inflation is set to have accelerated further last month as higher fuel costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East and more expensive electronics pushed up the cost of living.

The Office for National Statistics will reveal the latest rate of UK Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation on Wednesday.

It is expected to reveal that inflation rose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% a month earlier, according to a consensus of analysts compiled by Pantheon Macroeconomics.

It would point towards a continued upwards trajectory for inflation since reaching a 15-month low of 2.6% in June.

Economists have suggested that the fresh figures are likely to show the early impact of the breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire.

Oil and gas prices have ticked higher since the US-Iran ceasefire deal collapsed on July 8.

Oxford Economics’ Andrew Goodwin said he expects the data to show a significant uplift linked to higher petrol and diesel costs for motorists.

“Weekly data from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero suggests that fuel prices rose 7% month-on-month between July and August, and we expect this to add around 0.2 percentage points to CPI inflation,” he said.

Airfares are also likely to have swung higher in August following weaker pricing in July, with higher jet fuel costs also feeding into ticket prices.

Experts at Pantheon Macroeconomics also suggested that so-called “AI-flation” could also be a factor.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist for the company, said they believe higher electronics prices, linked to chip shortages amid the AI boom, could add 0.2 percentage points to inflation.

Analysts at Deutsche Bank said: “After broadly matching expectations in July, we see price momentum pushing up again in August.

“Some goods inflation, food inflation and a chunky rise in energy prices will likely see inflation take another small step higher to round up the summer.”

The banking giant predicted that CPI will peak at around 3.5% year-on-year in November as further price pressures, such as another rise in household energy bills in October, come into effect.

Projections for rising inflation have contributed to heightened expectations that the Bank of England could increase interest rates in the coming months.

University of Texas quarterback Arch Manning issued an apology on social media following criticism he received for laughing at an artificial intelligence-generated video that depicted Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian striking ESPN reporter Holly Rowe.

The incident began Tuesday when Manning posted a statement to his Instagram Story addressing remarks he made during a media availability one day prior, as reported by ESPN.

“In my press conference yesterday, I made an insensitive comment about an AI video,” Manning wrote. “There is nothing funny about it. It's easy to say I didn't mean it, but I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people. I do not take that lightly and am deeply sorry for that.”

The online backlash stemmed from comments Manning made on Monday when asked if he had viewed any fan-edited clips circulating online after Texas secured a 24-23 victory over Ohio State in Austin.

“I’ve seen a few AI edits of stuff, but that's about it. I saw an AI edit of Sark’s interview,” Manning told reporters on Monday while laughing. “Have y'all seen that one? That’s a good one. Of him slapping Holly Rowe? It’s hilarious.”

open image in gallery Following public criticism of his reaction to an artificial intelligence-generated clip showing Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian hitting ESPN sideline reporter Holly Rowe, University of Texas quarterback Arch Manning took to social media to apologize ( Getty Images )

The fabricated clip parodied a post-game interaction during which Sarkisian abruptly ended an on-field interview with Rowe by shouting, “Texas fight. Hook ‘em!” and walking away. In the deepfake version, the coach shouts the same phrase before striking Rowe, causing her to fall to the turf.

Following the public reaction to his remarks, Manning specifically directed his apology to the veteran broadcaster.

“I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments,” Manning said. “ have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment. I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward.”

open image in gallery ESPN reporter Holly Rowe stated on social media that she accepted the quarterback’s apology following a private conversation between the two ( Getty Images )

Rowe told her followers on X that she and the quarterback had spoken privately and that she accepted the apology.

“Thank you Arch,” Rowe posted. “I appreciate our conversation about this -- which will remain private. Apology accepted. We move forward with respect and kindness for one another.”

During the game that preceded the incident, Manning completed 23 of 37 passes for 195 yards and added 24 rushing yards in the team’s comeback win over Ohio State.

A prominent animal rights group is planning to meet with a top fashion executive who was filmed physically restraining two protesters during an altercation at a New York runway show, an incident that stunned many in the fashion world.

Moira Colley, senior director of media relations for People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals in New York, said Tuesday that the group has plans to meet with Steven Kolb, longtime chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, to discuss ending the use of wool and animal skins in clothing.

Kolb has apologized for his actions, which included forcefully restraining two PETA employees and putting his hand over their mouths, and is taking a leave from his job pending an investigation.

Colley said PETA's initial plan was to file a police report against Kolb. The group changed course after a visit to police and then consulting with attorneys, she said, and decided to seek the meeting with Kolb. He has agreed to meet, Colley said, adding that a time had not yet been set.

The group intends to show Kolb videos of how sheep are mistreated for the use of their wool.

“We are willing to drop everything if we reach an understanding that benefits the animals,” Colley said in a phone interview. She also said the group recognized Kolb’s previous involvement in getting fur banned from runway shows on the CFDA schedule — and hoped he would again “do the right thing.”

There was no immediate response Tuesday to a message sent to Kolb’s CFDA email address. The council is the fashion industry's main trade organization, and Kolb has worked there for two decades, becoming CEO in 2011.

Video of the incident from the Sunday runway show for Cos, a brand owned by H&M, quickly drew widespread attention.

It showed Kolb, who is well known and respected in the New York fashion world, forcibly restraining Andrija Barak and Mason Melito, identified by PETA as employees.

Barak was aiming to disrupt the runway show, calling out slogans about the use of wool. Kolb is seen in the video covering her mouth with his hands and restraining her with both his arms and a leg over her body as he seeks to let the show continue.

Separately he is seen pushing Melito and also putting his hands over his mouth.

Colley said the two were among six employees at the show. Three aimed to disrupt the runway, including Barak, and three were filming, including Melito.

News.content:

Federal agents have arrested a pair of suspects after 42 kilograms of fentanyl, a golden gun and a small alligator were found at a luxury apartment in downtown Los Angeles last week.

Marvin Angelito, 27, and Susan Gonzalez, 26, were arrested last Thursday — the same day agents raided their apartment, which federal prosecutors called a “known drug trafficking location.”

While executing a search warrant for the alleged stash house, agents found about 42.6 kilograms of fentanyl pills and powder, one kilogram of heroin and 7.2 kilograms of cocaine, the Justice Department announced Tuesday.

Agents also found guns, including a gold-plated Desert Eagle .50-caliber pistol with ammunition on the kitchen counter, and a small alligator in a glass tank with water, according to prosecutors.

open image in gallery Federal agents have arrested a duo after 42 kilograms of fentanyl, a golden gun and a small alligator were found at a luxury apartment in downtown Los Angeles last week ( DOJ )

open image in gallery Marvin Angelito, 27, and Susan Gonzalez, 26, were arrested last Thursday — the same day agents raided their apartment, which federal prosecutors called a 'known drug trafficking location' ( DOJ )

The alligator was seized by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The Independent has reached out to the agency for comment on the gator’s condition.

Lab equipment, including beakers, mixers, stirrers and torches, was also seized in the search, as was a hydraulic press, an AR-15 rifle with ammunition found in a hallway closet and a police radio, according to prosecutors.

Agents found the Olympic + Hill apartment building that the duo was living in through a confidential source who arranged to pay $125,000 for 500,000 fentanyl pills from an alleged drug trafficker, the Los Angeles Times reported, citing a criminal complaint charging Angelito and Gonzalez and an attached affidavit.

open image in gallery Agents reportedly found the Olympic + Hill apartment building that the duo was living in through a confidential source who arranged to pay $125,000 for 500,000 fentanyl pills from an alleged drug trafficker ( DOJ )

Angelito and Gonzalez were charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl. Both face a maximum sentence of life in prison if convicted.

They both made their initial court appearances Monday, when U.S. Magistrate Judge Karen L. Stevenson ordered Angelito to remain detained and Gonzalez to be released on a $15,000 bond. No pleas were taken Monday.

Angelito’s arraignment is scheduled for October 2 and Gonzalez’s arraignment is scheduled for October 9.

A bill that proposes to fix some of the biggest problems in college sports — spiraling spending, constant lawsuits and a transfer portal run amok — cleared a major hurdle Tuesday when the Senate voted 74-24 to halt debate and move the measure one step closer to a final up-or-down vote.

The Protect College Sports Act, a bill co-sponsor Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called “a bipartisan solution designed to bring order to the chaos” easily cleared the 60-vote threshold it needed to stop the filibuster.

Co-sponsor Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said the lopsided nature of the vote left her “cautiously optimistic” it could get through the House, which has failed repeatedly in passing a different version of a college sports bill.

There remains, however, a persistent block of opposition.

“What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation,” said Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn.

Notably, all four Black Democrats in the Senate — Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Angela Alsobrooks — voted against the bill that is strongly opposed by the NAACP.

The vote came a week after college football's most recent crisis — a scheduled meeting of school presidents in the Southeastern Conference to expel LSU over its now-canceled plans to place players on the roster who had participated in NFL training camps.

Calmer heads prevailed. The eligibility lawsuit that triggered the mess is the sort of litigation the bill would outlaw.

“That was probably like a big lamp for some people who saw it and said, ‘Oh my God, this is so out of control,’" Cantwell said in an interview with The Associated Press. “You can see how out-of-hand the situation was getting.”

Introduced in May, compromises finally got the bill to the floor in September

Cantwell and Cruz introduced the bill in late May and it nearly died without the support of the Southeastern and Big Ten conferences. Compromises helped get them on board, then it became a matter of getting the bill onto the floor of the busy upper chamber.

At around the time the vote took place, Cantwell released a report that outlined a “spending spiral” that has taken hold of college sports since name-image-likeness payments began.

Among its findings: There was a $519.9 million increase in institutional and government support of athletic programs between 2015 and 2025 among the 53 schools in the Power Four whose data was publicly available. The bill promises to harness that in a number of ways, including:

— Placing into law the 22% cap (around $21.5 million this year) on revenue colleges are allowed to share with their players — an amount agreed to in the House settlement that defined the rules over paying players. It would add a $27.5 million “retention pool” for schools to keep current players in a move that could bring some of the hard-to-regulate third-party NIL deals back in-house.

— Giving conferences the option of pooling their TV media rights, a move proponents say could raise between $4 billion and $8 billion in additional revenue. The SEC and Big Ten disagree and say they would not participate.

— Restricting players to one “free” transfer where they wouldn't have to sit out a year, which could limit bidding wars that take place year-round in the transfer portal.

— Placing into law the NCAA's new rule that allows players five years of eligibility, but no more.

Critics say the NCAA, which has struggled to police its business for the last 100 years, shouldn't be getting more power.

“Over and over again, courts have determined that colleges and the NCAA and conferences are violating the law,” Murphy said.

The bill, however, has gained support from a long list of sports leaders, including retired football coach Nick Saban and Deion Sanders of Colorado, and basketball coaches John Calipari of Arkansas and Mark Few of Gonzaga.

“I think this clears up about 75-80% of our issues,” Calipari said at a news conference in Washington on Monday, the eve of the vote. “Nothing is perfect. This is a bite out of the apple.”

There's a last-minute push before the elections

Though the bill passed on a bipartisan measure, some lawmakers view it as their best chance to do something with the uncertainty of the upcoming election looming. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber. Democrats are trying to flip the Senate in November’s midterms, which can complicate the legislative agenda.

“We’re going to get one shot at this, and I don’t know if we ever will again soon,” said another co-sponsor, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., just ahead of the vote. “We’ve got a moment.”

The bill, he said, could “define the trajectory of college athletics.”

___

Pells reported from Denver.

The House Oversight Committee voted Tuesday to recommend that billionaire Leon Black be held in contempt of Congress for failing to comply with a subpoena for testimony in the investigation of Jeffrey Epstein.

Republicans and Democrats joined unanimously in the bipartisan vote after Black refused to appear this month for a sworn deposition and produce requested nondisclosure agreements. Black sued the panel, asking a federal court to block the subpoenas.

Black is the former chief executive of a private equity firm that lawmakers say funneled millions to Epstein. Republican Rep. James Comer, the chairman of the Oversight Committee, said Black is “hiding behind litigation to delay having to provide answers to the American people.”

“No one is above the law,” Comer of Kentucky said. “We have no choice but to hold him in contempt.”

The panel's ranking Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, said Black's behavior is “unacceptable.”

“We are going to stand up,” he said, and remind people that “subpoenas are not suggestions.”

The recommendation to hold Black in contempt would next go to the full House for a vote. If approved, it would send the contempt finding to the Justice Department, with the possibility of prosecution.

The House is scheduled to break later this week until after the midterm election in November, making next steps uncertain.

Black’s attorney said earlier this month that the committee is “on a fishing expedition.” The lawsuit claims the committee overstepped its authority in issuing the subpoenas.

Epstein investigation churns in Congress

The investigation into Epstein has become one of the signature developments of this Congress, a rare moment of bipartisan action. Survivors of Epstein's alleged sexual abuse have told personal stories of being young women in a trafficking enterprise organized by Epstein and his colleague Ghislaine Maxwell.

Black is among several prominent figures, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, who have been asked to appear as part of the probe.

In June, Black did appear for a voluntary interview at the committee. Lawmakers said later that he refused to answer their questions about the nondisclosure agreements.

The committee issued two subpoenas seeking to compel Black to produce the NDAs and to appear for a deposition July 16. The committee said it had accommodated Black’s request to delay the deposition to Sept. 3, but he refused to appear.

Black co-founded the private equity firm Apollo Global Management and stepped down in 2021 during the fallout over his ties to Epstein.

Lawmakers have alleged that Black paid Epstein $180 million during their yearslong relationship.

The lawmakers said Tuesday that Black's testimony would be crucial to their investigation as well as their recommendations going forward.

Comer said testimony from Black about Epstein and Maxwell would be “invaluable.”

Garcia said hearing directly from Black would help the committee understand the role of big banks in trafficking enterprises as it probes how the legal and law enforcement systems can do better to protect victims.

A Georgia property owner is suing a Cedartown police officer who fatally shot her family’s donkey during a search operation late last month.

Hannah Israel filed the civil rights complaint on September 11 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia’s Rome Division, naming Officer Trenton Garner individually. Municipal agencies and the Cedartown Police Department are excluded from the litigation.

The filing stems from an incident on August 29, when police arrived at the Rockmart property while looking for a missing 12-year-old child. According to the court documents seen by CBS News, officers entered the fenced pasture without obtaining consent or securing a search warrant, and without notifying the owner prior to entry.

Described in the complaint as a young and docile animal that presented no danger, the donkey — named HeeHaw — was shot and killed by Garner. Israel contends the use of lethal force was unjustified and violated constitutional protections against unreasonable property seizure and unlawful search.

The official incident report filed by Garner offers a different perspective of the encounter. According to the officer, the animal charged at personnel and failed to retreat even after a K-9 handler deployed an electrical arc from a Taser to deter it.

A Georgia property owner has filed a lawsuit against a Cedartown police officer who fatally shot her family’s donkey, HeeHaw, during a search operation late last month ( GoFundMe )

Garner stated he discharged his firearm once to defend the handler and tracking team members before the animal retreated uphill and died.

Following the shooting, Israel stated that officers departed the scene without disclosing the animal’s location. A police supervisor then contacted her to report that the donkey had been dispatched, requiring her and a minor to search the property across multiple acres in the dark to find him.

The legal action outlines three primary federal violations: unlawful search, unconstitutional seizure, and property deprivation without due process. Seeking a jury trial, the plaintiff is asking for compensatory damages, punitive awards, legal fees, and court costs.

The lawsuit outlines three primary federal violations involving unlawful search, unconstitutional seizure and property deprivation without due process. Seeking a jury trial, the plaintiff is asking for compensatory damages, punitive awards, legal fees and court costs.

Israel has since launched a GoFundMe campaign to support animal care on the farm and establish a foundation in the animal’s memory, stating that all proceeds would go toward farm needs rather than personal expenses. By Tuesday, the campaign had surpassed its initial goal of $30,000, raising more than $159,000 from more than 2,200 individual donations.

Garner remains on administrative leave pending an independent inquiry by the Georgia Department of Agriculture's Law Enforcement Division. Authorities confirmed that the missing child who prompted the search was eventually located unharmed.

News.title: England cruise to victory led by ‘absolute freak’ Brook
News.content:
As Brendon McCullum watched from the England balcony with the newest member of his think tank, Kevin Pietersen, their captain Harry Brook put on a brutal display that married the best of those two great T20 batsmen. To McCullum’s pure aggression and power, Brook added Pietersen’s flair and sheer range of strokes.

Brook made 114 from 49 balls, his second ton in T20 internationals and his first in any format this summer, as his team continues to take shape. They smashed 254 for four from their 20 overs, setting up a win by 119 runs. Under Brook, England have now won 19 of their 22 completed T20s.

Brook said he and Pietersen have had a “couple of conversations”. But in the idle hours before this match, “I was actually watching his highlights earlier on my phone”. He added that Pietersen “was a phenomenal player”; his influence on his batting is clear, and will only grow now they are working together.

It proved the perfect warm-up. This was the second time he and his predecessor Jos Buttler have wrought utter carnage on this ground this summer. Against India in July, they racked up 257 for three, with that pair sharing 233. Then, Buttler made a big hundred, with Brook finishing 95 not out, having been starved of the strike. This time, Buttler made 80 as they put on only 128 from 60 balls, and they fell just short of the team score from July, but it was still their fourth highest ever. Brook, meanwhile, made sure he got to three figures, reflecting ruefully afterwards that he had “let myself down a couple of times” this summer, letting opportunities for big scores go.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit 19-year high as global bond rout intensifies
News.content:
The cost of UK government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007 in a fresh global debt sell-off.

The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose from 5.37pc to a fresh 19-year high of 5.41pc on Tuesday as rising oil prices risk reigniting inflation.

Mortgage experts have warned that residential and buy-to-let mortgage rates are set to climb towards 5pc, as market turmoil threatens to filter through to household finances.

Short-term debt costs have also jumped, with the yield on two-year UK bonds surpassing 4.9pc for the first time in three years.

The bond chaos came as Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, warned that Labour risked becoming “just a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

He told LBC that John Healey’s original plan for a “low drama budget” had been “torpedoed” by higher borrowing costs and “events over the last couple of weeks”.

He said: “I think that [the bond market turmoil] will mean some hard choices next month at the Budget.”

“Few hard choices so far, but one is looming on the horizon, how any hole to the budget headroom is made good on. Is that a question of tax rises, or is it a question of taking the knife to public spending.”

Mr Haldane has been advising Labour since Andy Burnham took power.

It comes as the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England face pressure to raise interest rates this week to combat rising prices.

Anthony Brinkman, a portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, said: “The recent gilt market movements seem to be intent on showing central banks they are out of time – the market is expecting action.”

Borrowing costs around the world are rising after a 20pc surge in oil prices so far this month.

Brent crude tipped above $109 a barrel this week after Houthi rebels in Yemen, considered a proxy for Iran’s forces, seized control of a key port in the Red Sea, threatening shipping.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the face of the inflation threat.

As a result, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has surged above 5pc for the first time since 2007.

News.title: AI could transform global inequalities or ‘widen the gap’, warns Bill Gates
News.content:
“AI could be a great equaliser, or [it could] widen the gap”, says Mr Gates. “This is not a long-range prediction. It’s a present-tense choice”.

“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident. After all, the market is an extraordinary engine of innovation, but a terrible guarantor of equal opportunity.

“With AI, the gap could grow even faster … That is what makes this moment so urgent. Things are changing rapidly, and the window to shape who benefits from AI, and how soon, is short”.

The key issue holding back the deployment of AI in the developing world revolves around the availability of local data and, in turn, the ability for the technology to scale in environments very different from where it is currently being created.

An app that is trained on billions of hours of American English, will struggle at first with British English (see your spell check) but is next to useless if your local language is Swahili or Chichewa.

More profoundly, an AI tool that allows a farmer in Hampshire to control his combine harvester remotely, will offer little to a smallholder in South Sudan who works the land by hand and faces a completely different array of pests, weather conditions and costs.

The same is true for health. “A community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital - and the AI supporting her needs to reflect that”, says Mr Gates.

He adds: “Most of the world is invisible to today’s AI models. These AI systems were trained primarily on what exists on the internet – and the internet reflects a deeply unequal world. More than 90 percent of the data used to train early, large language models came from English-language sources. The communities that stand the most to gain from AI are largely absent from the knowledge base these tools are built on. They are not just underserved. They are not in the picture at all”.

The new investment aims to help correct that. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, says investments are already being made with companies including Microsoft and Google to build databases of a much wider range of languages, for instance.

Africa alone has more than 2,000 languages, and for AI’s to be effective there they have to understand what and how people actually speak - “their dialects, accents, and slang, too”.

The investments, he says, are being made on the condition that the intelligence and knowledge they accumulate are made freely available for others to use.

Languages for AI “are true public goods, almost definitional public goods. They need to be freely available to everybody. Once they’re created, they are public goods that can be uploaded onto any AI,” said Mr Suzman.

News.title: Reynolds refuses four times to rule out tax raid on state pensioners
News.content:
The Business Secretary refused four times to rule out retirees paying tax on the state pension from next year.

Jonathan Reynolds declined to reassure pensioners that they would not pay income tax on the benefit for the first time, saying it was a question for the Chancellor.

The comments on Tuesday raised concern for millions of retired people expecting to see their state pension surpass £13,000 from April, forcing them to pay income tax.

However, pensions minister Torsten Bell later insisted Labour would not put up taxes on people who rely on the state pension.

It is still unclear how this will be implemented given the complexity of separating the tax arrangements of different groups of pensioners.

The rise under the triple lock guarantee would drag many pensioners into paying income tax for the first time because their state income would surpass the personal allowance of £12,570.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, said last year that people solely reliant on the state pension would not have to pay the tax.

However, Mr Reynolds was repeatedly asked on BBC Breakfast whether Labour would honour this commitment after the next increase in the state pension in April. He declined to answer four times.

He said: “I’m sorry, that is for the Chancellor and for a Budget.

“The majority of pensioners in this country don’t just rely on the state pensions. Some do, I accept that, but the majority don’t.

“Sometimes when this is looked at, we’re focusing just on the state pension side of this. You’ve got to consider the full range of income retired people in the UK have.”

However Mr Bell, the pensions minister, walked back from Mr Reynolds comments.

He said: “In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this Parliament.

“The Chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget.”

Former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb said only one in 16 pensioners would benefit from this policy.

He said: “Those on the new state pension can expect to see an increase of nearly £500 per year next April.

“But the sting in the tail is that this will take the standard rate of the new state pension above the tax threshold.”

The comments came after official figures on Tuesday indicated the triple lock will rise by 3.9pc from April.

Under the triple lock, the state pension rises each April in line with inflation, average wages or 2.5pc, whichever is highest.

Total pay, including bonuses, rose by 3.9pc in the three months to July, down from 4.2pc in the three months to June.

Pensioners may yet receive a bigger increase if September’s inflation figure is higher than 3.9pc. That will be revealed next month but a higher figure is thought to be unlikely.

News.title: Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon
News.content:
The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.
