The Durban refugees who had been sleeping outside a government office since May were moved on Tuesday. Five buses took 278 people to Gauteng province, about 570 kilometres inland.

How the Camp Formed

In May, people from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi and Rwanda were driven out of homes and businesses around Durban. Threats tied to an anti-immigration protest movement did it.

Some sheltered first near the central police station, then at an ecumenical church centre in the city. On 21 May the group was taken to the Home Affairs refugee reception office on Che Guevara Road for verification.

The Durban refugees then formed a camp on the pavement outside, and stayed there. Numbers ran between roughly 400 and 457 people.

The city verified them. Of 457 people checked, three lacked valid documentation.

That figure matters because of how the group has been described. These were not, with three exceptions, undocumented migrants.

Tuesday’s Move

The relocation was ordered by South Africa’s inter-ministerial committee on migration and carried out by Home Affairs. The municipality required the site to be cleared under its by-laws.

A departmental spokesperson said the move was to somewhere the government regards as a safe place. The head of immigration framed it as allowing reintegration, whether in Gauteng or elsewhere.

The destination is Lindela, at Krugersdorp. That facility is normally where South Africa holds people awaiting deportation.

Home Affairs says those moved are legally in the country and this is not a deportation. One South African outlet nonetheless described the buses as heading to Lindela for deportation.

That tension has not been resolved publicly. About 200 others from the camp declined the offer and chose reintegration in KwaZulu-Natal instead.

Durban’s seafront. About 200 people from the camp declined the move to Gauteng and chose reintegration locally instead. (Photo: “Durban South Beach Promenade” by RishHans, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

The Deadline That Is Not a Government Deadline

A date of 30 September has been circulating as a cut-off for undocumented migrants in South Africa. It is not a government measure.

It was set by a protest movement called March and March, led by Sphelele Shinga, as its own ultimatum. The movement says it expects very large demonstrations that day.

The same movement ran a 30 June deadline earlier this year. That campaign produced the displacement that created the Durban camp in the first place.

On 3 September the movement staged what it called a clean-up at the site. Police used teargas and rubber bullets.

It threatened court action over the camp on 13 September. No court order governing the site or the relocation has been granted.

The System Behind the Story

South Africa‘s asylum system carries a backlog that explains much of the friction. The refugee appeals authority held 161,000 cases at the end of 2025, of which 70,976 were active.

A further 82,348 asylum seekers were in the active caseload, and 55,190 people held recognised refugee status. The department reports cutting active appeals by 12.2 percent during 2025.

Long waits leave people documented but provisional for years, which is what most of the Durban refugees were. It is a status that invites exactly this kind of dispute.

Nobody has said publicly who paid for Tuesday’s buses. Nor has the department said how long people are expected to remain at Lindela.

What It Means for Anyone Living There

For foreign residents of South Africa, the practical lesson is about paperwork and proximity. Valid documents did not prevent this group being displaced, and did not prevent four months on a pavement.

What the Durban refugees did secure was a relocation rather than a removal. The three people without papers are the exception that proves how the system sorted them.

The next fixed date is 30 September, and it belongs to a protest movement rather than to the state. That distinction is worth holding on to as it approaches.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was moved from Durban?

Two hundred and seventy-eight people, mostly from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi and Rwanda, who had been sleeping on the pavement outside the Home Affairs refugee reception office on Che Guevara Road since May 2026. About 200 others from the same camp declined the move and opted for reintegration in KwaZulu-Natal.

Were they in South Africa legally?

Almost all of them. Of 457 people verified by the eThekwini municipality, three lacked valid documentation. The Department of Home Affairs has confirmed that those relocated are legally in the country.

What is Lindela?

Lindela Repatriation Centre in Krugersdorp, Gauteng, is South Africa’s main facility for holding people ahead of deportation. Home Affairs describes Tuesday’s transfer as a safety relocation of documented people rather than a deportation step, though not all South African reporting has accepted that framing.

Is there a government deadline of 30 September?

No. That date was set by March and March, an anti-immigration protest movement, as its own ultimatum for undocumented migrants to leave. There is no official South African government deadline on that date.

World.title: Uganda Invictus Games Exit Lasted Eleven Days and One Phone Call
World.content:
Uganda · Society

Key Facts — What the Invictus Games are An international sports event for wounded, injured and sick military personnel and veterans.

— Who founded them Prince Harry, in 2014. The first Games were held in London that September.

— What Uganda did It joined in July, withdrew on 3 September, and rejoined on 14 September.

— Why it withdrew Its military chief understood that the Games lacked the King’s endorsement.

— What changed his mind The King’s principal private secretary telephoned to say the King had no objection.

— Where the next Games are Birmingham, England, in 2027. Uganda would be the second African country to compete.

Uganda joined the Invictus Games in July as its 26th nation and the first from East Africa. Twelve days ago it walked out, on the belief that King Charles did not approve. On Monday his private secretary telephoned to say otherwise.

Ugandan soldiers. The country’s defence forces signed a partnership with the Invictus Games Foundation in October 2025. (Photo: “Amisom Uganda 07Btn 13 (6440671619)” by AMISOM Public Information, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

The Uganda Invictus Games withdrawal lasted eleven days. It began with a misunderstanding about what a British king thinks and ended with a telephone call putting it right.

The Sequence

The Uganda Invictus Games entry was announced on 7 July at a foundation event in London, with Prince Harry present. It became the 26th country in the Games and the first from East Africa.

On Thursday 3 September, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced the withdrawal on social media. He is chief of Uganda’s defence forces and President Yoweri Museveni’s son.

His stated reason was deference. In order not to be construed as being opposed to King Charles, he wrote, Uganda was withdrawing.

He added that Uganda would not participate in anything that did not have the King’s approval. The wording made clear he believed approval was absent.

On Monday 14 September, Sir Clive Alderton telephoned him. Alderton is principal private secretary to the King and Queen.

The message was that the King was moved by the consideration shown and had no problem with Uganda taking part. Uganda reinstated itself the same day.

Where the Misunderstanding Came From

Kainerugaba had been given to understand that the Invictus Games are a private charity rather than an official Royal Family initiative. On that reading, taking part could be seen as siding with Prince Harry against the palace.

Prince Harry’s office publicly attributed the withdrawal to a letter from the palace. That makes this as much a dispute inside the British royal family as a Ugandan decision.

The foundation is indeed a charity rather than a crown institution. Whether that means the King disapproves is a different question, and the answer came by telephone.

Uganda’s military spokesman confirmed the reversal. The King, he said, was moved by the general’s sensitive consideration of the King’s opinion.

Uganda would be the second African nation to compete at the Invictus Games, after Nigeria’s debut in 2023. (Photo: “Amisom Uganda 07Btn 05 (6440676355)” by AMISOM Public Information, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

What the Games Are

The Invictus Games are an international multi-sport event for wounded, injured and sick serving personnel and veterans. Prince Harry founded them in 2014 and the first edition was held in London that September.

Twenty-five nations took part before Uganda joined. Nigeria was the only African participant, debuting at the 2023 Games in Dusseldorf.

The Uganda Invictus Games link was formalised in October 2025, when the defence forces signed a partnership with the foundation. The 2027 Games are in Birmingham, less than 300 days away.

Exact dates for the Birmingham edition have not been confirmed in the reporting on Uganda’s reversal. That detail remains outstanding.

The Relationship Underneath It

The episode is small but it sits on a strained relationship. Britain sanctioned three Ugandan officials in April 2024 under its anti-corruption rules.

Those were Anita Among, the speaker of parliament, and two former ministers of state for Karamoja affairs. The measures were travel bans and asset freezes.

The stated grounds were the theft of iron sheets from a government housing programme meant for Karamoja communities. Ugandan officials have argued the real motive lay elsewhere, in British objections to Uganda’s anti-homosexuality law.

Kainerugaba himself is not under British sanctions. He is, though, a prolific and unpredictable user of social media, which is where the withdrawal was announced.

Why a Small Story Is Worth Reading

A country joined a charitable sports event, left it over a perceived royal slight, and returned after a phone call. Nothing material changed in between.

What the Uganda Invictus Games episode shows is how thin the channel is between a British palace and an East African general. One letter created the problem and one call solved it.

For the wounded Ugandan soldiers who would compete, the eleven days were the whole story. They are back in training.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Uganda withdraw from the Invictus Games?

General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defence forces, announced the withdrawal on 3 September 2026 after being given to understand that the Games were a private charity without King Charles III’s endorsement. He said Uganda would not take part in anything that lacked the King’s approval.

What made Uganda rejoin?

On 14 September 2026, Sir Clive Alderton, principal private secretary to the King and Queen, telephoned Kainerugaba to say the King was moved by the consideration shown and had no problem with Uganda’s participation. Uganda reinstated itself the same day.

What are the Invictus Games?

An international multi-sport event for wounded, injured and sick serving military personnel and veterans, founded by Prince Harry in 2014 with a first edition in London that September. They are run by the Invictus Games Foundation, a charity rather than a crown institution.

Is Uganda the first African country to take part?

No, the second. Nigeria debuted at the 2023 Games in Dusseldorf. Uganda is the first East African country and the 26th nation overall, and would compete at the 2027 Games in Birmingham.

Sources: allAfrica on Uganda rejoining the Games, Reporting on the original withdrawal, IBTimes UK on the letter that preceded the withdrawal, Pulse Uganda on Uganda joining in July, ICTJ on British sanctions against Ugandan officials

World.title: Saxophone Still Getting Louder For Jimmy Rojas: 3 years for boutique burglary; Still facing charges for breaking police cameras
World.content:
Saxophone Still Getting Louder For Jimmy Rojas: 3 years for boutique burglary; Still facing charges for breaking police cameras

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City resident Jimmy Estuardo Rojas has been sentenced to three years in prison after changing his plea to guilty for burglarizing a Mahogany Street boutique where police reportedly caught him inside with bags packed with merchandise.

Rojas appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, September 15, where he changed his original not-guilty plea and admitted to burglarizing Jay’z Pick & Wear Boutique at the corner of Mahogany and Jasmine streets.

The Magistrate sentenced Rojas to three years imprisonment, effective Tuesday.

The burglary occurred in the early morning hours of September 22, 2025. Police responding to a report of a burglary in progress arrived at the business and, with the owner present, entered the building believing the intruder was still inside.

According to the facts of the case, officers found Rojas inside the boutique along with several bags containing items taken from the business.

Investigators later determined that entry had allegedly been gained by damaging wooden boards at the rear of the building.

Rojas initially pleaded not guilty after being charged, but reversed that plea nearly a year later. The conviction is his first for burglary, although he has had previous encounters with the criminal justice system.

He still has another burglary charge pending in connection with the March 2026 break-in at the security booth of Saint Luke Methodist Primary School. Police alleged surveillance footage captured Rojas during that incident. He pleaded not guilty and was denied bail.

Rojas is also before the court on damage-to-property charges after police alleged that surveillance cameras and related equipment valued at almost $49,000 were damaged at two locations in the Saint Martin de Porres area in August. He has pleaded not guilty to those allegations.

Those matters remain pending before the court and are separate from Tuesday’s burglary conviction.

World.title: Mexican businessman fined for illegal entry into Belize; US$10,500 undeclared cash now under scrutiny
World.content:
Mexican businessman fined for illegal entry into Belize; US$10,500 undeclared cash now under scrutiny

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Mexican businessman who pleaded guilty to an immigration offence on Tuesday remains in police custody after authorities discovered he was carrying US$10,500 in cash which he allegedly failed to declare upon entering Belize.

Rafael Moran Gama, 40, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to failing to present a visitor’s permit on demand to an Immigration Officer.

Gama was fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, payable forthwith, in default six months imprisonment. When informed of the default sentence, Gama reportedly expressed concern about being sent to prison.

His problems, however, did not end with the immigration charge.

According to Immigration personnel present at court, police have custody of US$10,500 found among Gama’s belongings and he is expected to be interviewed by personnel from the Belize Tax Service Department regarding the money and why it was not declared when he entered the country.

At the Central Bank’s fixed buying rate of US$1 to BZ$2, the cash amounts to approximately BZ$21,000. Official Financial Intelligence Unit guidance states that Belize increased its traveller cash-declaration threshold in 2016 from BZ$10,000 to BZ$20,000, with declarations to be made to Customs officers when entering or leaving the country.

That means Gama was carrying approximately BZ$1,000 above the declaration threshold. Carrying more than BZ$20,000 is not itself prohibited, but the amount must be declared to Customs. The FIU has identified failure to declare funds at or above the threshold as an offence under Belize’s customs framework.

Gama told the Chief Magistrate that he travelled by taxi from Mexico to the Corozal Free Zone, where he later accepted a ride from a taxi bearing Belizean licence plates into Belize City.

He claimed that when they reached the Belize side of the border he was sleepy and handed his passport to the taxi driver, but could not say whether the driver ever presented it to Immigration authorities.

Gama was later encountered during a police operation in Belize City at around 8:00 a.m. and detained. During the processing of his belongings, authorities recorded the US$10,500 in his possession.

He was escorted back to the Queen Street Police Station following his arraignment pending the financial interview.

Gama told the court the seized cash is all the money he currently has available and that he needs access to it to pay his $1,005 court fine.

Once the immigration fine and the outstanding matter concerning the cash are resolved, authorities are expected to arrange for Gama to be returned to Mexico.

No charge relating to the US$10,500 had been announced as of Tuesday afternoon.

World.title: Extortion case against Immigration Officer Monique Escalante discontinued after High Court rejects hearsay evidence
World.content:
Extortion case against Immigration Officer Monique Escalante discontinued after High Court rejects hearsay evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The extortion case against interdicted Immigration Officer Monique Meisha Escalante has been discontinued after the prosecution was unable to secure the testimony of the Jamaican national who accused her of taking US$3,000 at the Philip Goldson International Airport.

Escalante, 34, appeared before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, where the Director of Public Prosecutions’ Office entered a nolle prosequi after the court refused to admit a statement from virtual complainant Jahnoi Shaun-Dhee Richards as hearsay evidence.

The matter had been proceeding through a voir dire—a hearing to determine the admissibility of evidence—because Richards could not be located to testify.

The Crown called four witnesses in an attempt to establish the circumstances surrounding Richards’ statement and his absence from Belize. Prosecutors told the court that repeated telephone calls to Richards went unanswered, an email received no response, and attempts to contact him through social media were also unsuccessful.

At the close of the Crown’s evidence, Escalante’s attorney, Leslie Hamilton, made a no-case submission, arguing that prosecutors had failed to establish the legal basis necessary to admit Richards’ statement in his absence. Justice Pilgrim upheld the defence submission and declined to admit the statement.

With its principal witness unavailable and his statement excluded, the Crown entered the nolle prosequi, discontinuing the prosecution. Escalante was subsequently discharged from the extortion charge. The outcome is not an acquittal, however, and the prosecution could potentially bring the matter again if Richards becomes available and the necessary evidence can be presented.

Escalante was originally charged in March 2024 after Richards, then 27, alleged that while entering Belize through the PGIA on March 15, 2024, he was instructed to place money inside his passport and eventually handed over US$3,000. Public reporting at the time stated that airport surveillance footage was reviewed during the investigation and that several other immigration officers were detained and questioned before being released.

Escalante pleaded not guilty after being arraigned and was granted $8,000 bail with conditions, including surrendering her travel documents, reporting weekly to police and having no contact with Richards.

Richards reportedly left Belize following his stay, and despite efforts by prosecutors to locate him, he did not appear to give evidence in the High Court proceedings.

Escalante left court Tuesday with documentation confirming that the prosecution had been discontinued, bringing the case against her to an end for now.

World.title: Briceño says Guatemala billboards are tourism ads, not political messaging
World.content:
Briceño says Guatemala billboards are tourism ads, not political messaging

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño says the controversial Guatemala billboards appearing across Belize City should be viewed as tourism promotion, even though he acknowledged that their wording may be “a bit misleading.”

The Prime Minister was responding to growing public criticism of the s, which feature Guatemalan scenery alongside the message encouraging people to visit and return.

Briceño said his understanding is that the billboards are part of a standard campaign promoting Guatemala as a travel destination.

His comments come after Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton demanded that the billboards be removed immediately, describing them as a political provocation and an affront to Belize’s sovereignty and national identity.

The controversy has gained added attention because it comes only days after renewed tensions in the Sarstoon and as Belize marks its 45th anniversary of Independence.

Briceño, however, did not adopt that interpretation.

Instead, he sought to separate the s from the territorial dispute, saying that while the wording may raise questions, he understands the intention behind them to be tourism related.

The matter has also raised questions over the approval process for billboards within Belize City, where s generally require municipal approval.

For now, the Prime Minister’s position is clear: the message may not have been perfectly framed, but he does not view the campaign itself as a political challenge to Belize.

World.title: Laguna Rio offers lagoonfront living in San Pedro with residences from US$169,000
World.content:
Laguna Rio offers lagoonfront living in San Pedro with residences from US$169,000

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A new residential development on Ambergris Caye is offering buyers an opportunity to own a private lagoonfront residence while remaining just minutes from the heart of San Pedro Town.

Laguna Rio, a Blue Ocean Belize development, features waterfront residences designed around open spaces, natural light, coastal materials and outdoor living. Resale prices currently start at US$169,000.

The residential community sits on the lagoon side of Ambergris Caye and combines access to the water with proximity to some of San Pedro’s most important services and attractions.

According to the development information, the Boca del Rio Bridge is approximately three minutes away, Central Park is five minutes away, Ambergris Hope Hospital is seven minutes away, John Greif II Airport is eight minutes away and the San Pedro International Ferry Terminal is approximately 10 minutes away.

One available configuration, Studio A, offers approximately 646 square feet, with one bedroom, one bathroom, a full sized kitchen, living area, laundry closet and verandah.

Laguna Rio is designed for both full time island living and buyers looking for a second home or real estate investment in Belize.

Another major feature is direct seller financing through Blue Ocean Belize.

Financing options include plans starting with 30 percent down, while other structures offer lower fixed interest rates or longer repayment periods. Final terms and availability are subject to confirmation by Blue Ocean Belize.

Interested buyers can contact Blue Ocean Belize at +501 636 5752, toll free at +1 800 928 6890, or email [email protected].

World.title: Man who likes to play with guns and little girls given no jail-time once again as psychiatrists insist he has ‘the mind of an 8-year-old’
World.content:
Man who likes to play with guns and little girls given no jail-time once again as psychiatrists insist he has ‘the mind of an 8-year-old’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-two-year-old Mark Stephen Godoy Jr. has avoided an immediate prison sentence after pleading guilty to two counts of unlawful sexual intercourse with a 14-year-old girl, with High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim instead imposing three years’ probation after considering Godoy’s significant intellectual disability.

Godoy admitted to having sexual intercourse with the girl on two occasions in March 2024, when he was 20 years old and she was 14.

Justice Pilgrim initially assessed the offences at a five-year starting point under the sentencing guidelines, finding the harm to the victim to be high and noting significant psychological effects. The provisional sentence was later reduced after the court considered the absence of violence, coercion or grooming, as well as Godoy’s guilty pleas, lack of previous convictions, remorse, family support and intellectual impairment.

The court ultimately found special circumstances justifying a departure from an immediate custodial sentence and placed Godoy under the supervision of a Community Rehabilitation Officer for three years. He must report as directed, comply with reasonable instructions and notify the supervising officer of any change of residence.

Public reporting on Monday’s ruling similarly said Justice Pilgrim considered imprisonment disproportionate in light of Godoy’s permanent intellectual limitations and warned that the probation order was not simply a “slap on the wrist.” A breach or new criminal offending could return him to the High Court for sentencing.

The case followed months of litigation over whether Godoy was legally competent to face the charges. Crown Counsel Kirk Brown, representing the Director of Public Prosecutions, fiercely contested the defence position and argued that although Godoy had intellectual limitations, he could understand the charges and participate in the proceedings with appropriate assistance.

Two psychiatric reports had identified intellectual impairments, with evidence before the court placing some aspects of Godoy’s functioning around the developmental level of an eight-year-old. The medical experts considered him unfit to stand trial, but Justice Pilgrim ruled in June that the legal test was different from the clinical assessment. He found that Godoy could understand the proceedings, make a plea, instruct counsel and give evidence if questions and concepts were simplified.

Godoy subsequently pleaded guilty to the two USI counts on July 29.

According to the facts, Godoy began communicating with the girl through Facebook Messenger and Instagram sometime after February 14, 2024. He allegedly told her he was 20 and she told him she was 14.

They later met on March 1 and again on March 5, 2024, and had sexual intercourse on both occasions.

The court’s decision comes months after a separate Magistrate’s Court matter in which firearm and ammunition charges against Godoy were struck out after he was also found incompetent to stand trial in that proceeding.

World.title: Father of newborn twins fined $105 after pleading guilty to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine
World.content:
Father of newborn twins fined $105 after pleading guilty to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 54-year-old security guard and father of recently born twins pleaded guilty Monday to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine after police allegedly found the drug in his pocket during a stop and search.

George Clinton Sanchez of Zacaranda Street appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on one count of possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Sanchez was on Marigold Lane in the Saint Martin de Porres area at around 9:50 a.m. on Sunday, September 13, when officers stopped and searched him.

During the search, police allegedly found two small pieces of a white substance suspected to be crack cocaine inside Sanchez’s left pants pocket. The substance was later weighed at 0.2 grams.

Sanchez pleaded guilty and became emotional while addressing the court, explaining that he is the father of newborn twins and asking the Senior Magistrate for leniency.

As a first-time offender, he was fined $100 plus $5 cost of court, bringing his total penalty to $105.

World.title: One week after being charged for knife, Basil Willis remanded for allegedly trafficking crack
World.content:
One week after being charged for knife, Basil Willis remanded for allegedly trafficking crack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Less than a week after being fined for carrying a four-inch knife in public during prohibited hours, 58-year-old Basil Earl Willis is back before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court — this time accused of possessing crack cocaine with intent to supply.

Willis, a car washer of Black Orchid Street, was arraigned on three charges: possession of 5.4 grams of crack cocaine with intent to supply, possession of 20 grams of marijuana, and resisting lawful arrest.

The charges reportedly stem from a police operation on Marigold Lane on Sunday, September 13.

Willis pleaded not guilty to all three counts.

The prosecution objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the drug-trafficking allegation, Willis’ criminal history and the prevalence of illegal drugs in the community.

Willis told the court he was not a flight risk and promised to attend every court date.

Despite the objection, the Senior Magistrate granted him bail of $2,000 plus one surety in the same amount. His bail is subject to a condition that he not be arrested and charged with another offence while the case is pending.

Willis is due back in court on October 28.

The new allegations come only days after Willis pleaded guilty to possession of an article with a blade. Police said he was riding a bicycle along Mahogany Street at about 4:50 a.m. on September 4 when officers found a four-inch knife tucked into his waistband.

During that case, Willis reportedly told police, “I always have my knife on me because yuh neva know.” He was fined $150 plus $5 cost of court and given until October 30 to pay.

Willis has pleaded not guilty to the latest charges, and the allegations against him have not yet been proven in court.

World.title: Raheem Sterling pleads guilty to dangerous driving after Lamborghini crash
World.content:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 02: Raheem Sterling #17 of Chelsea FC looks on during the pre-season friendly match Borussia Dortmund at Soldier Field on August 2, 2023 in Chicago, Illinois. Justin Casterline/Getty Images/AFPJustin Casterline / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Footballer Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving after he crashed his Lamborghini on a motorway in May.

The 31-year-old also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen for analysis when he appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, about 50 miles southwest of London.

Sterling, who attended court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top, was arrested after crashing on the M3 on the morning of May 28.

Police said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

READ: Raheem Sterling arrested for suspected drug-driving

The winger won 82 England caps, the last of which came at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

Sterling made his senior debut at Liverpool before joining Manchester City in 2015, winning four Premier League titles and other silverware at the Etihad.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but subsequently fell out of favour and spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Arsenal.

Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February, playing eight times in the Eredivisie.

World.title: JAMAICA gets Disney boost
World.content:
Disney Cruine Line’s Disney Destiny will make its inaugural call on Jamaica next month.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Jamaica’s tourism industry is set to receive a big boost on October 13 when one of Disney Cruise Line’s top modern vessels, Disney Destiny, makes its inaugural call at Falmouth’s historic cruise port bringing just under 2,800 passengers to the island.

The announcement was made by Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose during Monday’s opening of the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) at Moon Palace Jamaica in Ocho Rios.

The arrival of Disney Destiny adds to the growing roster of Disney Cruise Line vessels calling on Jamaica, alongside ships operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Princess Cruises, and Virgin Voyages.

From January to July this year, according to data shared by Rose, Jamaica recorded 234 cruise calls and 736,372 passengers. Montego Bay, Falmouth and Ocho Rios accounted for most visits, while four ships also called at Port Antonio and Kingston.

Rose pointed out that the cruise industry remains an important partner, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa — which hit sections of Jamaica last October — and reminded that it could provide a pathway to attracting visitors for longer stays.

“It’s often said you can come down, get a little taste of Jamaica on the cruise ship, then we can convert them, or they go back home and say that was too much of a teaser, and they come back,” he said.

The JTB official said cruise visitors are encouraged to venture beyond established resort centres, particularly towards Kingston and Port Antonio, to experience a wider range of the Jamaican product.

Reacting to news of Disney Destiny’s impending visit, Chukka Caribbean Adventures deputy executive chairman and Jamaica Tourist Board member John Byles pointed to the benefit it will bring to local artisans and attractions. According to Byles, Disney passengers tend to leave the ship and spend on Jamaican tourism experiences.

He welcomed the impending Disney Destiny call, describing it as a sign of the company’s growing trust in Jamaica.

“It is always very heartening to see the confidence that a brand like Disney continues to show for the Jamaica product and Jamaica destination,” Byles told buyers and suppliers attending the first day of JAPEX, a staple on the tourism calendar.

The trade show is being held under the theme ’Jamaica Reimagined’. Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brian Heron used his address to stress that Jamaica’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa must lead to a stronger and more adaptable tourism industry.

“Resilience is not simply about recovering, It is truly about what comes next,” he said.

He noted that changing travellers, technology and artificial intelligence were reshaping how people discover and experience destinations, requiring Jamaica to embrace innovation without sacrificing its authenticity.

The JHTA head said Jamaica’s strongest differentiator remains its people, pointing to the warmth of the welcome, culture, creativity, music, spirit, and food.

Officially declaring the trade show open during an address delivered virtually, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett stressed the importance of adapting to shifts in the global tourism marketplace, strengthening competitiveness and building resilience while safeguarding the characteristics that make Jamaica distinctive.

“An event like JAPEX is never just a trade show. Last year, JAPEX facilitated an estimated US$100 million in contracts and business negotiations. Behind that figure are real hotels, real workers, real families, and real communities. That is precisely why, in fact, we do this,” Bartlett said.

World.title: Veteran journalist Balford Henry passes
World.content:
HENRY... his quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter

THE local media fraternity has lost one of its calmest and most easy-going veterans, Balford George Henry, who died on Monday after a brief illness.

He was 74.

Henry’s quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter.

Henry served both national newspapers, The Gleaner and the Jamaica Observer, in several capacities. He also served as consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS) and worked at

New York Daily News, WLIB Radio in New York as a correspondent.

Henry was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

In a 2011 interview with JIS the unflappable Henry said he simply loves to write, and responded to the call to the fourth Estate during the summer of 1971, while a sixth former at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

“At that time, The Gleaner advertised for trainee journalists. I was among scores of young people from across Jamaica who sat the initiative tests, coincidently held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School auditorium. Fortunately, I was among the handful of successful candidates,” he recalled.

At that time, The Gleaner was the only institutionalised daily newspaper in the country and, in the absence of a school of journalism in Jamaica and indeed, the wider region, the North Street facility prided itself as the nursery and training ground for print reporters.

“I was exposed to the veterans of the craft, people like Ken Allen, Calvin Bowen, LK Southerland, and Editor-in-Chief Theodore Sealy. Barbara Gloudon, in particular, discovered very early in my career that I enjoyed writing features, and encouraged and nurtured my efforts,” said Henry in the JIS interview.

He recalled that the training period was tough, with the late Fitzroy Nation “being the only other member of my group to survive that ordeal”.

Henry further honed his skills as a Commonwealth Press Union (CPU) Fellow, London, 1977; earned a journalism diploma as a Thomson Foundation scholar in Cardiff, Wales, 1977; and was one of 12 journalists from around the world chosen by the World Press Institute (WPI) for a fellowship at Macalester College, St Paul, Minnesota, in 1983.

Early in his career Henry reported on sittings of the then Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC), as well as major social and cultural activities and events.

Later, as a veteran labour relations reporter, he covered industrial relations issues including major strikes and disputes during the volatile 1970s.

The recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry had also been the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youth in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in that country in 1977.

He had also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of the funeral of the late reggae icon Bob Marley in 1981; as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature entitled: ‘Fall of a Superstar’, on the rise and fall of Jamaican reggae singer Junior Byles.

In 2011 Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

Reacting to his passing, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness expressed sadness and said he remembers Henry as a committed journalist who understood the responsibility that comes with telling Jamaica’s story.

“His work reflected a deep knowledge of our politics, our people and the issues affecting our country,” Holness said in a post on Instagram.

“His passing is a loss to Jamaica’s media fraternity and to the many people who knew and worked with him over the years. I extend my heartfelt condolence to his family, friends, colleagues and the wider journalism community,” the prime minister said.

Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Minister Olivia Grange also expressed sadness at Henry’s passing, describing him as “a first-rate journalist” who was committed to his craft.

Grange said Henry was an “outstanding writer and questioner whose easy-going demeanour belied the penetrating nature of his questions”.

“I had great respect for Balford. He was always professional in his interactions and in his journalistic pursuits. He was sharp, he was keen, he could be tough, but he was always fair,” Grange said, and offered condolence to his family and colleagues.

Journalist Wilton Dyer, who was already at The Gleaner when a very young Henry arrived in 1971, remembers “a very quiet, contemplative man” who brought a “very dilligent, single-minded approach” to journalism.

“He was very efficient and driven,” Dyer said, recalling that Henry quickly developed a “mastery of labour relations and parliamentary reporting”.

Dyer also recalled that Henry was steeped in Jamaican music and also produced a record of his own called Bits of Paper.

By the mid-1970s Henry was among the leading Jamaican entertainment writers, said Dyer.

Fellow veteran journalist Garfield Myers remembered Henry as a workaholic.

“He was one of those who, when I went to The Gleaner in July 1973, had been there for a couple of years — very young man, a couple of years older than me — and he was one of those who showed me the way,” said Myers, a former Observer sports editor who still writes for the newspaper from St Elizabeth.

He said that Henry became very adept at labour relations and trade union coverage, which was a very important beat back in those days.

“Over time he graduated to Parliament and became one of the better parliamentary reporters, and mastered that beat. He was a very good reporter. Some journalists graduate to become editors but Balford was a reporter par excellence. Trying to make him into something else wouldn’t work,” Myers said.

Observer Executive Editor, Publications Vernon Davidson also commented on Henry’s mastery of parliamentary reporting, noting that he often returned from a long day of covering the legislature with stories missed by some of his colleagues.

“We could always depend on Balford to deliver, regardless of how long the sittings were, as he had an exceptional eye for detail and the type of patience required to cover Parliament,” said Davidson who also worked with Henry at The Gleaner in the early 1980s.

“Bally also provided excellent coverage of politics and would be our point reporter during the annual budget debates,” said Davidson who recalled that Henry joined the Observer in November 2003, left for JIS in 2009, and returned to the newspaper in 2012.

“He was a quiet fountain of knowledge and we are poorer for his passing. We extend our deepest condolence to his family, friends and colleagues,” Davidson said.

Henry is survived by his widow Claudia Stockhausen-Henry and was the father of two sons and two daughters.

World.title: Music in her bones
World.content:
Reggae songstress Sevana strikes a pose during an intimate gathering on Friday evening to celebrate her latest single, Jeans an’ Marina.Karl McLarty

If one were to choose a word to describe Sevana, multi-talented would certainly be in the running.

The Jamaican creative has spent years moving between worlds, so much so that when things appear quiet on one front, chances are something else is unfolding behind the scenes.

And if her recent absence from the musical spotlight left anyone wondering where she had been, Sevana has a simple explanation.

“When we’re quiet one place, we’re working in the next,” she said.

On Friday, the singer welcomed specially invited guests into an intimate, house party-style gathering at Cherry Drive Estates for the release of her newest single, Jeans an’ Marina.

The relaxed setting was fitting for a song inspired not by glamour or exclusivity, but by Sevana’s memories of community, simplicity, and the kind of Jamaican togetherness that requires little more than good company, music, and somewhere to gather.

It also marked Sevana’s re-emergence into a space she insists she never truly left.

“I was working on a lot of acting projects while you weren’t actively hearing from me on the entertainment scene, but I was still making a lot of music,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Sevana has been acting since 2017, but in recent years has deliberately positioned herself “a little deeper into that world”.

Her growing résumé includes an appearance in the Robert Nesta Marley biopic Bob Marley: One Love, while she is also featured in UK series Possession, now streaming on Sky TV, in which she plays an escaped revolutionary woman. She has also landed her first starring role in a feature film, Threads of Us, which she said is currently touring the United States.

“I have different projects that I’m pushing at the moment,” she explained.

But for all the creative lanes she has been exploring, there remains one that feels particularly like home.

“Music is my first love, and it is the thing that has continued to save me time and time again,” Sevana shared. “It’s not something I can let go. It’s in my bones, it’s in my blood and I love it. I will never stop.”

Her return, then, is perhaps less of a comeback and more of a refocusing. Sevana said she resisted the urge to release material simply for the sake of remaining visible, choosing instead to build a catalogue she genuinely believed in.

“Navigating the entertainment industry, it takes a lot out of you, especially if you’re trying to do multiple things at once,” she said. “I was really committed to putting together a body of work that I could be really proud of once I hit the ground running again.”

She wanted, she explained, to feel excitement about everything she eventually shared. “So I wasn’t in a rush to push any singles or anything until now.”

That patience has brought her to Jeans an’ Marina, a record whose roots stretch far beyond the studio and all the way back to Sevana’s childhood in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland.

The inspiration was partly sparked by what she witnessed following last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

Even amid the sombre mood that engulfed sections of the country, Sevana found herself reflecting on the way Jamaicans instinctively pulled together.

“That’s the vibe I was going for on this single. I wanted it to feel like a coming together,” she said.

But the feeling was familiar. Growing up in Savanna-la-Mar, Friday nights offered Sevana an early lesson in what community could look like when stripped of pretence.

“Every Friday night the community would gather in the square under the street light to just hang out,” she recalled. “We’d play dominoes, ludo, listen to music, buss a one beer and just relax.”

There was no dress code. No pressure to manufacture an image for the evening. Nobody needed an elaborate outfit or an exclusive invitation.

“It never felt like pressure to get all dolled up or anything like that. You could wear weh yuh have, and everybody had jeans and merina. You would put it on and just come out and have fun,” she said.

It is that uncomplicated sense of belonging that Sevana has attempted to bottle in the new single.

“The idea back then was for the community to come together and heal each other, and that’s what this song is about — being unified and arite,” she said.

The singer then went on to share that Jeans an’ Marina is not a standalone return to music. It is the opening note of what she hopes will be a sustained new chapter with her next single expected at the end of September. Sevana then plans to release new music every month heading into 2027, tracks that may eventually culminate in something much bigger.

World.title: Inaugural Ultimate a hit with the athletes, says Coe
World.content:
COE... it seems in large part to have worked pretty well Photo: Naphtali Junior

BUDAPEST, Hungary (AFP) — The inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest worked “pretty well”, according to World Athletics President Sebastian Coe, who hailed the “uniquely positive” feedback from athletes.

Coe had dubbed the three-day Ultimate, bringing together 381 athletes from 65 federations in competition for unmatched prize money totalling $10 million, as an “incubator for change”.

An all-black in-field, a long jump pit filled with pink sand, enhanced graphics and quick-fire coverage unashamedly aimed for television, and particularly a younger audience, were all features of the flashy new competition.

“At first inspection, and it’s early, it seems in large part to have worked pretty well,” Coe told journalists in Budapest.

“The athletes have been uniquely positive. At first perusal I think we’re in decent shape.

“We are an innately conservative sport and I just think we’ve moved slightly away from the risk-adverse end of that spectrum — not probably by much, but it’s a start.”

Coe added that there had been a “really good vibe” at three sell-out evenings of action and the competition looked “less last week”.

Jamaican sprint legend Usain Bolt claimed 19 global titles in a storied career, but said he wished the kind of prize money on offer at the Ultimate Championship had been available when he was competing.

“It’s big,” said Bolt. “It’s good for the sport and it incentivises athletes to come out here and do the best, to show up and to be ready.”

The Ultimate pitched 26 Olympic champions from the 2024 Paris Games against 26 World champions from Tokyo last year and 25 Diamond League winners from the 2026 season.

“It’s a good step, a first step to changing track and field for the better,” said Bolt. “I think the athletes are loving it. It’s a different energy, a different vibe.”

With 28 disciplines delivered in a fast-paced, made-for-television format, Coe described the current crop of athletes as one “for the ages”.

“For the last two or three years, I’ve sensed that we’ve now got a far broader bandwidth of talent across all our disciplines.”

The 2028 edition of the Ultimate will follow the July 14-30 Los Angeles Olympics, Coe confirmed.

“Where at all possible, we wanted our world championships and now the Ultimate to be the denouement of the season,” he said.

“That’s important and again the athletes have welcomed that.”

Coe entertained more than 20 International Olympic Committee members in Budapest as well as federation presidents of rowing, table tennis and volleyball.

“We all learn from each other,” he said. “Not everybody that watches the 100m wants all of the 100m. That’s how much it’s changed.”

There were ringing endorsements for the Ultimate from athletes in Budapest.

“They have built a great show and it has a different kind of vibe. I love it,” said Norway’s 400m hurdler Karsten Warholm.

Men’s 100m and 200m champion Kenny Bednarek added that “everything is a little bit more exciting than at the World Championships”.

“This event is awesome and it is cool that World Athletics has $10m to invest into its athletes. I want it to be the prize for every championships!” said American Nikki Hiltz, third in the women’s 1,500m.

There was some concern pre-competition about the field events, with no place for shot put, discus or women’s hammer throw.

“The championship is worse off for not having the other field events,” said Britain’s Jazmin Sawyers, second in the women’s long jump.

Sawyers added, however, that the event had been a “wow moment” for her and she would use her prize money of $75,000 to finance another year in the sport and buy a new sewing machine.

Coe acknowledged that the choice to cut some events had been tough.

“There was some nervousness going in about what it was going to mean for us, inevitable discussions that some disciplines are not there,” he said.

“But that’s not set in tablets of stone; it could look different next time.”

World.title: MOVING ON UP!
World.content:
Lavanya Williams

JAMAICA’S rising sprint sensation Lavanya Williams is crediting her mother for helping fuel her breakout season, and says strengthening her mental conditioning will be a key focus for the 2027 campaign.

Williams, one of the fastest women in the world this year, ended her season over the weekend after competing in the women’s 100m and 200m at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Hungary.

The 20-year-old missed out on a place in the 200m final after finishing seventh in her heat but was able to make the final of the 100m. She finished seventh in a stacked field which featured Olympic and World Champions Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, Julien Alfred and Sha’Carri Richardson.

“This is the experience I always wanted, coming on the big stage, running with the big dogs, as you can see. I came out with a seventh place finish but it has been good,” Williams told World Athletics.

Williams’ performances at the Ultimate Championship earned her US$16,000 ($2.5 million), adding another highlight to an impressive second season as a professional athlete since leaving William Knibb High.

Williams, who is coached by former Jamaica sprint star Michael Frater at the Dynamic Speed Track Club, shattered her personal best in both sprint events.

In the 100m she lowered her personal best from 11.45 seconds set in 2025 to 10.90, which she did at the Felix Sanchez Classic in the Dominican Republic last month. It was the fifth time she had gone under the sub-11-second mark this year, making her the 15th-fastest Jamaican woman of all time in the process.

In the 200m her personal best improved from 24.38 last year to 22.44, earning her a spot at the Commonwealth Games this summer in Scotland where she reached the final and finished just shy of the podium in fifth.

Williams didn’t finish the year empty-handed of silverware, however, as she won relay gold at the Commonwealth Games and the World Athletics Relays, as well as 100m gold and 200m silver at the North American, Central American and Caribbean (NACAC) Under-23 Championships in Mexico.

Williams believes her desire to please her mother made her a better athlete this year.

“This season I told myself that I really need to get on the worldwide radar, and I really wanted to make my mum proud,” she told The Inside Lane UK.

“She did a lot for me. She always talking about, ‘I want my dream house, I want my this, I want my that’, and when I thought about everything [and] not going to college I’m like, ‘Nah, I got to step up and get in the game.’ ”

Williams will be hoping to get her first taste of a major championship when she looks to qualify for next year’s World Athletics Championships in Beijing.

Though happy with her performances so far, Williams says she will have to go a step further to compete with the best in 2027.

“My season has been great. Part of it has been smooth sailing, [other] parts can get a bit demotivating at times because you know how the body works as an athlete. However, it has been good.”

“[My biggest takeaway] is being ready mentally. You can be ready physically but sometimes, mentally, if you’re not there you won’t go far.”

World.title: Fashion Radar: ‘Sākred
World.content:
‘Sākred founder and principal Shelly-Deane Neil makes a statement in the Tie-Side Wrap Set. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Tuesday Style Fashion (TSF) stops by ‘Sākred for this week’s spotlight on retailers. Under the Fashion Radar today is principal Shelly-Deane Neil.

TSF: ‘Sākred is officially open. What inspired you to create the boutique, and what does the name mean to you?

Shelly-Deane Neil (SDN): ‘Sākred was really inspired by my own journey with fashion and faith. As my relationship with God grew, the way I viewed how I dressed began to change, but my love for fashion didn’t. I still wanted to feel feminine, modern, confident and a little edgy. I just wanted what I wore to reflect who I was becoming.

I realised there was space for a brand that spoke to women like me — women who have standards but still genuinely love fashion. I wanted ‘Sākred to show that choosing modesty doesn’t mean losing your personal style.

The name ‘Sākred came from God, and it means “set apart”. For me, it’s not about saying the clothing itself is sacred; it’s about the woman wearing it understanding that she is. That idea really became the foundation of the brand and our approach to modern, modest fashion.

TSF: What gap did you see in the market that made you say,“This needs to exist”?

SDN: The gap became really clear to me here in Jamaica. As my own standards around clothing began to change, I realised how difficult it was to shop locally for pieces that gave me the coverage I wanted while still feeling modern, elevated and fashion-forward. In Jamaica, we have a very vibrant fashion culture, but a lot of what is readily available tends to be more revealing, particularly when it comes to occasion wear and going-out pieces. On the other hand, when you do find more modest options, they don’t always feel as current or aligned with the woman who still wants to make a fashion statement. I felt there was room in the Jamaican market for something in between — a brand where a woman could find pieces that respected her standards without asking her to sacrifice her sense of style.

TSF: Walk us through the process of bringing Sakred from an idea to a physical space.

SDN: Bringing ‘Sakred from an idea to a physical space was probably one of the most hands-on things I’ve ever done. There was so much that I had to learn, research and figure out along the way.

The sourcing process alone was a journey. Before I ever got on a plane, I spent countless hours researching, seeing pieces I liked, trying to get a glimpse of tags, tracing where garments were made, researching manufacturers and following one lead to another trying to figure out where I needed to go and who I needed to meet.

Then came the actual travelling. I travelled for hours, walked for hours, visited different suppliers, went through rack after rack and looked at hundreds of pieces to find the few that actually felt like ‘Sakred. I wanted to touch the fabrics, see the quality for myself, meet suppliers and understand what I was buying. And because our pieces are intentionally limited, I wasn’t trying to buy everything… I was looking for the right things.

At the same time, I was learning the operational side of the business. There were things I could have easily handed over to someone else, but I wanted to understand how my own business worked. Then there was finding the space, overseeing the build-out, developing the brand, hiring, merchandising and all the details that go into actually opening the doors. So when people walk into Sakred now and see this beautiful finished space, I think what they don’t see are all the hours behind it; the research, the travelling, the walking, the mistakes, the learning, the suppliers I had to find, and the things I had to teach myself along the way.

Sakred was very much built hands-on, from the ground up, and I think that’s part of what makes seeing it physically exist now so special.

TSF: How involved were you in the aesthetic and design of the store itself?

SDN: I was involved in absolutely everything. I chose the colour palette, the furniture, the fixtures, the lighting, the mirrors, the racks, the placement of the clothing — down to the smaller details of how everything would work together. I was very particular about creating a space that felt clean, modern and elevated, but still warm and inviting.

TSF: How would you describe your own personal style, and how much of it is reflected in Sakred?



SDN: I would describe my personal style as feminine, chic and a little edgy. I love a clean, polished look, but I also like something unexpected — whether that’s the silhouette, a detail, the way a piece is styled or simply the confidence it gives you when you put it on. And honestly, a lot of that is reflected in Sakred. When I’m sourcing, one of the first things I instinctively ask myself is, “Would I wear this?” I think that’s why the collection feels so cohesive, because there is a very clear point of view behind what makes it onto our racks. At the same time, I’m conscious that Sakred isn’t my personal closet. I’m choosing for different women, different body types, different ages and different lifestyles, so I’ll absolutely select pieces that may not necessarily be something I would wear myself, but still embody the Sakred woman.

TSF: How do you curate the pieces that make it onto Sakred’s racks?

SDN: I’m very selective about what makes it onto Sakred’s racks. I’m not sourcing simply because something is trendy or because I think it will sell. It has to feel like Sakred. I look at the silhouette, especially the quality of the fabric, the fit, the details and, of course, the level of coverage. But modesty for me isn’t necessarily about a specific hemline or neckline, it’s about the overall presentation of the piece and how it can be styled.

And then there’s simply instinct. I know the Sakred aesthetic, so sometimes I’ll see something and immediately know: “That’s Sakred.” Other times, something can be beautiful, but it just doesn’t belong on our racks. The goal is to curate a collection where every piece earns its place.

TSF: Name three ‘Sakred must-haves.

1. A little black dress is timeless. It’s one of those pieces every woman should have because you can dress it up, dress it down and make it completely your own.

2. Statement sets are a big part of Sakred. I love that they give you an effortless, complete look, but you can also separate the pieces and create entirely different outfits.

3. And definitely one of our shorts sets. They’ve become a hot commodity at Sakred. They’re comfortable and easy to wear, but still give you that polished, put-together look. I think those three capture ‘Sakred perfectly: Modern, feminine, versatile and always with a little edge!

TSF: Are there plans to expand beyond the store — perhaps into private styling, and events?

SDN: Absolutely. ‘Sakred is already my label, but I would definitely like to expand into creating original ‘Sakred pieces. I wouldn’t necessarily call myself a designer in the traditional sense — I’m much more visual. I can look at a piece and immediately see how I would change it, whether that’s adjusting the silhouette, changing a detail, adding something or taking something away to make it feel more elevated.

So I see the natural evolution being working alongside designers and manufacturers who can take my creative direction and translate it into original pieces for the brand. Beyond that, I definitely see ‘Sakred growing through events, collaborations and curated experiences. I want women to be able to experience the brand in ways that go beyond simply shopping. We’ve only just opened, so I’m being intentional about allowing the brand to grow organically, but there is definitely a much bigger vision for Sakred. The physical store is really just the beginning.

World.title: Balford Henry, award-winning veteran journalist, dies at 74
World.content:
Veteran journalist Balford Henry (right) being conferred by Governor-General Sir Patrick Allen with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

KINGSTON, Jamaica – Award-winning veteran journalist Balford Henry, whose career spanned more than five decades of reporting, has died at the age of 74.

He died on Monday after a short illness.

Henry entered journalism in 1971 as a trainee reporter with the Gleaner while in sixth form at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

Early in his career, he reported on sittings of the Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC) before making his name as a labour relations reporter and later a parliamentary journalist.

He also covered major social and cultural activities and historical events, including Bob Marley’s funeral in 1981.

Henry also served as a senior reporter with the Jamaica Observer and a consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS).

A recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry was the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youths in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in the country in 1977, according to the JIS.

He also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of Marley’s funeral as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature on reggae singer Junior Byles entitled, ‘Fall of a Superstar’.

In 2011, Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

He leaves behind two daughters.

World.title: Germany’s embattled leader Merz cancels New York trip amid mounting domestic pressure
World.content:
Merz had planned to fly to New York on Sept. 22 — two days after the elections — where he was to be awarded the Henry Kissinger Prize by the American Academy in Berlin and was scheduled to address the U.N. General Assembly. Next week is the U.N.’s so-called high-level week, during which numerous heads of state and government will address the General Assembly and hold important meetings.

Signs that the chancellor would cancel have dripped out during the past few days. Initially, Merz’ presence at the award ceremony for the “Henry Kissinger Prize” was canceled so that the Chancellor could still address a parliamentary group meeting on Sept. 22.

At that meeting right after the elections, many critical voices are expected — especially if, as feared, Merz’s Christian Democratic Union suffers a poor result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The party could even fall below the 5% threshold required to enter parliament. For Merz to fly abroad to accept an award in the midst of his biggest crisis as chancellor would not be good optics.

The fact that the entire trip has now been canceled underscores just how serious even the Chancellor’s Office views the domestic political crisis and the need to grapple with the future of the government and its leadership. Instead of Merz, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul will address the United Nations. Merz had already been represented by Wadephul at last year’s U.N. General Assembly.

Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report.

World.title: EU demands answers as France pushes for billionaire’s Russia sanctions release
World.content:
Foreign ministers are huddling with Paris on the issue Tuesday and Wednesday, said two EU diplomats, who expressed skepticism about the move at a time when Moscow is stepping up strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure and threatening neighboring countries. “Talks are ongoing to find a solution. Russia has given us no reason to allow any delistings,” one said.

Paris initially cast its advocacy for Usmanov, who has been sanctioned by the EU, the U.S., the U.K. and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as a concession to Slovakia — which had long advocated his removal from the list.

However, French officials and diplomats have since been given lines by the Élysée, acknowledging that Paris has “a specific national security issue and wish[es] to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.” That could include the release of French nationals jailed by Azerbaijan, a close ally of Uzbekistan, as reported by the FT.

“We don’t want to send the message that if you are a Russian oligarch wanting to get off the sanction list, [you should] hold some Europeans hostage,” Dutch MEP Thijs Reuten said.

Member states lobbying for vested interests in sanctions talks is nothing new, said another diplomat. “But the fact it’s France, which aspires to be a leader in the EU on the foreign affairs side, means they [are held to] a different standard.”

Ambassadors received no intel on a behind-the-scenes deal during Monday’s meeting. “Maybe there is a legitimate case to be made, but Coreper doesn’t know why the French are doing this,” they said.

World.title: Welsh leader of Farage’s Reform UK quits after arrest
World.content:
Dan Thomas was elected to the Welsh parliament as leader of the opposition in May.

LONDON — The Welsh leader of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK resigned Tuesday after being arrested on suspicion of assault.

Dan Thomas, who led the party in the Welsh parliament, said in a statement he was standing down from his role for “personal reasons.”

“Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account,” he said.

World.title: Ursula von der Leyen’s diplomatic faux pas with Mark Carney
World.content:
“We said that obviously from our side, given that … he’s going to be there for her speech, it would be great if she could be there [for his],” Wilkinson told POLITICO, adding: “They found a way to make it work, which I think is good for everybody.”

The episode comes amid the most carefully choreographed week on the Commission president’s calendar — and as Brussels and Ottawa are trying to deepen ties.

Speculation has swirled that Canada is seeking “associate membership” in the EU — even though no such status exists. Carney has denied pursuing such a standing, while a Canadian official, granted anonymity to speak freely, said it had actually been a European suggestion.

Anatomy of a snub

The back-and-forth started with a simple scheduling problem.

Von der Leyen had been supposed to meet Carney in Strasbourg on Tuesday, according to an EU official.

That meeting was pushed to Wednesday, the official said. “We had thought we had more time on Tuesday. There was an aligning of schedules — so now we will spend an extra night here.”

World.title: US to divert $52 million in military aid from Europe and Middle East to Trump-friendly nations in Americas
World.content:
The Trump administration is redirecting $52 million in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to help back US-aligned governments in the Americas.

 

The US State Department notified Congress on Tuesday that it would divert the funds from Iraq, Tunisia and NATO members Slovakia and North Macedonia to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Panama.

The US State Department said the funding would go towards combatting "narcoterrorism in our backyard" and helping "continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that it would "prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere."

The impacted countries are still expected to receive some assistance despite the change, although the exact amount is unclear.

Trump has increasingly turned his attention to the Americas since his return to the White House in January 2025, carrying out strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats coming from the region and launching an operation to capture former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. He has also sought to gain access to Venezuela's oil industry - striking a major oil deal with Caracas in August.

But Trump has also worked to deepen relations with governments he considers aligned to his goals as he looks to build the US' presence in the region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made a trip to South America last week as part of this push, meeting with the conservative leaders of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador to pledge further support and cooperation.

In Europe, however, Trump has made no secret of his wish to reduce the US' role, repeatedly hitting out at European NATO allies over their defence spending and threatening to withdraw American forces from the continent.

Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella, left, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio embrace during a bilateral agreements signing ceremony in Barranquilla, Colombia. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

In August, the State Department said it also planned to announce a $1 billion security package for new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's right-wing administration.

The office of the spokesperson for the department said the package aimed to help Washington and Bogotá achieve "our shared goals."

Trump has long been complimentary of de la Espriella, calling him a "smart, strong, and tough leader" and promising the "total support and strength of the United States behind him."

World.title: At least five killed and more than a dozen injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine
World.content:
At least five people have been killed and more than a dozen have been injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the last 24 hours.

 

The mayor of Kyiv, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday afternoon that at least 12 people had been injured in strikes on the Ukrainian capital since the morning, with one critically injured person dying in hospital.

Kyiv police said warehouses, a business center and a fast-food restaurant were damaged in attacks on the city, with Ukrainian media reporting that the restaurant was a McDonald's.

In the southern city of Kherson, a 74-year-old woman was killed by a Russian drone strike, Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Region Military Administration, announced on Telegram.

Two men, aged 38 and 60, were also wounded in a drone attack on the Kherson region on Tuesday morning, per local authorities.

In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration, Mykhailo Semkin, said early on Tuesday that another man was killed and a woman was injured after an attack that reportedly targeted the power grid.

Two others were killed and one person was injured in strikes on Sloviansk in the eastern Donetsk Oblast, authorities said.

Moscow launched 200 drones overnight at Ukraine as it continued its attacks on the country, with 187 intercepted, Ukraine's armed forces said.

Russian oil refinery struck

For its part, the Ukrainian military reported attacks on Russia's Syzran oil refinery, as well as on the Atlant Aero facility in the city of Taganrog, which reportedly specialises in the making of unmanned aerial vehicles and components.

In an operation carried out by Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, including its deep strike units, the Syzran refinery's primary crude oil distillation unit and tank farm were hit, the Ukrainian General Staff said.

Local residents ride the bikes in the frontline town of Druzhkivka, Donetsk region, Ukraine, Sept. 12, 2026,. AP Photo - Iryna Rybakova/Ukraine's 93rd Mechanized Brigade

Ukraine launches counteroffensive

It comes as a Ukrainian unit's commander announced that it had launched counteroffensive against Russian forces near the eastern Ukrainian city of Lyman.

The city of Lyman remains one of the few in the region of Donetsk not to have been occupied by Russian forces since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but Russian forces have been making efforts to encircle it for months.

Military analysts say that its occupation could facilitate Russia's advance towards taking the Ukrainian strongholds of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

But the commander of Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, Andrii Biletskyi, said in a video on Telegram that the unit had launched an "offensive operation" and that Ukrainian forces had cleared an area of around 75 sq km.
