World.title: Duterte due in ICC courtroom to assess if fit for murder trial
World.content:
DETAINED AT THE ICC. Rodrigo Duterte attends his first call at the ICC via video link from the Scheveningen prison where he is detained, on March 14, 2025.

Judges will hear arguments about his health and ability to stand trial, which is scheduled to begin in November. His lawyers have argued that he suffers from cognitive decline and is not well enough.

THE HAGUE, Netherlands – Former president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to appear in public for the first time on Wednesday, September 16, since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges related to his war on drugs.

Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for creating, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.

On Wednesday, judges will hear arguments about his health and ability to stand trial, which is scheduled to begin in November. His lawyers have argued that he suffers from cognitive decline and is not well enough.

Duterte’s lawyer and family did not respond to requests for comment.

ICC judges said in January that Duterte’s health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.

Duterte’s warrant says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including when he served as mayor of the southern Davao City.

ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown, the details of which were reported in a Reuters investigation.

According to police, 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defense and told supporters he was ready to “rot in jail” if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way
World.content:
ABS-CBN Corporation, which has not turned a profit since it lost its broadcast franchise, has P6 billion in new money coming in, the largest show of confidence in the company since the shutdown of 2020. Then on Tuesday, September 15, it announced that around 200 employees will be losing their jobs.

This will be the 6th straight year the workforce shrinks. ABS-CBN went into the shutdown with 11,071 workers, counting regular employees, project and program-based staff, independent contractors and talents together. By the end of 2025, it came down to 3,646, made up of 2,009 regular employees on permanent contracts, 206 project employees, 582 program-based employees and 849 independent contractors. Nearly 5,000 went in the first round alone, a figure that ABS-CBN president and CEO Carlo Katigbak gave shareholders at the 2020 annual meeting.

Those two things were put out side by side in ABS-CBN’s September 15 official statement. It called the new investments “a vote of confidence in the future of the company” in one paragraph, and in the next said it has been “a difficult year for the content industry,” blaming the Middle East conflict, high inflation and low economic growth for weaker advertising and consumer spending. Then it announced “the difficult decision to implement a retrenchment program to keep ABS-CBN on strong financial footing,” covering “around 200 people or 7% of the company’s workforce.” At a town hall meeting on Tuesday, according to sources familiar with the meeting, Katigbak told employees this would be the last retrenchment under his leadership.

So if investors are finally putting P6 billion into ABS-CBN, why are 200 employees going out?

Fresh money, in pieces

The P6 billion is fresh capital going into a company in trouble. It will arrive in tranches through 2026, released as the existing owners and the new one, I&C Holdings Corp., settle terms between them. Salaries, on the other hand, fall due every month.

I&C is taking P3.5 billion of it. ABS-CBN describes the firm in its own August 12 statement as a fully Filipino-owned private investment holding company “that invests for long-term company turn-around.” Crème Investment Corporation, Mantes Corporation, and Presta Holdings Company Inc., representing three branches of the Lopez family, are taking P2.2 billion between them. Lopez Inc. is taking P300 million. “This substantial investment is a vote of confidence in ABS-CBN,” chairman Mark Lopez said when the agreements were signed.

What the money buys are newly issued common and preferred shares that do not exist yet. They have to come out of an increase in ABS-CBN’s authorized capital stock, which shareholders are due to vote on at a special meeting on September 30 and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has to approve afterward. ABS-CBN has told the exchange the public float will be diluted, meaning the shares held by ordinary investors will account for a smaller slice of the company. The same meeting is expected to expand the board from seven directors to nine.

Where the P6 billion goes first

ABS-CBN told the exchange the proceeds are for working capital, for strengthening the balance sheet and for general corporate purposes. In plain terms, most of it is for paying what the company already owes. Some of it will likely go to repaying the bank loans coming due.

The books show how much that is. At the end of June, ABS-CBN held P1.31 billion in cash against P8.64 billion in loans falling due within 12 months. Its short-term obligations exceeded the assets it could quickly turn into cash by P14.2 billion, a gap that had widened from P12.4 billion at the end of December. Shareholders’ equity, which is what would be left if the company sold everything and paid everyone, had gone below zero, to minus P1.08 billion from a positive P747 million six months earlier.

So the P6 billion dropped into that picture pushes equity back above zero and gives the company something to show its banks. It will not change what the business earns next year.

The hole underneath

The media company itself was not only losing money. It was losing more than the year before, and by the middle of this year, its everyday operations had stopped producing any cash at all.

Revenues in the first half of 2026 fell 17% to P6.88 billion, and the net loss more than doubled to P1.83 billion. The clearest measure was EBITDA, which strips out interest and the paper cost of ageing equipment to show whether a business generates cash from running itself. In the first half of 2025, it was positive P568 million. In the first half of 2026, it was negative P498 million.

ABS-CBN has a fair answer to part of this. The first half of 2025 carried election advertising, BINI‘s sold-out Philippine Arena concert, and a strong Star Cinema release, none of which repeated. And the company says that setting political advertising aside, content revenues were flat. It expects the second half to improve on the back of BINI’s world tour and the rest of its film and live-events slate. But that does not explain the cost side, where salaries and wages rose to P2.5 billion from P2.4 billion. Personnel and talent costs rose to P1.82 billion from P1.65 billion, even as revenue fell.

Where the losses are

The easy explanation would be Sky Cable, whose cable and broadband revenues fell 42% to ₱1.12 billion as subscribers kept leaving.

The numbers point elsewhere. Sky cut its operating costs 25% in the first half and halved the personnel costs to P257 million. And it ended the period still generating cash from operations with EBITDA of positive P11 million. The content business went the other way, to negative P509 million, with a net loss of P1.24 billion against P535 million a year earlier.

The heavier pressure sits in the part of ABS-CBN that is supposed to be its future.

Six years of this

The cutting started in 2020, years before any new investor appeared. Katigbak set out the scale himself at the August 2026 annual meeting. Leaving Sky aside, general and administrative expenses plus manpower costs fell from around P15 billion in 2019 to P6.9 billion in 2025, a reduction of 54%, while debt fell from P20.5 billion to just under P8.5 billion, a reduction of 58%.

The workforce came down with it. After the 2020 retrenchment the company and its subsidiaries counted 5,870 people at the end of 2021, then 5,701, then 5,279, then 4,022 after the restructuring that followed the collapse of the Sky Cable sale to PLDT, and 3,646 at the end of 2025. Regular employees, the ones on permanent contracts, fell from 3,899 to 2,009 over those 4 years. In its 2025 sustainability report, ABS-CBN puts its employees at 2,797 and its attrition rate, including retrenchment, at 32%.

“We recognize that we are not yet where we need to be,” Katigbak told shareholders in August.

Letting people go costs money

Retrenchment is not a saving that starts immediately. Separation pay goes out first and the lower payroll shows up afterward, which is why a company short of cash can find it hard to afford.

ABS-CBN has been carrying that cost for years. It paid roughly P1.1 billion in separation benefits during the 2020 retrenchment. Its audited 2025 financials show that the parent company still owes P874 million to employees retrenched and separated in earlier rounds, down only P70 million from the P944 million owed a year before.

The ABS-CBN retirement fund that normally pays those benefits is nearly empty. At the end of June, it held P61 million against P3.53 billion owed to employees. Two years earlier, the fund held P228.5 million. For 2026, ABS-CBN expects to put P60.4 million back in.

A company holding P1.31 billion in cash against P8.64 billion in loans coming due cannot easily write separation checks for 200 employees, while a company with P6 billion committed incoming capital can. This means the new money is not what makes the retrenchment unnecessary but part of what makes it payable.

The banks are watching

There is a 3rd audience for the announcement. Almost all of ABS-CBN’s debt now sits in the column for obligations due within a year, P8.4 billion of it at the parent company, because a standstill agreement with its lenders ran out at the end of 2025. The P5 billion owed to the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) and the P4.75 billion owed to UnionBank have been extended in short increments since, most recently to May 31 and June 30 of this year.

The company is in talks to refinance those loans on longer terms, including removing the requirement that it hold a broadcast franchise. Its interim accounts still carry a formal warning that there is material uncertainty over whether ABS-CBN can continue operating as a going concern, and among the steps management lists in response is continuing cost control that reduces general and administrative expenses and employee costs.

Still unknown

The statement gave a number and stopped. The company has not said which divisions the 200 come from or how many will go from each, how much it expects to save every year, or how much the separation packages will cost. It has not given a current headcount, or a headcount that separates ABS-CBN from Sky. Nor has it said how the P6 billion will be split between the loans falling due, the money owed to employees from earlier rounds, and the day-to-day running of the business.

And one question the disclosures do not touch: Was this reduction already in the plans and projections shown to I&C Holdings and the Lopez investors before they signed? There is no evidence any of them demanded it, and ABS-CBN was cutting costs long before I&C appeared. But money that arrives in tranches, on conditions, from an investor that describes itself as backing long-term turnarounds, comes with a view about what a company should cost to run.

What ‘last’ means

Katigbak’s promise to employees at the town hall meeting — that this would be the last retrenchment under his leadership — can mean two different things. It can mean ABS-CBN has finally reached a size it can sustain, or it can mean only that there will be no further retrenchment for as long as he is chief executive. Only the first is a statement about the business.

The test is the arithmetic. The company has to reach the point where what it earns covers what it spends, and the first half of 2026 moved away from that point rather than toward it.

The 200 will not be the first to leave with money still owed to them. People let go in the earlier rounds are still owed money years later.

Strengthening a balance sheet means paying down what a company owes, and the money owed to former employees sits on that balance sheet alongside bank loans. The P6 billion may well be what clears both.

“We owe it to our banks, our employees, our partners to make good on all our obligations to them,” Katigbak told shareholders in August. On September 30, the shareholders are due to vote on the capital increase the P6 billion depends on. ABS-CBN has not said which divisions the 200 come from, or how much of the new money goes to the people it has already let go. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: Billions on paper: How much of Luzon Corridor’s $20-B pipeline will become real?
World.content:
Rappler worked with an independent research analyst to see how much of the Luzon Economic Corridor pipeline is actually moving from pitch to pavement, and found that most of it is still in the planning stage

First of 2 parts

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself offered perhaps the best test for the billions of dollars in projects pitched to investors under the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC).

“The success of the LEC will not be measured by the number of meetings that we hold or projects that we announce,” Marcos told investors and officials packed into the Grand Hyatt Manila on Thursday, September 10. “It will be measured by what we finance, by what we build, what we place into operation.”

That’s a demanding standard for the investment dealbook unveiled at the inaugural LEC Investment Forum, which lays out opportunities across the economic belt stretching from Subic Bay and Clark through Metro Manila all the way to Batangas.

On paper, there’s plenty to build. The dealbook contains 31 individually detailed opportunities, plus 13 industrial parks seeking businesses and locators. But only 18 of the 31 projects disclose an opportunity value. Rappler’s tally puts those at roughly $17.6 billion to $20.7 billion (P1.11 trillion to P1.30 trillion)*, depending on which end of disclosed ranges is used, while 13 projects still have no price tag at all.

Much of the pipeline is the basic machinery an industrial economy needs: railways, ports, airports, power plants, pipelines, warehouses, water systems, and telecommunications.

Rappler visualized the projects with disclosed values below, using the upper end where the dealbook gives a range. Click on a sector or hover over a project for more details.

Only four projects account for roughly four-fifths of the dealbook’s disclosed value at the upper end:

$4.1 billion (P257.6 billion) Sangley Point International Airport

$4 billion (P251.3 billion) North-South Commuter Railway operations and maintenance opportunity

$3 billion (P188.5 billion) Metro Manila Subway O&M concession

$3 billion to $6 billion (P188.5 billion to P377.0 billion) Subic-Clark natural gas ecosystem

Looking at these highlighted projects alone also shows that much of the pipeline is not made up of entirely new projects created under the LEC. Several of the biggest transport and energy projects were already in the government’s infrastructure pipeline before being folded into the corridor.

Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan flagged this as another reason to be cautious about treating the dealbook as a fresh wave of investments.

“I also flag that much of the pipeline is not new. Many of the transport and energy entries are long-standing JICA, ADB, and DOTr projects now rebranded under the corridor,” Punongbayan told Rappler. “All in all, there remains a huge gap between the corridor’s vision and its promised pipeline.”

How much is actually committed?

To look beyond the headline values, Rappler collaborated with Cesar Tolentino, an independent research analyst and strategic adviser, to assess how far the projects have actually progressed using the dealbook and other publicly available project information.

Tolentino’s analysis quantified about $21.4 billion (P1.34 trillion) across 20 projects with identifiable investment values. But only about $5.1 billion (P320.4 billion) could be classified as pledged, already being spent or implemented, or completed. Roughly $15.5 billion (P973.8 billion) remained at what Tolentino groups in the visualization as the planning stage, where the stated project value could not yet be verified as committed investment.

“Even if there is documentation confirming a minimum investment amount of $21.4 billion for the Luzon Economic Corridor, [only about] $5 billion is either pledged, work-in-progress (being spent), or completed (spent). A majority of the declared investment amount is up ‘in the air’ and cannot be confirmed as committed,” Tolentino told Rappler.

That does not necessarily mean the projects will not push through. Many are still at the point where investors are being sought, procurement has yet to happen, or feasibility studies and other project preparation are still underway.

Tolentino said this makes it difficult to treat the full value of the project list as investment that can already be expected to enter the country.

“There’s a rule of thumb that Chinese businessmen use: ‘You only count the money that is on-hand,’” he said, referring to funds already received or backed by a contract. A pledge without a contract, by comparison, remains work in progress.

Being listed in the dealbook itself also does not mean an investor has already written a check, or that the project itself is new to the LEC. Some of the corridor’s largest entries are longstanding government infrastructure projects that have since been grouped under the initiative. The document also does not provide a common methodology for what it calls an “opportunity value.”

In some cases, the figure appears tied to building or expanding infrastructure; in others, it is attached to a long-term operations and maintenance concession. For projects looking mainly for customers or offtakers, it’s not always clear whether the number refers to capital expenditure, total project value, expected contract revenues, or another measure.

In other words, the roughly $20-billion (P1.26 trillion) headline is better understood as the scale of opportunities being marketed, rather than an actual $20-billion investment already committed to the Philippines.

The projects are also at very different stages. For instance, the proposed 212-kilometer Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas freight railway is undergoing studies expected to finish only in early 2029. Feasibility work for the Metro Manila Subway Phase 2 is likewise targeted for 2029, while the $175-million (P11-billion) National Data Center remains at pre-feasibility stage.

Others are further along. The Department of Agriculture has secured an initial $65 million (P4.08 billion) for the Clark National Food Hub. A $20-million to $25-million (P1.26-billion to P1.57-billion) insulated-panel factory expansion in Pampanga already has civil works completed and equipment in transit, while development of a $30-million (P1.88-billion) Subic fuel depot began in May.

That wide gap between early-stage concepts and implemented projects is exactly the challenge the government now has to close. US Ambassador Lee Lipton said it best during the forum: “Ideas are easy. Closing a deal is hard. Getting projects to the finish line is even harder.”

Why the Philippines needs the investment

The Philippines urgently needs to attract more capital, with foreign investment already weak and continuing to lose momentum.

Foreign direct investment net inflows reached just $3.38 billion (P212.36 billion) from January to June 2026, down 17.8% from $4.12 billion (P258.86 billion) in the same period a year earlier, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Full-year FDI had already fallen 13.6% in 2025 from 2024.

DECLINE. Data form the BSP shows that foreign investments in the Philippines have been declining since 2024, with H1 2026 also being lower than the same period from 2025. Chart from BSP.

Economy Secretary Arsenio Balisacan has also repeatedly said the country needs stronger investment if it wants to generate more productive, better-paying jobs rather than depend so heavily on consumption and services.

The LEC is one attempt to solve that problem by packaging infrastructure, industrial land, incentives. and government support into a single investment proposition backed initially by the Philippines, US, and Japan, and now a wider group of partner countries.

There was also genuinely new money around the forum. The Philippines and the US signed a $60-million (P3.77-billion) Millennium Challenge Corporation Threshold Program grant, while the US Trade and Development Agency announced project-preparation support for Subic ship repair expansion and an AI-enhanced public Wi-Fi pilot. Those commitments are more concrete than expressions of interest, although project-preparation funding should still not be considered financing for the eventual full-scale infrastructure.

At the same time, Manila is not putting all its eggs in the US-led basket.

Just days before the LEC forum, the government’s economic team was in Hong Kong for the Belt and Road Summit, pitching the Philippines to investors and seeking deeper investment ties with the Hong Kong and China market.

“Hong Kong is a global financial center and a gateway to Asia. The Philippines is a fast-growing economy with talent, scale, resources, and a strategic location in the region. Our strengths complement each other,” Finance Secretary Frederick Go said at the Philipping-Hong Kong briefing.

The finance chief also emphasized that the country’s next chapter of growth would be built with the private sector and partners across the international business community, a chapter the government hopes will eventually be driven by AI, data centers and other high-tech industries.

But can the Philippines move beyond today’s pipeline of mostly basic infrastructure and actually attract the high-tech investments it’s banking on? (To be concluded) – Rappler.com

NEXT: Part 2 | High-tech dreams, low-tech reality of the Luzon Economic Corridor

*$1 = P62.829 based on the September 14, 2026 rate of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

World.title: Basilan vice governor’s son takes 4th District seat in BARMM Parliament
World.content:
JOINING THE RACE. Jay Hataman Salliman files his certificate of candidacy for the position of 4th District representative of Basilan to the Bangsamoro Parliament on May 5, 2026.

Jimael Salam Datumanong Salliman, better known as Jay Hataman Salliman, is also a lawyer and former Basilan provincial board member

MANILA, Philippines – Another Hataman is assured of a high-ranking seat representing Basilan province, this time as the province’s 4th District representative to the Bangsamoro Parliament.

Jimael Salam Datumanong Salliman, better known as Jay Hataman Salliman, is the son of Vice Governor Jim Hataman Salliman. Salliman topped the Basilan 4th District representative race during the 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections on Monday, September 14.

The 29-year-old lawyer and former Basilan provincial board member obtained 41,675 or 81.51% of the votes. This is based on Basilan’s certificates of canvass from the Commission on Elections’ website.

He ran under the Bangsamoro Federalist Party alongside his relative Abrar Hataman, who won his bid for representative in Basilan’s 3rd District.

Salliman won by a landslide over four other candidates.

Coming in second is Alzad Sattar, who chairs the Bangsamoro Peoples Party and is a former member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament. He got 8,364 or 16.36% of the votes.

Next is Bangsamoro Party candidate Monar Ibno, who placed third with 562 or 1.1% of the votes.

Moro Islamic Liberation Front Joint Action Group leader Omar Gapor Muallam came in fourth place, with 424 or 0.83% of the votes. He ran under the MILF’s political party, the United Justice Bangsamoro Party.

In last place is Bangsamoro Empowerment and Social Transformation Party candidate and Lantawan resident Pendatun Mohamad, with 101 or 0.2% of the votes.

As the winning candidate for Basilan 4th District representative, Hataman will serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026 to June 30, 2031. He will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament.

Basilan was the last province to transmit its certificates of canvassing after pre-shaded ballots were found in Maluso town on Monday. This prompted the Commission on Elections to place the town under its control and delayed the start of voting there to Tuesday, September 15.

The 32,000 registered voters in the municipality make up half of the 67,000 from the 4th District. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Calls for New Chapter in Kazakhstan–South Korea Ties, Signs $19 Billion in Deals
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and South Korea signed commercial agreements worth $19 billion during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Seoul on Sept. 15, with both sides seeking to expand cooperation in investment, industry, urban development and cultural and humanitarian ties, Akorda reported.

“Our goal is the comprehensive development of bilateral relations,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during talks with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

Speaking about the outcome of his visit, Tokayev highly assessed the current state and prospects of cooperation between the two countries.

“As for bilateral relations, during this visit, commercial agreements worth $19 billion were signed. We are satisfied with our work with Korean investors and are ready to continue working with them. There are good plans for the construction of hotels, an oil refinery and urban development. Particular attention is paid to strengthening cultural and humanitarian ties,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev also highlighted the high level of coordination between Astana and Seoul on the international stage, noting that the two countries share common positions on global sustainable development and security.

“Our states share common positions on issues of global sustainable development and security,” Tokayev said.

Lee reaffirmed South Korea’s commitment to further deepening bilateral cooperation, pointing to the growing alignment of the two countries’ foreign policy priorities.

“The Republic of Korea and Kazakhstan are broadening the scope of their external cooperation and pursuing pragmatic diplomacy focused on national interests and tangible results. Kazakhstan is an important partner for us in the area of economic security. The country is not only rich in energy and natural resources, but also has significant potential in promising high-tech industries,” Lee said.

He added that South Korea was ready to support the modernization of Kazakhstan’s industrial sector by leveraging its advanced industrial and digital technologies.

“Amid an increasingly unpredictable international environment, our two countries should strengthen cooperation by bringing together our respective strengths and capabilities and actively creating new opportunities for mutually beneficial growth,” Lee said.

President Tokayev expressed gratitude to Lee for the invitation to visit South Korea, describing the country as a strategic partner of Kazakhstan. He noted the longstanding ties of friendship and mutual understanding between the two peoples, as well as close cultural and humanitarian links, stressing that there are no contradictions or disagreements between Kazakhstan and South Korea.

He said the two countries are pursuing ambitious projects across a range of sectors and highlighted the importance of the Kazakhstan-Korea business forum held in Seoul with the participation of representatives of the two countries’ business communities. Among the projects discussed was the further development of Alatau City, which Tokayev described as an important initiative for Kazakhstan.

“The provisions concerning the status of this city have been incorporated into the Constitution. Korean companies will be provided with all legal guarantees. More than 120,000 ethnic Koreans live in Kazakhstan. All conditions have been created for them, and they are active members of our society,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted the historical significance of General Hong Beom-do, a Korean independence movement figure whose remains were returned from Kazakhstan to South Korea in 2021. Tokayev said he was well acquainted with Hong Beom-do’s history and described him as a hero and patriot. He noted that preserving the general’s memory and returning his remains to South Korea demonstrated mutual understanding between the two countries.

“It is remarkable that even after more than a hundred years, the Korean people have not forgotten their general. Bowing to his memory, we returned his remains to his homeland, thereby fulfilling our civic duty,” Tokayev said.

Lee warmly welcomed Tokayev and emphasized the importance of his visit to Seoul. He thanked Kazakhstan for the decision to return Hong Beom-do’s remains and expressed appreciation for the way ethnic Koreans were received in Kazakhstan.

“We are grateful for your decision to return the remains of General Hong Beom-do, who played a special role in the history of Korea and in protecting the Korean people during difficult times. Korean citizens were warmly welcomed in Kazakhstan at the time. We are grateful to you and the Kazakh people for this,” Lee said.

The two presidents said they were ready to cooperate long-term and provide comprehensive mutual support when needed. Following the talks, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and South Korea and giving it new practical substance.

Earlier, Tokayev met with South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong-sook, congratulated her on her recent appointment, and wished her success in the post. Tokayev said Kazakhstan-South Korea relations are developing steadily within the framework of their strategic partnership, with numerous mutually beneficial initiatives being implemented. South Korea is among Kazakhstan’s top 10 trade and investment partners, while more than 1,000 joint ventures with Korean capital operate in Kazakhstan.

“However, there are still many important tasks ahead of us. Therefore, I am confident that, working together as one team, we will successfully implement all the plans we have outlined,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev said Kazakhstan had created favorable conditions for business and investment, including for small and medium-sized enterprises alongside major Korean corporations. He noted the role of the Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Scientific-Technical Cooperation and the Business Council, as well as the bilateral legal framework supporting cooperation.

Tokayev thanked Han Seong-sook for taking part in the roundtable of Kazakh and Korean business representatives and expressed confidence that the agreements signed during the event would contribute to expanding bilateral ties.

He also said his upcoming talks with Lee were intended to open a new chapter in the history of Kazakhstan-South Korea relations.

Tokayev outlined several priorities for further government cooperation, including a target to double bilateral trade turnover.

“It is important not only to increase volumes, but also to qualitatively change the structure of trade and expand the range of goods with high added value. Therefore, I consider it highly relevant to develop a Comprehensive Program for Trade, Economic and Investment Cooperation between Kazakhstan and Korea for 2027-2030,” the President said.

He also proposed preparing a separate roadmap for industrial cooperation, incorporating the most promising localization projects and initiatives to export products to third-country markets.

Tokayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s commitment to comprehensive strengthening of its partnership with South Korea.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans $60 Million Tokenization Pilot for Alatau City Projects
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to tokenize up to $60 million in real estate and logistics projects by the end of 2026, launching its first major test of digital assets as a new source of financing for the economy, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at a Sept. 15 government meeting.

The plans include up to $50 million for the Iconic Tower complex and $10 million for the Birlik logistics center in Alatau City in the Almaty Region. Both are expected to be issued through the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange’s digital infrastructure.

Kazakhstan also plans to link its nationwide regulatory framework with the separate regimes of the Astana International Financial Centre and Alatau City, creating what officials describe as a single digital asset market.

Under that model, authorities are considering a regional payments and settlement hub with Binance. Suleiemenov said the project would involve establishing a Binance legal entity in Kazakhstan and obtaining a top-tier payment organization license, potentially allowing the hub to serve clients across the Commonwealth of Independent States, Eastern Europe and Asia, Suleimenov said.

The projects are part of a 65-measure plan approved by the government on Sept. 15 to expand Kazakhstan’s regulated digital asset market.

Kazakhstan plans to tokenize major infrastructure projects, real estate and commodity assets to attract investment. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the National Bank to compile a priority list of assets for tokenization and establish rules intended to protect investors.

“The digital assets sector is a completely new area of Kazakhstan’s economy. The basic conditions for the development of the digital assets market have already been established. We are now in the process of forming a comprehensive ecosystem,” Bektenov said.

“We have major infrastructure projects, real estate, commodities and other assets. Tokenization can be used to attract additional financing for these projects,” he added.

The government seeks to attract investment and bring more cryptocurrency activity into the regulated economy under the new plan. It also calls for expanding the use of the digital tenge, exploring digital instruments for cross-border payments and developing a more tightly regulated cryptocurrency-mining industry.

The National Bank expects the initial pool of tokenized assets to include government securities, corporate bonds, real estate, infrastructure projects and mineral deposits. Suleimenov called on the Finance Ministry, Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund, Baiterek Holding, KASE and the Central Securities Depository to prepare the first large-scale issuances.

What is tokenization

Tokenization records rights to an asset on a digital ledger. It can divide assets such as real estate, infrastructure or corporate debt into smaller digital units that investors can buy and trade. Supporters say the technology could accelerate transactions, reduce administrative costs and make investments previously dominated by large institutions accessible to a wider range of investors.

Larry Fink and Rob Goldstein of BlackRock have compared tokenization’s current development to that of the internet in 1996, noting that the technology could advance more quickly than many expect. They do not expect it to replace conventional finance soon, but envision the two systems gradually converging.

They portrayed that transition as a bridge being built from two sides: traditional financial institutions on one side and stablecoin issuers, fintech companies and blockchain networks on the other.

Global trends

The World Economic Forum describes 2026 as a “defining moment for digital assets.” It said clearer regulation, wider institutional adoption and greater interoperability are moving blockchain beyond experimentation and into the infrastructure supporting digital financial markets.

Tokenized real-world assets remain a small part of the global digital asset market. Boston Consulting Group estimates that around $30 billion in such assets are publicly visible, compared with roughly $3 trillion in cryptocurrencies and $300 billion in stablecoins. Under the firm’s more expansive scenarios, tokenized assets could represent nearly 16% of global investable assets by 2035, although the outcome would vary considerably by asset class.

According to Suleimenov, the digital assets market now has approximately 750 million users worldwide. Stablecoin transaction volume reached $50 trillion in 2025, while the market for tokenized assets expanded 12-fold over the past three years.

“Three major trends have emerged globally. The first is a shift from prohibition and observation toward licensing, supervision and common international standards. The second is the integration of digital assets with banks, payment infrastructure and capital markets. The third is a move toward practical applications,” Suleimenov explained.

Digital assets are increasingly used for cross-border payments, custody services and the tokenization of real and financial assets.

“Kazakhstan’s objective is to create a competitive, regulated market, with transactions, liquidity and capital concentrated within the country,” he added.

Steady progress

Suleimenov said Kazakhstan began building a regulated digital asset market in 2022. Then, it allowed cryptocurrency exchanges licensed by the Astana International Financial Centre to work with local banks. The parliament followed with a digital assets law in 2023.

By the end of 2025, AIFC-based providers had processed $10.6 billion in transactions and attracted approximately 215,000 users, according to figures cited by Suleimenov. The framework, however, remained limited to the financial center and did not cover the wider domestic market.

The National Bank expanded its approach in July 2025 by launching a regulatory sandbox where companies could test digital asset products under its supervision.

“The sandbox now includes 34 projects across 14 areas. Among them are stablecoins, tokenization, cryptocurrency exchanges, custody and services connecting cryptocurrencies with conventional currencies,” Suleimenov said.

Legislation that took effect on May 1 extended regulation nationwide and formally recognized digital financial assets, including stablecoins and tokenized real and financial assets. It also introduced licensing requirements for tokenization platforms, cryptocurrency exchanges and exchange services. Suleimenov described it as Central Asia’s first comprehensive nationwide regulatory framework for digital assets.

A presidential decree in July expanded the effort by seeking to establish a fully-fledged digital assets industry, encouraging the transition of digital asset transactions to the country’s regulated ecosystem and launching the tokenization of the economy and diversifying sources of financing for the economy.

Key figures

The National Bank has authorized the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange to operate platforms for issuing and trading digital assets. Its digital platform has recorded 34,000 transactions worth 20.5 billion tenge (US45.9 million) in an exchange-traded fund linked to bitcoin futures.

Three newly introduced cryptoasset ETFs have generated 650 transactions worth one billion tenge (US$2.2 million), according to Suleimenov.

Three licensed cryptocurrency exchange operators have also processed around two billion tenge (US$4.5 million) during their first two months of operation, while five more companies are seeking licenses.

Yerkegali Yedenbayev, chief authorization and fintech officer at AIFC’s Astana Financial Services Authority, said Kazakhstan’s citizens are estimated to hold around one million cryptocurrency wallets worldwide, suggesting that much of their trading still takes place through foreign platforms.

He said the center’s regulated digital asset providers currently serve nearly 270,000 clients, up from 53,000 in 2023.

“Today, there are 35 providers operating in the AIFC that offer services in the digital assets sector. Among them are 11 digital asset exchanges, including Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, and Bybit, the fourth-largest crypto exchange. In addition, there are 16 investment service providers and eight payment organizations, including three stablecoin issuers,” Yedenbayev said.

“While the volume of transactions in the licensed market reached $320 million in 2023, this figure reached $10.5 billion by the end of last year. In the first half of this year, the volume of transactions reached $5.5 billion. Thus, in a short period of time, the regulated market has grown more than 30-fold,” he said.

Digital tenge

The newly adopted plan also calls for wider use of the digital tenge, the central bank’s digital currency. Unlike cryptocurrencies, it is issued by the National Bank.

Bektenov instructed the Finance Ministry and the National Bank to examine its use in government procurement, corporate transactions and programmable contracts, which could automate payments when predetermined conditions are met.

“Unlike cryptocurrencies, the digital tenge is a centralized digital currency issued by the National Bank and is therefore legal tender. Its use should improve the efficiency of public spending and support the development of digital financial services. Digital contracts could help automate payments in government procurement and corporate transactions,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Binur Zhalenov, deputy governor of the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK), said the digital tenge has the potential to transform how money moves. Most of the real-world use cases of digital tenge will be related to government spending, including public procurement and social spending.

What needs to be done

Suleimenov said the plan’s success would depend on competitive tax rules, more targeted compliance controls by banks and a sufficient supply of high-quality assets for tokenization. He said concerns involving an individual transaction or customer should not result in banks freezing all accounts held by a licensed digital asset provider.

The concern echoes findings reported earlier. Ainur Zhanturina, founder of RISE Research, said limited access to banking services was the principal barrier identified in the organization’s survey and interviews with Kazakhstan’s digital asset companies.

“Many banks are unwilling to work with companies in this sector, viewing them as higher-risk clients, which complicates transfers and account management,” Zhanturina said.

Сryptocurrency mining

While the digital tenge and tokenization are intended to expand Kazakhstan’s financial infrastructure, the plan also addresses a more established and energy-intensive part of the digital asset industry: cryptocurrency mining.

Kazakhstan has 76 licensed cryptocurrency miners and five accredited mining pools, with around 470,000 pieces of mining equipment registered with the government, said Vice Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov.

The country’s mining pools reported producing approximately 3,600 bitcoins in 2025, four times the volume recorded in 2023. According to Baitursynov, tax revenue from the industry rose to 22.4 billion tenge (US$50.1 million) in 2025 from nine billion tenge (US$20.1 million) two years earlier.

Bektenov said Kazakhstan should focus on regulating energy consumption and taxation rather than simply expanding mining capacity. He instructed officials to examine the use of gas- and coal-fired generation to supply mining centers.

“According to international studies, by the end of 2025, our country had entered the world’s top 10 in terms of its share of global Bitcoin mining. Now, our priority should no longer be focused on the quantitative growth of mining capacity,” said Bektenov.

He emphasized that the policy should focus on creating a more effective operational model that ensures control over energy consumption, transparent taxation, and the industry’s integration into the global digital economy.

“It is necessary to establish a fully-fledged digital mining industry comprising exchanges, digital instruments, tokenization, asset storage, and payment solutions,” he added.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Doubling Kazakhstan-South Korea Trade, Expanding Industrial Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for Kazakhstan and South Korea to double bilateral trade and deepen cooperation in advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, energy, transport, artificial intelligence and other high-value sectors. Speaking at the opening of the Kazakhstan–South Korea business roundtable in Seoul on Sept. 15, Tokayev said bilateral trade exceeded $3 billion last year and could be doubled through joint efforts by the two governments and businesses.

“This visit provides a good opportunity to consolidate the progress achieved and give new impetus to bilateral cooperation,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized that Kazakhstan and South Korea had built strong relations over the past three decades based on mutual respect, trust and friendship. According to him, South Korea is now among Kazakhstan’s major trade and investment partners, with Korean companies playing an increasingly prominent role in the country’s economy.

Korean companies have invested more than $12 billion in Kazakhstan, while more than 1,000 companies with Korean capital operate in the country, including Samsung, Kia, Hyundai, Lotte, Doosan Enerbility and Shinhan Bank.

Industrial partnership enters a new stage

Tokayev identified industrial cooperation as one of the strongest foundations of Kazakhstan–South Korea economic relations. The countries’ joint industrial portfolio currently comprises 51 projects in automotive manufacturing, machinery, metallurgy and other sectors worth more than $4 billion.

Kazakhstan also produced nearly 170,000 vehicles in 2025, setting a national record, while local production of Korean consumer electronics is also expanding, including Samsung household appliances.

“Our goal is to create a fully integrated industrial ecosystem encompassing localized components, advanced materials, electrical equipment and electronics, with a focus on serving the broader Eurasian market,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev also said Kazakhstan was closely following South Korea’s new industrial strategy under President Lee Jae Myung, including the Three Mega Projects and Seven Major SEED initiatives.

Urban development opens opportunities for Korean companies

Construction and urban development were highlighted as another promising area of cooperation.

“Kazakhstan is currently entering an important stage of infrastructure development. We intend to significantly accelerate the pace of construction throughout the country – from transport and utility systems to housing and social infrastructure. I consider this one of the key priorities of my work as President,” he said.

Tokayev noted South Korea’s international experience in construction, engineering and infrastructure development and invited Korean companies to participate in large-scale projects across Kazakhstan. Potential areas include hospitals, children’s rehabilitation centers, multifunctional medical centers, modern schools, sports facilities and transport infrastructure.

The Kazakh President said the government would prepare a specific list of infrastructure projects to create new mutually beneficial ventures and advance investment initiatives.

Critical minerals could create new value chains

Critical minerals represent another strategic area for expanding bilateral cooperation, according to Tokayev. Kazakhstan’s significant reserves of strategic minerals create opportunities for cooperation with South Korean companies in advanced industries and other high-value sectors.

“We propose a ‘resources–technology–industry’ model for jointly developing complete value chains,” Tokayev said.

He highlighted the planned creation in Almaty of a Center for Technological Cooperation in Rare and Rare-Earth Metals as a step toward turning cooperation in the sector from resource exploration into concrete industrial projects.

Energy remains an important component of Kazakhstan–South Korea cooperation, with Tokayev highlighting growing Korean interest in Kazakhstan’s energy sector. He identified further opportunities in gas processing, petrochemicals, energy infrastructure and renewable energy. Tokayev also proposed expanding cooperation in peaceful nuclear energy, particularly in developing small modular reactors.

As one of the world’s largest uranium producers, Kazakhstan has significant potential in the nuclear energy sector, while SMRs are gaining increasing attention as an emerging energy technology.

Kazakhstan seeks greater Korean role in Middle Corridor

Tokayev said Kazakhstan was investing heavily in railways, roads, ports, terminals and other infrastructure to increase the capacity, speed and reliability of the country’s transport links between Asia and Europe.

“We believe the time has come to expand Korea’s participation in the development of the Middle Corridor,” he said.

The President highlighted the activities of Korean logistics companies, including CJ Logistics and LX Pantos, which are developing logistics centers, multimodal terminals, warehouse facilities and digital supply-chain solutions in Kazakhstan.

Tokayev also welcomed cooperation between Kazakhstan’s Shin-Line and Lotte Global Logistics to develop new logistics opportunities.

AI cooperation targets regional technology leadership

Artificial intelligence and new technologies were identified as another major area for future cooperation. Tokayev stressed that human capital would be central to Kazakhstan’s AI strategy and highlighted cooperation with Seoul National University of Science and Technology on establishing Kazakhstan’s first Institute of Artificial Intelligence.

“Our goal is to position Kazakhstan as the main computing center of Central Asia and a bridge between Europe and Asia,” Tokayev said.

He said Kazakhstan was ready to deepen cooperation with global technology companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, including supplying materials and components for microelectronics and semiconductor production.

Human capital remains central to partnership

Tokayev emphasized that technological and economic cooperation would depend on developing human capital. Universities in Kazakhstan and South Korea currently maintain academic cooperation through more than 230 agreements, laying the groundwork for expanding research and educational partnerships.

He also said Kazakhstan’s next stage of economic modernization would focus on new industries, technologies, research capabilities and human capital. South Korea’s own transformation into a global economic and technological power, he noted, provides valuable experience for Kazakhstan as it pursues its modernization agenda.

“I am confident that today’s event and the agreements being signed will give a powerful impetus to a more ambitious partnership,” Tokayev said, calling on Korean businesses to increase investment in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Astana AI Film Festival Attracts More Than 8,000 Entries From 125 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana AI Film Festival (AAIFF 2026) will take place from Oct. 1 to 3, bringing together AI-generated films from 125 countries and offering a combined prize and investment pool of US$2.75 million, organizers said at a briefing in Astana.

More than 8,000 films were submitted to the international competition, highlighting the rapid growth of AI-assisted filmmaking and the expanding global community around the emerging field. The festival received 8,067 submissions from 4,756 unique creators. The total running time of the submitted works exceeded 100,000 minutes.

The competition is divided into two sections. A total of 3,138 films were submitted under the festival’s main theme, The Future Worth Living In, while another 4,929 entries were submitted to the open competition without thematic restrictions.

The United States led in submissions with 1,395 films, followed by Kazakhstan with 829, India with 702, China with 550 and South Korea with 349. The United Kingdom, Indonesia, Japan, Brazil and France also ranked among the countries with the highest number of entries.

AI filmmakers experiment with new forms

The submitted works span 19 genres, with participants using artificial intelligence not only to generate visual content but also to experiment with storytelling, genres and the creation of cinematic worlds. The longest film submitted runs for four hours and three minutes, while one project combines five separate fictional universes.

“Just a few months ago, we were launching an international competition, and today we have received more than 8,000 works from 125 countries,” said Almas Zhali, co-founder of the festival and chairman of the AAIFF board.

“These are no longer isolated AI experiments – we are seeing full-fledged films, complex stories, characters and entire universes. This scale shows how quickly AI cinema is developing,” he said.

The participants include emerging directors and independent teams alongside established figures in the international AI creative industry. Among them are AI production studio The DOR Brothers, which has more than 370,000 followers, director Zack London’s Gossip Goblin project and Robert Gaudette, whose works have previously been presented and recognized at international film festivals.

Organizers estimate that participants spent more than $4 million using more than 80 generative AI models. Among the most widely used tools were Suno AI, Seedance 2.5, Kling, Wan 2.6, GPT Image 2 and ElevenLabs.

All submitted films undergo mandatory plagiarism checks.

Festival offers $1.75 million in prizes

The main thematic competition will distribute $1.75 million in prize money, while another $250,000 will be distributed among five categories in the open competition. A separate $1 million investment fund has also been established for promising AI teams. Entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of Coinbase, former general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, and founder of The Network School, provided the capital.

“We want strong projects to continue after the festival. That is why, in addition to the prize fund, there is a separate investment capital,” said Aizatulla Hussein, co-founder of AAIFF.

The investment is intended to help selected creators continue production, scale their projects and develop them from Kazakhstan. Selected teams will have an opportunity to join Astana Hub, he said.

AI cinema still searching for its identity

Despite the rapid growth of AI-generated filmmaking, the field has yet to develop a distinct and consistent form, according to Hussein.

After reviewing thousands of submissions from different countries, organizers found no single established model for AI cinema. Some filmmakers use AI to reproduce traditional cinematic forms, while others create experimental works that are difficult to classify within conventional filmmaking.

“The trend and the form itself are only taking shape and being explored. Previously, trends could remain for months, but now everything changes practically every day,” Hussein said.

He noted differences in the approaches taken by creators from different countries. South Korean submissions, for example, frequently featured noir and horror aesthetics, as well as stories set in office environments. Chinese creators more often turned to animation and demonstrated distinctive visual approaches, he said.

Kazakh filmmakers also showed recurring themes, with national motifs and visions of the future appearing in many submissions. Yurts, the steppe and robots feature in some of the country’s science-fiction-inspired works. Hussein said it remains difficult to draw a clear line between entertainment content generated with AI and what can be considered full-fledged AI cinema.

“Some try simply to reproduce traditional cinema, while others experiment in ways that do not look like cinema at all, but are very interesting,” he said.

He expressed hope that the festival could contribute to defining a new form and potentially even a new name for this emerging type of entertainment and filmmaking.

AAIFF 2026 will take place from Oct. 1 to 3 as part of AI Month, a series of events dedicated to artificial intelligence. For the first time, finalists will have an opportunity to present their AI-generated films to audiences on a large cinema screen in Astana.

The festival program will also include business sessions, panel discussions and master classes for filmmakers and industry representatives. The awards ceremony and announcement of winners will take place on Oct. 3.

World.title: Kazakhstan, South Korea Advance Investment Cooperation Ahead of Central Asia–Korea Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and South Korea are advancing a growing portfolio of investment and industrial projects, including 67 initiatives worth a combined $6.9 billion in Alatau City and 51 joint industrial projects, as the two countries prepare for the first South Korea–Central Asia Summit in Seoul on Sept. 16.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev held a series of meetings with the leaders of major Korean companies, while senior Kazakh officials engaged with Korean businesses and government representatives on projects spanning automotive manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, hospitality, artificial intelligence and space technologies.

Alatau City emerges as major platform for Korean investment

During a meeting with Lotte Group Chairman Shin Dong-bin, President Tokayev highlighted the company’s longstanding contribution to Kazakhstan’s economy, including its activities in the food industry and the modernization of production facilities in Almaty and Shymkent.

Lotte also plans to expand its presence in logistics and hospitality. Tokayev welcomed the signing of an agreement to build the first Lotte-branded hotel in Almaty and noted the potential for further expansion. Shin confirmed Lotte’s plans to invest in food production, logistics and hospitality and said the company intends to participate in Alatau City development projects, including the Iconic Complex.

The development of Alatau City was also central to Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev’s meetings in South Korea with representatives of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), Lotte Hotels & Resorts, Doosan Enerbility and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI).

With KEPCO, the sides discussed the development of Alatau City’s power infrastructure, including electricity transmission and distribution systems, substations, integration with the national grid and local power networks. Doosan Enerbility and GGGI discussed the development of the city’s own generation capacity. One option under consideration is a 2×250-megawatt gas-fired power plant, with the potential for a subsequent transition to hydrogen. Doosan Enerbility could serve as the project’s technology and EPC partner, with a public-private partnership mechanism being considered.

Lotte Hotels & Resorts also discussed a multifunctional complex in Alatau City featuring an L7 by Lotte hotel. The project, valued at more than $200 million, is expected to include a 180-room hotel, office space and residential apartments.

Kazakhstan and South Korea explore new digital and space projects

At a meeting with Hanwha Group Vice Chairman Kim Dong-won, Tokayev outlined Kazakhstan’s efforts to build a national artificial intelligence ecosystem and develop digital infrastructure. He invited Hanwha Group to implement joint projects in Kazakhstan and use the country as a technological platform for entering Central Asian markets.

Separately, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev visited CONTEC Space Group’s assembly and testing complex in Seoul. The sides discussed CONTEC’s potential investment in the Galam project, joint satellite and component production, and development of a network of ground stations.

One proposal is to establish a manufacturing hub in Kazakhstan for satellite components, with subsequent supplies to markets in Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. The sides are also considering localizing the production of large ground-based antenna systems.

Another area of cooperation is using artificial intelligence to process satellite imagery, potentially expanding the use of Earth observation data for practical applications. A Kazakh subsidiary of CONTEC is expected to be established in the near future, with further details of the partnership expected to be presented during Tokayev’s state visit to South Korea.

Hyundai seeks deeper automotive localization

During a meeting with Hyundai Motor Group President and Head of Strategy and Planning Sung Kim, Tokayev discussed expanding investment and industrial and technological cooperation.

Representatives of Hyundai Engineering and Kia also took part in the meeting. Tokayev identified a longer-term goal of turning Kazakhstan into a major regional center for automobile production and exports, with an emphasis on developing full-cycle manufacturing.

Electric mobility was also identified as a promising area of cooperation, including electric vehicle and component production and the development of charging infrastructure.

Hyundai Motor Group confirmed its intention to expand its presence and deepen production localization in Kazakhstan. Hyundai Engineering said it is ready to develop cooperation in the oil and gas sector, industry and infrastructure, while Kia representatives said they intend to cooperate on developing a national Kazakh automotive brand.

Several agreements were exchanged following the meeting, including between QazaqGaz, Hyundai Engineering and SICIM Kazakhstan on constructing a gas processing plant in western Kazakhstan, and between Hyundai Motor Company and Astana Motors on producing a new Hyundai Tucson model.

KIND to support Alatau City and transport infrastructure

Tokayev also met with Kim Bok-hwan, president and CEO of the Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND). The meeting focused on KIND’s potential involvement in the development of Alatau City. Tokayev emphasized the project’s potential and called for greater Korean participation in infrastructure and investment initiatives in the new city.

He also invited KIND to participate in Kazakhstan’s large-scale plans to modernize social and transport infrastructure. The sides also discussed establishing a Kazakh-Korean joint investment fund to attract Korean capital and technology to infrastructure and energy projects in Kazakhstan.

The sides also discussed potential KIND participation in modernizing the country’s transport and logistics system, including the development of the ports of Aktau and Kuryk and projects involving the construction and renovation of regional airports.

The meeting was followed by an exchange of documents, including a memorandum of understanding between Caspian Group and KIND, an agreement between Alatau City Authority and KIND on developing a master plan for Alatau Smart City, and a strategic agreement between Qazaqstan Investment Corporation and KIND.

The series of meetings comes ahead of the first Korea–Central Asia Summit, which will bring together South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and the leaders of all five Central Asian states in Seoul on Sept. 16.

The summit is expected to provide a high-level platform to strengthen cooperation between South Korea and Central Asia, while business meetings involving Kazakhstan and major Korean corporations underscore the growing focus on investment, technology transfer, infrastructure and industrial cooperation.

World.title: Building Capabilities for Future of Agriculture
World.content:
How Eurasia Group is developing people and advancing technology adoption to support the future of agriculture in Kazakhstan

In 2026, Eurasia Group received a HUMANRISE Award for Digital AgroLeaders — an educational initiative that has been introducing students to modern agriculture and preparing a new generation of professionals for an increasingly technology-driven industry for more than 15 years.

HUMANRISE recognizes achievements in human capital development and employer branding. For Eurasia Group, however, the value of Digital AgroLeaders extends far beyond HR. As a long-standing John Deere dealer and partner, Eurasia Group sees its role not only in bringing advanced agricultural technologies to Kazakhstan, but also in developing the people and capabilities needed to put those technologies to work. Advanced equipment, precision ag solutions, connectivity, and data can only deliver their full value when the industry has people who understand these technologies and know how to use them effectively.

Digital AgroLeaders helps build this technology readiness before young professionals even enter the workforce.

Technology adoption starts with people

Agriculture in Kazakhstan is undergoing a significant technological transformation. Precision ag, automation, connected machines, and data are creating new opportunities to improve productivity, operational efficiency, resource use, and decision-making.

At the same time, the skills required across the industry are changing. Technical professionals need to understand increasingly sophisticated equipment and digital systems. Agronomists need to know how to turn data into actionable insights. Farm managers need to understand the value of precision technologies and make informed, data-driven decisions. And the industry increasingly needs professionals who can bring equipment, agronomy, connectivity, and digital solutions together across the production system.

Developing this next generation is also part of a broader sustainability challenge. Agriculture in Kazakhstan must become more productive and efficient while responding to climate pressures, water scarcity, rising input costs, and workforce shortages — challenges that are increasing the importance of both advanced technology and new professional capabilities.

For a John Deere dealer, market development includes customer engagement, service support, equipment demonstrations, and helping customers adopt and get more value from technology. Digital AgroLeaders adds another dimension to this work: building the capabilities of future market participants before they even begin their professional careers.

Digital AgroLeaders: building technology readiness since 2010

In 2010, Eurasia Group launched its first student competition focused on John Deere equipment and technologies. Over the past 15 years, the initiative has evolved into an educational ecosystem that brings together students, universities, faculty, agricultural businesses, and industry experts.

Participants work on real-world business challenges, attend master classes, explore modern agricultural technologies, and gain access to mentorship, internships, and career development opportunities.

For students, this provides practical experience that complements their university education. For the agricultural industry, it helps create a generation of professionals entering the workforce with a deeper understanding of precision ag, connected machines, digital agriculture, and the role data can play in improving farm performance.

For Eurasia Group, the ambition goes beyond developing future employees. Digital AgroLeaders is designed to help young people see agriculture as a modern, innovative, and attractive industry in which they can build meaningful careers and contribute to the future of Kazakhstan.

2026: reaching a new scale

In 2026, Digital AgroLeaders reached the largest scale in the project’s history. More than 2,500 students from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan participated in the initiative — more than twice as many as the previous year — while the program also expanded its geographic reach.

As a result, thousands of future agronomists, engineers, technical specialists, IT professionals, and agricultural leaders have had the opportunity to experience modern, technology-enabled agriculture beyond the university classroom.

The long-term value of this reach goes beyond the number of students involved. By introducing future agricultural professionals to precision ag, connected machines, and data-driven farming early in their careers, Digital AgroLeaders helps build a broader base of knowledge and technology readiness across the industry. Over time, these capabilities can support faster technology adoption, more effective use of advanced solutions, and stronger decision-making across Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector.

“We believe that technology alone does not transform an industry — people do. Bringing advanced equipment and digital solutions to the market is only part of the equation. We also need to develop the knowledge and capabilities required to unlock their full potential. Digital AgroLeaders reflects our long-term commitment to developing people, supporting innovation, and contributing to a more productive and sustainable future for agriculture in Kazakhstan,” said Sergey Glokke, COO of Eurasia Group.

External recognition of a long-term strategy

In 2026, this approach received external recognition through the HUMANRISE Award.

For Eurasia Group, the award recognizes more than 15 years of investment in the next generation of agricultural professionals. It also reflects a broader approach to market development — one in which technology, knowledge, and people advance together.

The long-term partnership between Eurasia Group and John Deere is an important part of this approach, combining technology expertise with knowledge transfer, capability development, service support, and customer adoption.

The HUMANRISE Award recognizes the success of Digital AgroLeaders, but the initiative’s greater value lies in its long-term impact: helping build the skills and technology readiness that will support a more productive, innovative, and sustainable future for agriculture in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 38th Among 70 Countries in IMD Global Competitiveness 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 38th out of 70 countries in the 2026 World Competitiveness Ranking published by the International Institute for Management Development (IMD) in June. The ranking, compiled by the IMD World Competitiveness Center, assesses countries based on four main factors: economic performance, government efficiency, business efficiency and infrastructure.

Kazakhstan ranked 23rd in government efficiency and 23rd in business efficiency. The country placed 43rd in infrastructure and 57th in economic performance. Overall, Kazakhstan moved down from 34th place in the 2025 ranking. However, its 2026 position remains higher than its 43rd-place ranking in 2022.

Kazakhstan ahead of several major economies

Kazakhstan ranked ahead of several countries in the 2026 competitiveness ranking, including Spain in 39th place, Portugal in 40th, Poland in 41st, India in 44th, Italy in 45th, Türkiye in 57th and Argentina in 58th.

Singapore topped the ranking, followed by Hong Kong and Switzerland. Taiwan and the United Arab Emirates completed the top five. Mongolia, Botswana, Nigeria, Namibia and Venezuela occupied the lowest positions.

The ranking provides a comparative assessment of countries’ economic conditions, institutional and business environments and the infrastructure supporting their economies.

Earlier, Kazakhstan ranked first among Central Asian countries in the Legatum Prosperity Index 2026, placing 66th out of 161 countries globally.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Rybakina Makes History Twice, Tops WTA Prize Money Standings
World.content:
ASTANA — Elena Rybakina has added another distinction to a landmark season, topping the Women’s Tennis Association’s 2026 prize-money standings after becoming the first player representing Kazakhstan to reach the No. 1 singles ranking, according to the WTA.

Rybakina has earned over $10 million in prize money this season, according to WTA figures, putting her nearly $2.8 million ahead of second-placed Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus, with Czech Republic’s Linda Noskova in third.

The biggest boost came in New York, where Rybakina won her first U.S. Open title on Sept. 12, defeating two-time defending champion Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2. The victory earned her a record $5.5 million in prize money and 2,000 ranking points.

Rybakina officially became the PIF WTA World No. 1 on Sept. 14, becoming the 30th woman in WTA history to reach the top spot and the first man or woman from Kazakhstan to do so.

The achievement is especially significant for Rybakina because the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation played a decisive role in the early stages of her professional career. Speaking to the WTA after her U.S. Open victory, she recalled that she had been considering offers from U.S. universities when the federation noticed her at a tournament and backed her.

“Kazakhstan has given me so much. The opportunity to try myself in the professional tour, it was a big decision for me and my family. Somehow, the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation saw me on one of the tournaments where I had a good run. They believed in me, and a lot of other people in Kazakhstan believed in me and helped me on my way. I’m very grateful. It’s a history for the whole countr, and I just can’t wait to go there and celebrate with all the people who follow me, who love me, and most importantly, people who believed in me from the very beginning.” she said.

The 2026 season has been Rybakina’s most successful to date. She has won the Australian Open and U.S. Open, and reached the finals at Indian Wells and Toronto. She is the first singles player to qualify for the 2026 WTA Finals, where she will defend her title.

Rybakina’s rise also marks a broader milestone for Kazakhstan’s tennis development. The WTA noted that, as her career has progressed, more children across Kazakhstan have begun taking up the sport and attending new tennis facilities.

“I always say there are so many kids that are coming to the tennis facilities. They all want to play tennis, which is a great thing. I just want to celebrate such an achievement for the country all together,” she said.

World.title: EU to urge Syria to withdraw recognition of Georgia’s occupied regions
World.content:
Syria to withdraw recognition of Abkhazia

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that during talks with the Syrian leadership, the EU intends to raise the issue of Syria withdrawing its recognition of the independence of Georgia’s Russian-occupied territories — Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

This is stated in a letter in which von der Leyen responded to an appeal from Georgia’s Coalition for Change, an informal political group bringing together pro-Western liberal parties. The coalition currently includes Akhali, Girchi-More Freedom, Droa, the Republican Party and the Activists for the Future movement.

Syria recognised the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia on 29 May 2018, under Bashar al-Assad. At the same time, Syria announced that it was establishing diplomatic relations with both regions. Georgia responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Coalition leader Nika Gvaramia said at a briefing that the coalition had asked the European Commission president to make the withdrawal of recognition of Georgia’s and Ukraine’s occupied and annexed territories one of the key issues in talks with Syria.

According to Gvaramia, von der Leyen’s letter states that the EU remains committed to Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Gvaramia said this position is particularly important for Georgia because Syria needs European assistance. “Therefore, such pressure could play an important role in the decision to withdraw the recognition,” he said.

He also recalled that on 30 July, the government of Nauru officially withdrew its recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

Four UN member states currently recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia: Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

What the Coalition for Change said in its letter to Ursula von der Leyen

“For more than three decades, Abkhazia and so-called South Ossetia have been under Russia’s illegal occupation, while the decisions to recognise them adopted by the Assad regime directly undermine Georgia’s sovereignty,” the letter says.

The coalition believes that EU cooperation with Syria’s new government creates an opportunity to reverse these decisions and restore respect for Georgia’s internationally recognised borders.

The coalition said it is ready to assist the European Union in this process by providing information and helping establish contacts.
