World.title: Parents should 'urgently' discuss sexual choking with their children
World.content:
Sexual choking or strangulation is common among young people and following the recent death of a 16-year-old girl from Sydney, parents may be wondering how to talk to their children about the risks.

The girl is believed to have lost consciousness and had a seizure as a result of asphyxiation after allegedly being choked during consensual sexual intercourse.

Research from 2024 surveyed 4,702 young Australians aged 18 to 35 and found 57 per cent had been strangled during sex.

There is an "urgent" need for parents to discuss the risks of sexual strangulation with their children, says Vanessa Hamilton, a sexual health educator and author of Talking Sex: A Conversation Guide for Parents.

"This is such a serious issue. The average age of exposure to pornography is 13 years old — and as young as eight — in Australia.

"Our kids need us to help navigate that. They have a human right to accurate information about their bodies and respectful relationships."

Ms Hamilton says even younger children can be taught about protecting their necks in a non-sexual context.

What is sexual strangulation and what term should I use?

Sexual choking or strangulation is when pressure is applied to the neck to restrict air or blood flow during sex, explains Jackie McMillan, senior project officer at Women's Health NSW who worked on the sexual violence project It Left No Marks.

Warning after possible death from sexual choking Experts are calling for greater education on the risks of strangulation after the death of a Sydney teenage girl, which the ABC understands is related to a suspected sexual choking act.

People may also call it breath play, using a chokehold, being pinned, or suffocated.

Ms McMillan says sexual choking is a high-risk sexual activity and there is no safe way to engage in it.

Risks include serious injury, brain injury and death. There can also be legal consequences, even if the activity is consensual.

Medical experts and safety advocates prefer the more accurate term "strangulation," but colloquially it is referred to as "choking".

Ms McMillan says that "starting with the language of violence" can turn young people away.

"If you talk to young people about sexual strangulation, they think it's something they're not doing. They think strangulation is about violence, they think the term is stigmatising and not about sexual expression," Ms McMillan says.

Chanel Contos, founder and CEO of Teach Us Consent, says using the more recognisable term choking can be a way to open a dialogue, before explaining why strangulation is more accurate.

"Using the correct term helps convey the seriousness involved," she says.

'Providing information is not giving permission'

Chanel Contos founded Teach Us Consent to help young Australians practice affirmative consent and respectful relationships. (ABC News: Callum Flinn )

Young people want practical, honest information about sex, Ms Contos says.

"What the actual physical risks are, how to say no without being shamed for it, and how to raise boundaries with a partner before anything happens, rather than navigating it in the moment.

"Ultimately, the education they're asking for comes back to consent … as an ongoing and informed conversation."

Ms Hamilton says parents needn't worry that talking about sex will encourage their children to become sexually active.

"Providing information is not giving permission.

"The research shows the more information young people have, the less likely they are to go out and do it.

" When they understand the complexities of what is happening, they make better decisions. "

She says lessons about consent and body safety should begin in infancy, for example using the correct names for body parts and narrating nappy changes, and continue throughout a child's life.

What to say to children about sexual strangulation

Learning about strangulation can begin with young children in the context of play, Ms Hamilton says.

"You can say 'You never touch anybody's neck. Never prevent someone from breathing.'"

Ms McMillan says: "We talk about heads and necks being precious in football … we can talk about the neck being a delicate area."

Why teaching consent should start in infancy Narrating nappy changes is one way parents and caregivers can strengthen bonds and start lessons around body safety early.

As children age and have access to the internet, Ms Hamilton says parents can be more specific.

In the 2024 research referenced earlier, respondents said they found out about sexual strangulation most commonly in pornography (61 per cent), but also through movies, friends and social media.

"We should be talking about respectful, pleasurable partnerships, what it looks like to have a positive sexual encounter," Ms Hamilton says.

"What they are seeing in scripted pornography isn't an accurate view of what a pleasurable sexual encounter is."

Ms Contos says the most important starting point for older children is that "there's no safe way to engage in strangulation" and to explain the risks.

"Many young people report being strangled without any conversation or agreement at all, and even when someone believes they've consented, they're often unaware of just how serious the risks are, meaning their 'consent' is uninformed.

"It's also important to emphasise that saying no to strangulation doesn't make someone boring … there is nothing prudish about sex without violence."

Ms McMillan says some good opening questions for older children might be:

I hear some people are putting their hands around other people's necks during sex, what do know about that?

Is anything happening during sex or with your friends having sex that is worrying you? Or you'd like to know more about? We can find out together.

Is the conversation different for boys and girls?

Experts say it can be easier to talk to children about consent during mundane moments of the day, rather than having a formal "sit-down" talk. (Pexels: Nicola Barts)

Parents can discuss the gender expectations behind sexual strangulation, Ms Contos says, and unpack what messages that might send about women's and men's roles in relationships.

"Girls, who more frequently say they've been strangled without their consent, therefore need to understand their right to say 'no' to things they are uncomfortable with, even to people they may love or want acceptance from.

"Boys are more likely to absorb the message that initiating this is expected or even normal, and need to understand that this is not something they're supposed to be doing by default."

Ms Hamilton says we need to support boys to recognise harmful messages they receive online from the manosphere, for example.

" They are being given misinformation which is really unhelpful. "

Teaching kids about media literacy should start young, says Ms Hamilton.

"You turn on commercial radio and it's full of rubbish you can call out and encourage kids to think critically about."

Ms Contos says children are exposed to media presenting an unequal dynamic between men and women everywhere.

"Building that critical lens early means that when they do encounter pornography, they're already equipped to question what they're seeing rather than absorb it as normal."

Where and when to have these conversations

Ms Hamilton says parents should look for "teachable moments".

"Be ready to see the opportunities, such as when you hear something on the radio.

"Talking in the car is a great place as you are facing forward and not looking at each other."

For unexpected questions, Ms Hamilton recommends approaching with honesty.

"Say, 'Wow I didn't expect that question and I don't know how to answer. Give me a bit of time as it's an important one.' Or 'Let's look into that together.'"

Resources our experts recommend for parents include:

For parents who feel they have waited longer than they should have to talk about sex with their child, Ms Hamilton says to acknowledge that.

"Say things like, 'No-one spoke to me about this and I don't want this to be the case for you. I'm sorry I haven't brought this up already.'"

World.title: Renshaw reveals secret behind milestone ODI century
World.content:
Matt Renshaw admits he may not have posted his first ODI century had he opened the batting for Australia against Zimbabwe.

Batting at six, Renshaw starred for the tourists in Harare, making 109 off 94 deliveries, as Australia recorded a 59-run win in the first of three ODIs.

The ODI ton was his first for Australia across any format since his only Test century in 2017, when he opened the batting against Pakistan at the SCG.

He recently returned to the Test arena, after a three-year absence, and again opened the batting in Australia's innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Aussies defeat Zimbabwe Matt Renshaw plays a starring role with the bat, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

But he played down the batting order in his nine ODI matches prior to Harare.

Renshaw said avoiding the pressure of opening the batting helped him score his century.

"Higher up the order I [get] a bit giddy,'' Renshaw said.

"For me, my tempo when I come in the middle overs is just trying to hit the gaps, hit where the fielders aren't.

"With spin being a very big factor in that middle period … I see it as my strength. I really understood my role. It made it really simple for me."

Renshaw was named in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming series against South Africa.

Australia will face the Proteas in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

The next ODI against Zimbabwe will be played on Friday in Harare.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Democrats probe Russian-funded wedding parties for Donald Trump's son
World.content:
Democrats in the US Congress have launched an investigation into reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of President Donald Trump's son earlier this year.

The Democrats' move comes on the heels of an article revealing that the wedding festivities of Donald Trump Jr were funded by a wealthy Russian businessman with strong ties to President Vladimir Putin and the Russian government.

ProPublica reported that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association (IBA), paid for lavish wedding festivities in the Bahamas in May.

"Why is a Russian oligarch and friend of Vladimir Putin financially supporting the president's son?" US representative Robert Garcia wrote in a social media post on Tuesday, local time.

Umar Kremlev was honoured by Vladimir Putin for his services to boxing in April. (Reuters: Kristina Solovyova)

"What does Umar Kremlev expect in return for funding this three-day wedding in the Bahamas?"

Mr Garcia is the senior Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

He is expected to chair the panel if Democrats win a majority in the House of Representatives in November's midterm elections.

A representative for Mr Trump Jr declined to comment.

Bettina Anderson has revealed on social media Umar Kremlev had funded the post-wedding celebrations. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

His wife, Bettina Trump, said in an Instagram post on Monday, local time, Mr Kremlev was a friend who had extended an "extraordinarily generous wedding gift", stressing that Mr Kremlev had paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.

Mr Kremlev and the IBA did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday, local time.

The president, who did not attend his son's wedding, said in a statement that he did not know Mr Kremlev.

He added that the wedding controversy was "not a big deal".

US Attorney-General Todd Blanche also brushed aside the potential conflict of interest when asked about it, saying he would not investigate.

Loading...

"The president doesn't know who this person is," he said.

"I like that it's fun to talk about this issue and the rhetoric around it, but I think all the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it."

Mr Garcia and other leading House Democrats have already been gearing up for probes into Mr Trump, his family and ethics questions that have arisen since the start of the president's second term in January 2025.

Trump is not shy of collecting spoils The US president's most-recent filings indicate he pocketed more than $US2.2 billion last year through ventures ostensibly run by his family.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer called the wedding arrangement "so corrupt, so venal, so endangering our national security".

In a speech to the Senate, Senator Schumer added: "You're dealing with a Russian oligarch, not just a cousin who's giving you a gift."

"Sometimes a wedding gift is a bribe from a foreign autocrat," he said.

In the first year of his second presidential term, which began in January 2025, Mr Trump reported $US2.2 billion ($3.1 billion) in revenue, with more than half coming from cryptocurrency ventures.

In the previous year, his personal income was reported at $US622 million.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Ed Sheeran's support acts quit US tour after Macklemore dropped
World.content:
Four supporting acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour have abruptly quit in solidarity with rapper Macklemore, who has been dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.

Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, Danish band Lukas Graham, and US artist Finneas posted on Instagram that they were pulling out.

Rowe and Lukas Graham would have been replacements for Macklemore on Sheeran's remaining US dates, while Beoga had been performing several songs — including some the Irish folk band co-wrote — with Sheeran around the middle of each set.

Finneas is one of the acts to announce they are pulling out of The Loop tour. (AP: Jordan Strauss/Invision, File)

Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said on Instagram.

"I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."

Pressure mounts on Sheeran

The moves by his fellow artists put enormous pressure on Sheeran, who has tried to avoid politics and taking a side in the Gaza conflict, arguing that his fans do not come to his shows to hear politics.

Rowe and Beoga each cited their country's history in their statements explaining their decisions.

"We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be," Beoga said.

Aaron Rowe has pulled out of the tour, citing his support for Palestinians. (AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision, File)

Rowe called Sheeran a friend and said the British singer-songwriter changed his life.

"But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he said, adding that he could not "stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up".

Meanwhile, Lukas Graham, the band that had hits with Mama Said and 7 Years, expressed gratitude to Sheeran and called it "a difficult decision".

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, seemingly referring to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.

Emails seeking comment were sent to Sheeran and the tour's promoter, the Messina Touring Group.

Crisis started with Macklemore being dropped

Sheeran weighed in on Macklemore's removal after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments onstage during their tour, saying the promoters made the decision.

The British singer also said he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza.

Macklemore dropped from Sheeran tour Macklemore says he has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour over pro-Palestinian comments made on stage earlier this month.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote on Instagram on Tuesday, local time.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran's statement came a day after Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after saying "Free Palestine" while introducing his protest song Hind's Hall at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it is in no way criticism of you," he said during the concert.

Macklemore said on Instagram on Monday that New England Patriots owner and billionaire Mr Kraft had rallied support among some stadium owners and told Sheeran they would not allow him to perform at their venues if Macklemore stayed on the tour.

In a statement on Monday, Mr Kraft said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community".

Macklemore denies being antisemitic and says conflating antisemitism with criticism of Israel's actions aims to avoid Israeli accountability.

Mr Kraft's representatives did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about the other musical artists' actions.

Sheeran says 'I am not complicit'

A growing chorus of organisations and experts say Israel's wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide — an accusation Israel vehemently rejects.

Macklemore was scheduled to perform at eight of the 10 shows Sheeran has remaining on his stadium tour, which is scheduled to resume in Philadelphia on Saturday. Ahead are stops at Gillette Stadium, Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium and Indianapolis's Lucas Oil Stadium.

In his social media post, Sheeran said he "spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge", but that "the venue's and promoter's decision was final".

He wrote that he tried to use his music to "bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together" and that while he had personal views about "this devastating conflict", he chose not to speak publicly because people who came to his shows "do not expect a political forum".

"I am not complicit. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," Sheeran said.

" However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. "

AP/Reuters

World.title: It may be second in size only to Telstra. AI firm prepares for ASX listing
World.content:
AI data centre developer Firmus Technologies is courting investors in Asia and Australia ahead of a widely expected multi-billion-dollar share market float next month.

The company has been making headlines over its expansions and resulting community concerns, as well as through its partnerships.

Last week Firmus announced it had signed a multi-year deal with OpenAI for two new AI factory sites in Malaysia.

Firmus's AI factory in Singapore, which uses the company's technology to submerge its data clusters. (Supplied: Firmus)

At the same time, the company has been growing its presence in northern Tasmania with three data centre projects and a flurry of sports sponsorships, including with the Tasmania Devils AFL team.

One AI data centre is currently under construction in Launceston, where its parent company is headquartered, and another near George Town has council approval while a site at Wesley Vale is still awaiting approval.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff is shown around Firmus's Launceston facility by Mr Rosenfield and Mr Curtis. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Plans are also underway for projects in South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, Western Australia and the ACT.

Firmus already has significant operations in Singapore, and over the next 24 months, it says it hopes to have seven AI data centres across four countries.

Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The AI company and club say it's a natural pairing — but not all are convinced.

This narrative of aggressive expansion will stoke interest in its expected float on the Australian share market next month.

Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in an initial public offering (IPO), which could value the company at more than $50 billion, depending on what proportion of the company is sold.

If that pans out, it could make Firmus the second-largest float in Australian history, after the federal government raised $14 billion by selling a third of Telstra three decades ago, valuing the entire company at $42 billion.

Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis have sought to allay public concerns about the amount of energy and water the data centres would require. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Based on its share price yesterday, Telstra had a market value of $53 billion.

An important caveat for many of the figures being touted in the financial press for Firmus's float are that they are based on conjecture and hype.

The company's public offer document, the prospectus that potential investors will review, has yet to be lodged with the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).

Firmus Technologies has plans for data centres across Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The valuation reports are based partly on an invitation for a "roadshow" in Asian and Australian capitals sent out to potential investors by investment banks handling the float for Firmus.

The roadshow will help determine how much demand there is for stock, based on forecast earnings.

A spokesperson for Firmus declined to comment on the likely size of the capital raising, or how much of the company might be sold, which will depend on the demand.

'Mum and dad investors' also likely for IPO, expert says

Sam Baker, private wealth adviser at Shadforth Financial Group, told the ABC it was widely known Firmus had been looking to debut this year on the ASX.

"It now appears as if the company is fronting investors both in Asia, and soon to be Australia, as a preamble to looking to do an initial public offering of up to $7 billion," Mr Baker said.

"They're telling the story of the business, providing details, which will largely be provided in any prospectus for the initial public offering.

" But it's about sort of gauging interest as to what or whether investors would be interested and at what price they would be potentially prepared to pay for any shares in an initial public offering. "

The data centre under construction at St Leonards, Launceston. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Mr Baker said investors in Australia and overseas would likely be interested.

"In an initial public offering, they tend to have cornerstone or institutional investors, but I would expect a raising of this size will also be looking to attract retail, or mum and dad, investors," he said.

Mr Baker said while IPOs could be used for the founders to "cash out", it seemed Firmus was raising funds to support the rollout of its AI data centres across Australia and South-East Asia.

From Bitcoin to AI

Firmus's most advanced project is at St Leonards in Launceston, and it has approval for another at Long Reach, near George Town, in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone.

The company is seeking approval for another at Wesley Vale in Tasmania's north-west.

A visualisation of the Firmus AI data centre planned near George Town, in northern Tasmania. (Supplied)

Firmus has struggled to gain a social licence in Tasmania, but Mr Baker did not believe that would necessarily impact the IPO.

"Broader institutional investors are mainly focused on getting a return," he said.

" Whether or not there is some resistance across the retail shareholders, that will remain to be seen. "

Firmus began as a bitcoin miner in 2019, subsequently pivoting to data centre development.

Its co-CEO Oliver Curtis was sentenced to two years' jail in 2016 for conspiring to commit insider trading.

The trial heard how he shared in $1.4 million of illegal profits from insider trading using confidential information between May 2007 and June 2008.

Firmus co-CEO Oliver Curtis with his wife Roxy Jacenko. (Instagram: Roxyjacenko)

In October 2025, Mr Curtis was asked about his reflections on the ordeal and whether Tasmanians could trust Firmus.

"The experience of the past presents an opportunity for the future," he told ABC Radio Hobart at the time.

"It's all about resilience, it's all about how you get back on the horse, and it's all about basically making sure that you are completing what you believe you need to complete.

"For me, this is about more than an individual; this is about a company.

"I'm so fortunate we have a hugely amazing, talented team around us — and that's the story."

World.title: Kash Patel grilled for nearly five hours by US Senate
World.content:
FBI director Kash Patel has been grilled by the US Senate for nearly five hours over his controversial management of the agency, including the ousting of experienced agents.

Mr Patel's time at the FBI has been marred by his firing of veteran employees with little explanation.

Appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Mr Patel defended his tenure, saying the US murder rate had fallen to a 20-year low, according to FBI data.

Here are the main takeaways.

Patel defends Epstein files rollout

Mr Patel defended FBI investigators who worked on the Epstein files release, as part of the Congress-backed Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Survivors of the notorious sex offender said the FBI failed to investigate Jeffrey Epstein in 1996 when the agency was notified of the first allegations.

More than 30 of Epstein's victims have now brought forward a lawsuit against the FBI, despite attempts by the Trump administration to dismiss the case.

With a unanimous Maxwell vote, the US Senate issues a warning to Trump The bipartisan vote is non-binding, but it reveals the sentiment surrounding Jeffrey Epstein within Donald Trump's own party. Here's how.

They've also criticised the administration for publishing unredacted personal information in the released files.

Mr Patel told the hearing that the FBI had complied with the Transparency Act and "produced three and a half million pages of documents for the first time ever".

"We've also repeatedly stated if there's new information, we want everyone to come forward so that we can analyse that information as to what is and isn't remaining," he said.

Probe into bestiality hiring change

One of the stranger moments was when Mr Patel confirmed the FBI had quietly lifted restrictions on hiring applicants who were victims of bestiality in their childhood.

Similar changes were also made to those who had previously participated in prostitution.

Mr Patel denied the changes reflected a lowering of employment standards and insisted these were designed to prevent victims who had been forced to engage in that conduct from being automatically disqualified.

"We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked," he said.

"We did not want to make it an automatic disqualification for the FBI to consider you if you were a victim of these awful, heinous acts."

Loading...

The questioning spanned partisan lines, with Republican senator John Kennedy of Louisiana grilling Mr Patel about the rationale for a change the FBI director said subordinates proposed to him.

"When you saw bestiality, I say this with respect: The person who recommended it, why didn't you just say what planet did you parachute in from?" Senator Kennedy asked.

Mr Patel later added that previous regulations disqualified "any individual who participated on either side of it".

"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Senator Kennedy probed further. "So you disqualified the animal?"

"We have great canines, but we're not going to disqualify them," Mr Patel said, laughing.

Patel rallies against 'weaponised FBI', amid reported firings

The main reason for the hearing was reports that Mr Patel had been gutting the ranks of longstanding FBI staff.

Connecticut Democrat Richard Blumenthal pressed Mr Patel, noting the agents had participated in an FBI investigation into Mr Trump's retention of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.

Kash Patel was probed on his personal expenses. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"Do you think firing the president's political opponents is more important than retaining the decades of experience and expertise monitoring intelligence threats from Iran?" Mr Blumenthal asked.

"I think what's most important is not to have a weaponised FBI, and I will endeavour every single day to make sure we have no one there who is doing that," Mr Patel said.

He later suggested that the scope of firings had been overblown, saying many agents had retired.

Mr Patel also later refused to pledge the FBI wouldn't interfere in midterm elections.

"I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies," he added.

Heated questioning over Olympics partying, magazine lawsuit

Mr Patel was probed on his personal expenses, including partying with the US hockey team as they celebrated their Winter Olympics win in Italy.

Trump seems to mock US women's hockey team while congratulating men on gold After the US men's hockey team won gold at the Olympics, Trump's locker-room joke about the women's team sparks backlash online.

"What you'll never understand is the players, who are my friends, invited me to the locker room," the FBI director said.

"What you'll never understand is that during that trip, where 300,000 Americans went to Italy to participate in the games and watch them, not a single security incident occurred."

Mr Patel also defended his decision to file a defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic after it printed a story alleging he had a drinking problem that had interfered with his ability to do his job.

"As a personal private citizen, I am allowed to participate in my own defence, especially when there's a smear campaign," he said, before becoming heated.

"Everyone sees you for the complete and total fraud you are," Mr Patel told Senator Peter Welch, who asked whether FBI resources had been used to investigate The Atlantic's journalist.

World.title: Historic outback pub hits the market as restoration costs soar
World.content:
A heritage-listed hotel in Western Australia's Goldfields, infamous for its connection to the murders of two police officers a century ago, has hit the market with an asking price of more than $1 million.

It is the second time the Cornwall Hotel in Boulder has been listed for sale in the past decade, suggesting the overheated construction market and onerous heritage obligations may be turning off potential buyers.

The two-storey hotel was built in 1898, just five years after the discovery of gold at Kalgoorlie.

It takes its name from the 19th-Century Cornish miners who flooded into WA during the gold rush and built the pub from locally quarried stone.

The Cornwall Hotel received $992,090 from the WA government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund, but structural repairs did not begin until 2016. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Real estate agent James Brennan described the nine-bedroom hotel as a unique piece of Goldfields history, but conceded the interior "needs a lot of love".

He said a mining company needing workers' accommodation could be a potential buyer, as the city faced ongoing accommodation shortages.

"A property like this, it needs the right owner, someone who can bring it back to its former glory," he said.

"It really is hard to put a price on that history, and obviously it's a beautiful building … heritage does scare people at times, but there's definitely been a lot of interest."

The Cornwall Hotel in Boulder circa 1926. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

Pub's famous link to murders

The Cornwall Hotel's most famous former licensee was Evan Clarke, who turned king's evidence following the brutal murders of detectives Inspector John Walsh and Sergeant Alexander Pitman, who were after gold thieves, in 1926.

It was rumoured that following the murders, the bodies were taken to the hotel where they were dismembered before being set alight and thrown down disused mineshafts.

Detective Inspector John Walsh (left) and Detective Sergeant Alexander Pitman were on the trail of gold thieves when they were murdered. (Facebook: WA Police Historical Society)

The family of Jack Osmetti, a well-known local sportsman who ran the pub for around 50 years, bought it in 1927.

The hotel was badly damaged by fire during Kalgoorlie's 1934 race riots and again by a magnitude-5 earthquake in 2010, but has been extensively repaired.

Negotiations with insurers resulted in the building being propped up and fenced off for four years, until matters were finally settled in 2014.

The owners then applied for and received $992,090 from the state government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund, but structural repairs did not begin until 2016.

Stonemason's old watering hole

In the era when the Cornwall Hotel was built, stonemasons constructed enduring public and commercial buildings by combining cheap, highly skilled manual labour with traditional lime mortars and hand-dressed masonry.

Today, retired Kalgoorlie stonemason Ken Ball reckoned his 55-year occupation was a "dying trade" and that the demise of historic buildings was a sign of the times.

Ken Ball (left) and Eastern Goldfields Historical Society member Arthur Ward with a photograph of the Cornwall Hotel after the 1934 race riots. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"I've got a lot of good memories here," he said, standing outside the Cornwall Hotel.

"I did a lot of work at the old Boulder cemetery, so I would often stop in for a drink on the way home … obviously not since the earthquake, though.

"It's a shame to see beautiful old buildings like this wasting away, and you'd love to see them get a new lease on life, but finding tradesmen is hard enough, let alone heritage-qualified tradesmen."

Heritage projects 'astronomically harder'

The City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder offers grants of up to $50,000 to private owners of heritage-listed buildings, but uptake has been low in recent years.

While WA's shortage of skilled tradies is well documented, Kalgoorlie builder Tim Matthew said heritage projects were "astronomically harder" and typically required a specialised heritage architect.

"Even if you had an infinite budget, most builders I know don't have the time to spend weeks and weeks researching the heritage requirements," he said.

"And honestly, some of these grants don't scratch the surface to do anything meaningful."

Tim Matthew outside the heritage-listed Lord Forrest site, which reopened as a public park in 2017. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Matthew said a recent heritage project he consulted on was an historic WA pub seeking a roof replacement, which would involve replacing karri timber used for structural beams in the roof.

But karri timber has become much more expensive and harder to source since the WA government banned commercial native forest logging.

"Heritage projects are typically 100 per cent like-for-like replacement … if you use the wrong bolt that's a problem," he said.

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Heritage must find relevancy

Eastern Goldfields Historical Society life member Scott Wilson said it was important heritage buildings in Kalgoorlie-Boulder were preserved for future generations, but they needed to remain functional as well.

"We would support anyone going down the road of heritage grants because it is an arduous process," he said.

"Whether that is a mining company renovating it for workforce accommodation, or someone turning it back into a pub, it needs to stay relevant."

That relevancy could come down to simple dollars and cents and what is possible in the current market.

A spokesperson for Heritage Minister Simone McGurk said more than $27 million had been awarded to nearly 930 projects since 1997, and a "high number" of development applications continued to be received.

World.title: Fishers fund review in last-ditch effort to overturn gillnet ban
World.content:
Commercial fishers in north Queensland are hoping a new report will convince the state and federal governments to reverse a planned ban on gillnets within the Great Barrier Reef.

Operators in the fishing zone have commissioned a report they say shows their netting practices are likely to pass international sustainability standards.

Temporary licences were introduced in 2024 to allow commercial fishers to continue using gillnets ahead of the planned phase-out in 2027.

The Queensland Seafood Industry Association, working with the operators, would not release the full report to the ABC, saying it was "commercial in confidence".

It did, however, release a summary of findings, which the ABC verified as being accurate by the report's authors, sustainable seafood consultants FishListic.

Townsville commercial fisher Nathan Rynn says results from the report are promising. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Fisher Nathan Rynn said the association hoped to use the report to obtain a Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) "blue tick" on their boats and products to show the fishery was sustainable.

"I'm sort of positive about the net fishery moving forward, albeit the legislation issues," Mr Rynn said.

"I think we can overcome that and have the best-managed fishery on the planet … but we'll actually have the accreditation behind it, possibly."

Reef impact under review

According to the released section of the report, FishListic said it found the fishery would meet half of the MSC's standards without any conditions imposed and could pass others after further consultation.

The company reviewed the ecological risk of four threatened species that had interactions with the large mesh nets.

Great hammerhead sharks, scalloped hammerhead sharks, green sawfish and hawksbill turtles all returned a medium risk of being impacted by the nets, down from high risk under the current Queensland government assessment.

Several dolphin, marine turtle, and shark species listed as high risk under the 2021 study were not analysed in the FishListic report.

The company did not conduct site inspections but used public data, along with camera footage and data logs provided by fishers, to assess the MSC criteria.

Blue tick for consumers

The Queensland Seafood Industry Association's David Bobberman said the east coast inshore fishery produced between 200 and 300 tonnes of seafood annually.

Mr Bobberman said consultation and further research projects would likely be required before the fishery could receive a blue tick and "certified sustainable seafood" labelling.

"To be clear, it's not MSC-certified at the moment, but it's been pre-assessed, and the pre-assessor has given them a pass mark," he said.

Gillnets are anchored to the ocean floor and held vertically in the water. (Flickr: Virginia Sea Grant)

The MSC uses third-party auditors to conduct in-person reviews of fishing practices against international standards, following a pre-assessment.

Criteria include the sustainability of fish stocks, protection of marine species and habitat, and management strategy.

Mr Bobberman said the fishery impact had been greatly reduced since 2024 with fewer operators, and gillnetters now trained under a sustainable fishing program.

"We've gone from over 200 available licences to gillnet within the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park to 25," he said.

Mr Bobberman said he did not consider any alternative gear as viable replacements, with line fishing too limited, and tunnel nets "too selective" in when and where they could be used.

Wild barramundi and king threadfin salmon are target species for gillnet operators. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Minister investigating options

The office of Queensland Minister for Primary Industries Tony Perrett said in a statement it would "welcome" the opportunity to conduct a "robust review" of the report, but it was waiting to receive the full document.

It said Mr Perrett was investigating options available to Queensland that would comply with federal government bans.

However, the Federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said the phase-out of gillnets was being led by the Queensland government.

Fishers 'making a real effort'

Leslie Roberson, a researcher at the University of Queensland, said governments should be taking notice of MSC certifications.

"I think it does mean something to consumers. To the government, I think it should mean something," Dr Roberson said.

"The fishery has paid for an independent assessment of themselves so, obviously, people are going to have questions of whether that's biased.

"[So,] they've taken steps to get that reviewed [by MSC auditors]. They are making a real effort."

Leslie Roberson has worked with other fisheries hoping to obtain MSC certification. (Supplied: Leslie Roberson)

Dr Roberson said gillnetting had a bad reputation partly stemming from a lack of data.

She said information about protected species interactions was previously filled out by fishers without a "third party" to check them.

East coast inshore fishery operators have been required to use onboard cameras and log interactions with threatened species since February 2024.

Queensland government data shows 188 fatal interactions with endangered scalloped hammerhead sharks and seven narrow sawfish deaths in that time.

No other threatened species deaths were reported.

World.title: Redundant at 69: retirement without a plan
World.content:
Sponsored MoneySuper & retirementAMP Redundant at 69: retirement without a plan Sponsored by AMP Franki Hobson September 16, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most people downsize when they retire. Helen* went the other way, to nine acres in regional NSW, where her husband slashes the paddocks by tractor and she grows the vegetables she donates to a community centre. “I’m retired. I’ve got all the time in the world,” says the 71-year-old, laughing. But the date that time began was never hers to pick. Two years ago, after roughly 30 years with the same construction company, Helen returned from an overseas family funeral to a meeting with her manager. Her office role had been made redundant. She was 69. “It didn’t worry me at the time,” she says. “I thought, no, that’s good.” The fine print stung more: her contract recognised only 10 of her 30 years, and past retirement age the payout was taxed harder. After tax, including her long service leave, it came to about $30,000. Overcoming financial fear allows retirees to enjoy the simple pleasures. iStock The fear that kept her working



For years, Helen’s retirement remained a moving target. She originally planned to stop working at 55, but financial anxiety kept her working. Rather than quitting cold turkey, she cut back to four days, then three. “I didn’t want to jump straight from five days to zero,” she says. Remote work through COVID pushed the finish line even further back — until it was finally moved for her. It happens more often than people expect, says AMP general manager of guidance and advice Andrea Boss. “Retirement doesn’t always happen on your timetable,” she says. “Health challenges, caring responsibilities, redundancy or changing family circumstances can bring it forward unexpectedly.” The fear had deep roots. She salary sacrificed hard through her 50s, then watched the global financial crisis knock her balance. “That scared the hell out of me,” she says. The couple moved their super into cash, and left it there. “If I’d left it where it was, I’d probably have half a million sitting in super, not 250 thousand.” Her fix, in hindsight: “Just leave the super as it was and let it do its bit.” The instinct is common, and costly, says AMP chief investment officer Anna Shelley. “Cash is obviously stable, but over a long retirement its buying power is eroded by inflation,” she says. “A common approach is to spread money across different types of investments and keep enough in cash or other defensive assets for nearer-term expenses.” Income from multiple angles



No single payment replaced Helen’s salary. The household runs on a combination: her super, drawn as a lump sum when needed; a part Government Age Pension of about $400 a fortnight each; savings and her husband’s two remaining days a week working. Helen has about $250,000 left in super, a paid-off home, and a family that lives long: one of her sisters is 97. “If I live to 97, we’re going to run out of money,” she says. “But I assume we’re not going to live here on nine acres till I’m 97 either.” It’s a common concern; 58 per cent of Australians worry about running out of money in retirement, according to AMP’s 2026 Retirement Confidence Pulse. What they spend is shaped by who comes after. They have an adult child with ongoing support needs, and the couple’s planning considers him and their other children. “If it was just us, we could live quite comfortably and die with no money left, and that would be fine,” Helen says. “But I want to leave some money to my kids.” 10,000 days, calmer Retirement can now stretch 10,000 days or more, and Helen is filling hers deliberately: volunteering weekly at a community centre serving three-course meals for $10, and driving three and a half hours to watch her grandchildren play footy. The worries of her 50s have not eventuated. “I’m certainly calmer. There’s no pressure. If I didn’t do something today, it doesn’t matter.”



Her advice, when her daughter asks? “Salary sacrifice if you can afford to. And pay your house off.” While absolute certainty never arrived, confidence did. According to Ben Hillier, AMP’s director of retirement, spending your super isn’t a failure to protect your nest egg; it’s fulfilling its purpose. You built those savings specifically to fund this stage of life, so spending them means the plan is working. To understand how to turn your fears into retirement confidence, visit AMP Super’s Retire the Fear hub at amp.com.au/retirethefear *Names and some identifying details have been changed at the family’s request. This information is general in nature and does not constitute financial product advice. Readers should consider their own circumstances and seek independent professional advice.

World.title: Revealed: The secret backroom dealings behind $1.1bn lotto licence deal
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian budget Revealed: The secret backroom dealings behind $1.1bn lotto licence deal Kieran Rooney September 16, 2026 — 11:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A secret 40-year-extension of Victoria’s lotto licence was in the works for almost three years before it was announced, with The Lottery Corporation convincing the government it should be allowed to pay a premium in return for shutting out competitors for decades. In a new report released on Wednesday, the auditor-general raised concerns about the lack of transparency surrounding the deal and said there was uncertainty over whether taxpayers could have benefited from a bigger windfall through a competitive process. The Auditor-General reviewed the state’s decision to extend the lotto licence by 40 years. But the report did not identify any probity concerns and said the government sought to deliver value for Victorians when it chose to conduct “exclusive bilateral negotiations” with The Lottery Corporation, the existing operator, and collect $1.145 billion for the extension. TLC announced the shock 40-year deal on May 5 – the day the Victorian budget was released – through an announcement to the stock market. The government was immediately criticised for using the agreement to prop up the budget’s bottom line.



Auditor-General Andrew Greaves found the government believed that it could secure more money this way because TLC was willing to pay significantly more to extend its licence without a competitive process, and to secure a commitment that lotto taxes would not be raised without providing compensation. Related Article Updated

Victorian budget Lotto windfall boosts state budget amid warnings about election-year spending splurge A commercial adviser appointed to the process valued the licence at about $1.372 billion, which was $227 million less than finally collected, however the auditor-general cautioned that the higher figure was a “theoretical value” and not a like-for-like comparison to a price set by negotiation. The report cited internal departmental analysis that said a competitive process was “unlikely to deliver a better outcome than bilateral negotiations”, and that continuing with the current operator would minimise disruption to future tax income. Greaves did not dispute this but said it was impossible to say which method could have produced a higher payment because the price was not tested on an open market.



“We saw evidence that agencies actively assessed and negotiated proposals advanced by TLC. However, those mechanisms could not replicate the price discovery benefits of a competitive process,” he said. “As a result, while agencies sought to maximise value within a bilateral framework, it is not possible to know with certainty whether a higher premium could have been achieved under an alternative approach.” Gaming Minister Enver Erdogan said the report made clear the process to extend the licence was conducted properly. Justin McManus Wednesday’s report outlined the full timeline of events behind the deal for the first time, revealing that TLC initially approached the government in November 2023 with a proposal to pay an upfront premium in return for a 20 to 40-year extension. The government then authorised Treasury to explore reforms to the current licence, which at the time only allowed for an extension of one year.



Victorian Auditor-General Andrew Greaves. Victoria Auditor-General’s Office These discussions culminated in June 2025, almost a year before the deal was announced, when the government passed laws that paved the way for the multi-decade deal. Alongside this work, government agencies spent 2024 gauging market interest in the lottery licence and developing a negotiation strategy. A commercial adviser was appointed, and they argued TLC was likely to pay more for the licence for a range of reasons, including the fact that it was part of a national bloc of lottery corporations that already worked together. By November, the government decided to proceed with exclusive negotiations, but set a reserve price that would act as a minimum payment. If TLC could not match this floor price, they would revert to a traditional competitive process, with the intention that holding exclusive negotiations were guaranteed to deliver better value.



The auditor-general revealed that TLC was not only willing to pay this reserve price to avoid an open process, but forked out more cash to the state in return for an agreement on lottery taxes. The government promised it would compensate the company if it increased lottery taxes above current levels. Related Article Victorian Parliament Lotto extension was in the works months before laws allowed it That deal “resulted in a material increase to the premium TLC paid for the licence”, according to the report. Greaves did not find any significant integrity issues, but said the government’s approach meant the public had limited visibility over key decisions and the reasons behind them. Departmental chiefs told the auditor-general the secrecy was required for the negotiations to ensure the best value for money. Greaves said these were credible arguments, but that agencies needed to balance these objectives by making sure parliament and the public knew what the government was doing and why they were doing it.



The report recommended Treasury develop new rules that assessed how and when major commercial decisions could be disclosed to the public, which the department accepted in principle. Related Article Victorian budget Melbourne’s cooling housing market is turning into a billion-dollar budget crisis When the deal came to light in May, it sparked criticism from the state opposition, competitors and anti-gambling advocates because of its length and the fact that there was no public tender process. Speaking before the report was tabled on Tuesday, Premier Ben Carroll said he was confident that Gaming Minister Enver Erdogan had overseen the negotiation process correctly. An opposition spokesperson criticised the secretive nature of the negotiations, revealed in a report which came a month after the auditor-general exposed a previously undisclosed levy on public transport fares.

World.title: Renshaw’s maiden ODI century was great. But can he fire in Tests against South Africa when it counts?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Renshaw’s maiden ODI century was great. But can he fire in Tests against South Africa when it counts? Tom Decent Updated September 16, 2026 — 11:40am ,first published September 16, 2026 — 2:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Renshaw’s dad is trying to sell a book that he has written for cricket coaches. “He’s the biggest cricket nuffy I know,” Renshaw wrote on Instagram this week. “It covers all the principles and games that we did when I was a kid and still do now [at] training.” There is no mention on the cover – or the back – that Ian Renshaw is indeed the father of an incumbent Australian cricketer. But as far as timing goes, his son’s first international century in nearly a decade on Tuesday in Zimbabwe won’t do sales any harm.



Renshaw’s 109 from 94 balls at the Harare Sports Club, which helped Australia to a 59-run victory over Zimbabwe in the opening ODI of the series, came at No.6 against a modest attack and with the visitors wobbling at 4-107 in the 18th over. After bringing up his 50 from 55 balls, Renshaw put his foot down. An array of powerful aerial shots down the ground carried him to his maiden ODI hundred 31 balls later and Australia to 8-294. Australia’s batsman Matt Renshaw celebrates his century during the first ODI against Zimbabwe. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Nathan Ellis (5-31) then helped bowl Zimbabwe out for 235 in 45.1 overs before Renshaw’s day out took another unlikely turn as he snared the wicket of Brendan Taylor with a gentle off-spinner that was scooped to long-on. Of all the international centuries a cricketer dreams of making, one against Zimbabwe in an irrelevant ODI is nowhere near the top of the list.



But for Renshaw, ripping off an Australian helmet and raising his bat again carried plenty of symbolism. “I probably didn’t think I was going to play one-day cricket,” Renshaw said. “Batting at six, you’re probably not expecting to get a hundred. If you do, it’s probably slogging. “I was just playing my game. I know I play my best when I am nice and relaxed.” Almost a decade after announcing himself as one of Australian cricket’s brightest prospects, Renshaw is preparing for another crack at the toughest format of the game that he is yet to conquer. Matthew Renshaw at the Gabba in Brisbane after being named in the Australian Test team in 2016. Getty Images



The big question is whether he can kick on and churn out big runs as Australia’s opener in a three-Test series against South Africa, starting on October 9 in Durban. Jake Weatherald’s axing last month, after Australia’s dismal Test defeat to Bangladesh in Darwin, has handed Renshaw the keys at the top of the order against the same nation he made his international debut against 10 years ago in Adelaide. Later that summer, as a 20-year-old, Renshaw cracked 184 against Pakistan at the SCG. Australia appeared to have found its next long-term opener, a towering Queensland left-hander in the mould of Matthew Hayden. Later that year, Renshaw was dropped.



He was parachuted back into Australia’s XI in Johannesburg in 2018 for the Test immediately after the Sandpapergate scandal and has been in and out since. His past 10 Test innings - 5, 4, 22, 8, 5, 5*, 0, 2, 2 and 8 - read more like lottery numbers than the returns of a player about to open the batting for Australia in such a crucial series. Now 30, Renshaw is a far more rounded player than the youngster who was given a baggy green. His white-ball game, in particular, has come on enormously, culminating in ODI and T20 international debuts since October last year. But Test cricket remains the unfinished business.



Facing Zimbabwean spinners at both ends through the middle overs of an ODI is considerably different to seeing off a red ball in South Africa against fast bowler Marco Jansen and potentially Kagiso Rabada, pending his recovery from a hamstring injury. “It’s obviously a very different role,” Renshaw said of his opening duties. “It’s something I am trying to prepare for as well as I can. Mindset is the biggest thing. It’s about trying to get as much rhythm as you can before that Test series.” Australia had three Test representatives in their opening ODI: Renshaw, Travis Head (4) and Alex Carey (27). For the fourth innings in a row, including his three Test knocks against Bangladesh, Head chopped a ball back onto his stumps. It is becoming a bizarre trend for one of Australia’s most destructive batters. Loading



Josh Hazlewood was managed, while Cricket Australia said Cameron Green was not selected due to shoulder soreness. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket ‘Dire consequences’: BBL sell-off slammed amid fears for grassroots cricket Australia have two more ODIs against Zimbabwe and three against South Africa before a two-day warm-up match ahead of the Test series. Renshaw said he would begin facing red balls in the nets soon. But when he walks out to open the batting in Durban, he will have played one first-class match in the previous six months. David Warner’s 135 in Cape Town in 2014 remains the last Test century on South African soil by an Australian opener.



A decade after his own Test career began with such promise, you suspect Renshaw would happily trade any number of white-ball runs to be the man who breaks that drought. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Netflix’s ‘queen of screens’ hid a secret about her past. When it came to light, she froze
World.content:
Bela Bajaria, one of the most powerful people in Hollywood, on racism, being fired and why she’s embracing an aspect of her past she once concealed.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I gingerly broach the topic of Bela Bajaria’s time at Universal Television, she brushes aside my polite euphemisms and gets to the point. “Which part of [my time at] Universal?” asks Bajaria, whose role as Netflix’s global chief content officer makes her one of the most powerful people in Hollywood. “The getting fired part?” In 2011, Bajaria joined the television studio arm of NBC, then known as Universal Media Studios, which had been gutted by a previous regime. Her success in rebuilding it resulted in her promotion to president in 2015. But her success in creating and selling programs to rival platforms – also a key part of her job – became a sticking point. Bajaria started her career as an assistant at CBS in the mid-1990s. Today, she is one of the most powerful people in Hollywood. Joe Armao Among the hit series Bajaria helped bring to fruition at Universal are The Mindy Project and Brooklyn Nine-Nine for Fox, and Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt and Master of None for Netflix. “I always felt the decisions I made were best for the creator and best for the studio,” says Bajaria, in an exclusive interview with this masthead. “When you are the studio to a sister network and you sell outside to other places – and if those shows are successful – it causes tension.” Things came to a head in 2016, when Bajaria was sacked. At the time, it made no sense. After all, she’d created a slew of hit shows, treated people fairly and made what she believed to be the right decisions for the business. “Then you realise that it’s not so simple,” she says. “There are definitely tensions and personality clashes and lots of other things that happen.”



Cliches about learning from failure, she adds, “look nice stitched onto a pillow”. But they do not preclude the self-doubt that comes with being dismissed from a high-profile dream job. Twelve-hour roasted lamb shoulder served with crispy briwats, smoked eggplant, sticky lamb fat and lemony za’atar jus. Joe Armao “The reason I talk about the firing part is that some people look at me and my job now and go, ‘Oh, it’s all just great,’” Bajaria says. “But there were these big, huge lessons along the way. I definitely learned more from getting fired than I learned at any other time professionally. It gives you a sense of perspective about who you are and what you’re made of.” During her subsequent “summer of soul-searching”, Bajaria had a conversation with Ted Sarandos, now the co-chief executive of Netflix with Greg Peters. He told her not to take another job without speaking to him first. Soon, he offered her a role as head of licensing, co-productions and unscripted content. Turkish beef dumplings, braised beef shin, burnt butter with urfa pepper and smoked yoghurt. Joe Armao “I’ve worked in scripted TV for 20 years,” she told him. “You’re offering me a job, but I have no experience in any of those things.” “I just hire smart people,” Sarandos replied. “You’ll figure it out.”



It’s safe to say that Bajaria impressed her new boss: in 2023, she succeeded Sarandos as Netflix’s global chief content officer. According to the London Telegraph, she is “the woman who decides what the world is watching on TV”, while Forbes magazine labelled her “Netflix’s Queen Of Screens”. Bajaria and I are ensconced in a leather-upholstered booth at Maha, a moody, subterranean restaurant described by The Age Good Food Guide as Melbourne’s “gilded tiger of Middle Eastern fine dining”. We share several dishes including Turkish beef dumplings; roast zucchini and burnt red peppers; steamed warrigal greens with an olive oil and mustard dressing; and house flatbread with sumac butter and smoked hummus. The highlight is the slow-cooked lamb shoulder marinated in garlic sumac and cumin, so tender that it falls apart as we spoon it onto our plates. Roast zucchini and burnt red peppers, harissa and almond tarator. Joe Armao Despite an impressive drinks menu, we opt for water – in part because Bajaria is on a flying visit to Australia, to promote the first American National Football League regular season game played in this country. The match between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers drew 100,000 fans to the MCG, many of whom travelled from the United States. It was streamed live on Netflix and ESPN, and broadcast on Channel Seven. ‘When someone brought it up in an interview, I felt like some deep, dark secret was out.’ Bela Bajaria For Netflix, it marks a further dissolution of the once-solid boundaries between broadcast television and subscription video on demand. When the streaming giant launched in Australia in 2015, it trumpeted its high-end, ad-free original programming (House of Cards, Orange Is the New Black, BoJack Horseman) as its point of difference. Meanwhile, free-to-air networks played to their strengths: live sport, news and local programming. These days, it’s harder to tell the difference. Netflix now offers discounted subscriptions to viewers willing to watch ads, while investing heavily in reality shows, sport and other live events. In response, Australian broadcasters have beefed up their on-demand platforms. Two months before Netflix’s debut, Nine launched Stan, a direct rival that invests heavily in premium Australian programming. (Nine is the owner of this masthead.)



Related Article Streaming Next at Netflix: Co-CEO Greg Peters on live sport, AI and talking to your telly Globally, Netflix has more than 325 million subscribers, although household account sharing means its total number of users is significantly higher. While the company intends to increase its subscriber base, it can no longer rely on the rapid rate of growth it enjoyed in its early days – a situation made trickier by an international cost-of-living crisis. This has prompted Netflix to seek revenue from other sources, such as games, short-form video and podcasts (all of which are more amenable to daytime use, allowing Netflix to move beyond its reputation as evening-based entertainment). With all this in mind, would Netflix consider making a play for major Australian sports such as the NRL or AFL? Bajaria is not ruling it out. “I love that people in Australia love sports so much,” she says, pointing out that the immense popularity of World Baseball Classic in Japan – the only country in which Netflix has the rights to the tournament – could provide a model for other markets. “If there was [a sport] in Australia that was ‘right-sized’ in that way, we’re always going to look at it. It doesn’t have to be global.” Much has been written about Bajaria during her 30-year career. But there was one element of her past she vowed to conceal: her stint as a beauty pageant queen. Having already won Miss India LA and Miss India USA, she was crowned Miss India Worldwide in 1991. “I hid it very deeply because I thought there would always be misconceptions about my work ethic, drive, ambition and intellect,” she explains. “When someone brought it up in an interview, I felt like some deep, dark secret was out.”



She re-enacts the wide-eyed, frozen-in-fear expression that overcame her during that conversation. But as her career progressed – and she continued to defy the lazy stereotypes about pageant winners – she embraced her Miss India accomplishments. Related Article Streaming ‘It’s like Squid Game’: Why Netflix parted ways with content chief Que Minh Luu Bajaria was born in 1970 in London, a city with established South Asian communities. When she moved to LA at the age of nine, it was a huge culture shock. “There was definitely racism against Indian people in London,” she says. “But in Los Angeles at the time, there just weren’t any Indian people, so it was even weirder.” Her British accent amplified the unwanted attention, so she rid herself of it by studying popular American TV programs, from I Dream of Jeannie to Dallas. “I grew up with very Eastern, Indian values of community and village versus the hyper-individualism of LA,” she says. “And [other children in LA] had a much more casual relationship with their parents … TV really helped me learn about American culture... it also showed me the power of film and television because we watched the same shows, which connected me with the kids at school.” Competing in the Miss India contests, she now realises, allowed her “to become Indian on my own terms … I embraced my culture not just through my parents, but by meeting these Indian women from all around the world. I found my voice and learned to own my ‘Indian-ness’. By the time I entered the workplace, I’d already been out there in the world, being interviewed on stages. It ended up being an asset.”

World.title: A petrol can, a drill and six dead trees: Sydney tree vandal avoids conviction
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life A petrol can, a drill and six dead trees: Sydney tree vandal avoids conviction David Barwell September 16, 2026 — 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of poisoning six mature trees in a heritage-listed park in Sydney’s inner west has agreed to pay more than $116,000 to fund park improvements after admitting he drilled holes into the trees and poured petrol into them in a case residents said turned the site into a “tree graveyard”. The case became one of Sydney’s most closely watched tree vandalism cases, sparking community outrage and prompting calls for tougher penalties against people who illegally destroy public trees. A photo taken by a local showing a man appearing to drill into a tree at Allman Park. Facebook The settlement follows an incident on December 28, 2024, when Norman Sukkar was allegedly caught on camera using a cordless drill to bore large holes into six mature trees at Allman Park in Ashfield before pouring petrol into them. The trees, which stood along the boundary of the park, included five magenta lilly pillies and one tuckeroo, which at the time of the poisoning were mature trees standing about 11 metres tall.



Council arborists later found two trees had died, while the remaining four were in a state of “irreversible decline”, ultimately requiring all six to be removed. No permit had been issued for the clearing of the trees and no development consent was in place authorising their removal. Related Article City life Fight to save Hunters Hill trees after ‘calculated act of vandalism’ Footage of the removal was shared on social media, prompting widespread attention that inspired some resident to install “tree graveyard” signs at the site to mourn their loss. Sukkar was originally facing prosecution in the NSW Land and Environment Court after the Inner West Council commenced proceedings seeking up to $1 million in penalties. However, the council has discontinued the case after entering into an enforceable undertaking with Sukkar. Under the settlement, Sukkar has agreed to pay $100,000 to the council to fund improvements at Allman Park, including planting seven replacement trees, maintaining them for 12 months, additional garden bed planting and upgrades to drainage and pathways.



He has also accepted responsibility for the destruction of the trees and acknowledged that his actions breached planning laws, damaged the natural qualities of a heritage-listed park and undermined public confidence in the planning system. The undertaking notes that the conduct was witnessed and reported by a member of the public, helping the council pursue the enforcement action. A photo of the tree graveyard signage in Allman Park. Facebook Tree poisoning remains a persistent issue across Sydney, with councils regularly reporting attacks on public reserves and foreshore bushland. Local governments have long argued offences can be difficult to prosecute because offenders often act covertly, and substantial evidence is required. The issue was highlighted again last month when Yi Wang, director of gardening company Sydney Garden Home, pleaded guilty in the NSW Land and Environment Court to three offences under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act after illegally removing 287 trees from protected foreshore bushland at Woodford Bay Reserve in Longueville in November 2023.

World.title: Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant The creator of Top Paddock and The Kettle Black changed the way Australia thinks about cafes. Now, it wants to do the same with hotel restaurants — starting in South Brisbane. Matt Shea September 16, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Don’t know Nathan Toleman? Because he probably helped change the way you think about cafes. Toleman is founder of The Mulberry Group, the Melbourne-based hospitality powerhouse that was originally responsible for venues such as Top Paddock, The Kettle Black and Higher Ground. All have now been sold, but under Toleman’s stewardship they took the casual, bright but elegant style of all-day dining pioneered by Bills in Sydney, and step-changed it into ambitious, design-driven “breakfast restaurants”. Nathan Toleman and chef Gareth Woolcock outside High Ground. Markus Ravik “There were nice enough sandwich joints, and there were restaurants, but nothing in the middle,” Toleman says. “We were, like, ‘Why don’t we open a cafe with the elements of a restaurant at cafe price points?’ And then everyone thought, ‘Oh, there’s an opportunity’.” Now Toleman wants to do the same thing with hotel restaurants. And he’s starting in Brisbane. In October, Mulberry will open High Road Bar and Grill beneath Novotel Brisbane South Bank in South Brisbane.



Related Article Kosta’s Takeaway closes permanently in Newstead after just six months “When you look at the best hotels around the world, the first thing you want to do is go to the restaurant. Chateau Marmont [in Los Angeles], Chiltern Firehouse [in London] – the restaurants are as big a part of the experience as the hotel. There’s been almost this belief in Australia that you go to a hotel and then you go [outside] to find a good restaurant. I’m like, ‘Why don’t we change that?’” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up To be clear, there have for years been good hotel restaurants in Australia – Gowings at QT Sydney, Paper Daisy at Halcyon House in Cabarita and Raes on Wategos in Byron Bay, among many others – but overall Australian diners are yet to take this segment of the industry seriously. Within hospitality circles, hotel’s kitchens can sometimes be dismissed as being too beholden to the bureaucracy of stakeholders that come with that industry. “There’s been almost this belief in Australia that you go to a hotel, and then you go [outside] to find a good restaurant. I’m like, ‘Why don’t we change that?’” The Mulberry Group’s Nathan Toleman



“In a restaurant, some meat comes in on Monday, we do a special, it’s on the menu that night,” Toleman says. “In a hotel, you have to submit it, get the tech guy to update the point-of-sale, go to marketing. By the time you get it done, the meat’s gone. “We’re saying: if you want to be seen as a destination restaurant, you need to start acting like one.” High Road has been conceptualised with both locals and visitors to the nearby performing arts precinct in mind. The restaurant will have its own entrance, and its design is intended to capture the feel of a classic Queenslander house. Related Article Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead “It has this beautiful dappled light in the morning,” Toleman says. “So you have that Queenslander vibe where you have the house as the main restaurant, and the whole outer edge is designed to feel like the verandah of your house, so you can engage with these different experiences.”



The restaurant’s design will feature warm timbers and layered textures throughout. Expect marble-top tables, leather banquettes, an open kitchen with low-set counters, and full-height windows with timber Venetians. In the kitchen will be chef Gareth Woolcock, who has a background working in independent and hotel restaurants, both in Australia and the UK. Toleman says Woolcock’s restaurant and bar menus are yet to be finalised, but will reflect a lengthy recent history working in detail with local suppliers, and be based around a woodfired grill and oven. High Road’s design is intended to capture the feel of a classic Queenslander house. Markus Ravik For drinks, there will be an Australian-led wine list with a touch of European influence, alongside local craft beer and a cocktail menu that serves twists on the classics. It might sound like ambitious stuff for a southern restaurant group’s first play in the local market – but beyond The Mulberry Group, Toleman is also a partner in Lune Croissanterie with sister-and-brother team Kate and Cameron Reid. He spent two months in Brisbane in 2021 project managing the build of Lune South Brisbane. “I was here that whole time, experiencing the city,” he says. “And I was so impressed with the dining scene. Agnes is one of my favourite restaurants in Australia. There’s been so much focus historically on Sydney and Melbourne, but Brisbane is having this wake-up moment – we have the population, we have the produce, we have the people.”
