World.title: ASX erases early gains, tracking Wall Street as oil prices, bonds lift
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX erases early gains, tracking Wall Street as oil prices, bonds lift Staff writers Updated September 16, 2026 — 11:14am ,first published September 16, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket was treading water at the end of its first hour of trade on Wednesday, erasing early gains as elevated oil prices and rising yields kept investors cautious ahead of the US Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision. Energy stocks jumped. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.7 points at 8671.80 as of 10.58am AEST, with eight of its 11 industry sectors in the green. The benchmark lost 0.9 per cent on Tuesday, hitting its lowest level since early June as the oil-price driven inflation fuelled bets for interest rate hikes in the world’s largest economy. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.31¢. Wall Street lost ground on Tuesday. Bloomberg “If the Fed follows the futures market and hikes rates, our sense is that stocks are likely to see downward pressure over the near-term,” said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. “However, we’ve found that over a longer time horizon — six to 12 months after the first rate hike — stocks typically recover and push into positive territory.” Energy stocks led the morning’s gains, with oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos up 3.1 per cent and 2.6 per cent, respectively, as Brent crude settled almost 3 per cent higher overnight as outages at a key Saudi pipeline and Libyan oil fields added to supply risks in a market already hit by disruptions from the Iran war. Refiner Ampol rose 2.4 per cent.



Traders were watching for signs of how long Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline will remain closed after drone attacks halted operations last week. Saudi Aramco is delaying oil supplies to some European customers this month, people familiar with the matter said. “The combination of higher interest rates and elevated oil prices is like asking equities to run a marathon with ankle weights strapped on,” said Darrell Cronk at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. “Higher rates increase the discount rate investors apply to future earnings, while higher energy costs drain purchasing power from consumers and pressure profit margins.” The big four banks also bounced higher after their losses on Tuesday, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.6 per cent, National Australia Bank and ANZ Bank both up 1.1 per cent and Westpac up 1.3 per cent. Meanwhile, gold miners sent the materials sector lower. Northern Star Resources dropped 1.5 per cent and Evolution Mining lost 1.7 per cent as gold was trading around $US4290 an ounce, holding a two-day decline. Traders are now pricing in a 92 per cent chance of the Fed hiking rates to battle the fuel-led inflation. Raised borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest. Iron ore and copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto both ticked higher, up 0.3 per cent and 0.1 per cent, respectively. Tech stocks were lower, with software makers Xero and WiseTech down 1.3 per cent and 1.7 per cent, and family tracking app Life 360 down 6.1 per cent after rally on Tuesday.



Reliance Worldwide jumped 5.3 per cent after Brookfield Asset Management agreed to buy the plumbing supplies business in a deal that values it at around $4.1 billion. Buying Reliance Worldwide gives Brookfield exposure to the US construction and housing market, which generates around 60 per cent of Reliance’s revenue. On Wall Street overnight, US stocks slipped after oil prices and the bond market cranked up the pressure. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.8 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Wall Street felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the US bond market, climbed to 5 per cent from 4.97 per cent late on Monday and briefly touched 5.04 per cent overnight. It’s been jumping to its highest level in years, and Monday was the first time it breached 5 per cent since 2023. Higher yields mean everyone from the US government to households to businesses must pay more in interest to borrow money, which slows the overall economy. They also make people less willing to pay high prices for stocks because they can earn more from sitting in bonds, which are considered safer investments.



“The result is a market that must work harder to generate earnings growth just as investors become less willing to pay premium valuations for that growth,” according to Darrell Cronk, president of Wells Fargo Investment Institute. The last time the 10-year yield was consistently above 5 per cent was around the turn of the millennium, and it’s been a long march back since it bottomed out below 0.50 per cent in 2020. The pace has accelerated since February, after the war with Iran sent oil prices much higher. That raised worries about high inflation potentially lasting for years, which are layering atop longstanding concerns about the US government’s massive debt level and other issues. Oil prices rose further Tuesday following several sharp swings in the morning. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.9 per cent to settle at $US108.75. It remains well above its $US72 level from early July and from before the war with Iran began in February, as doubt continues about whether the fighting will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf anytime soon through the Strait of Hormuz.



Inflation remains high enough that the widespread expectation is that the Federal Reserve will announce on Wednesday [early Thursday AEST] that it will hike the federal funds rate for the first time in three years. Related Article Opinion

Sydney Sweeney There’s a seriously bad industry behind Sweeney’s seriously bad ad Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Traders are still betting on a slight chance that the Federal Reserve could hold off on hiking interest rates, though. If it does, the market could swing because investors may see it as a sign that the Fed is less committed to getting inflation lower. Fed officials will also release forecasts for where they see interest rates heading in upcoming years, providing another opportunity to inject uncertainty into the market. On Wall Street, stocks of companies that depend on customers having enough spare cash to spend on their products fell to some of the sharper losses.



Chipotle Mexican Grill dropped 5.9 per cent. Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and Longhorn Steakhouse, sank 4.3 per cent. Dollar Tree, whose customers may have less financial cushion than others, fell 5.4 per cent. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry sank after the US Senate voted to block legislation creating a new regulatory framework for crypto, while demanding more limits on President Donald Trump’s investments. The price of Bitcoin slumped 3 per cent to $US75,725.19 at 10.20am AEST. Coinbase Global fell 10.1 per cent, and Robinhood Markets lost 3.4 per cent. Several artificial-intelligence stocks meanwhile held steadier following their worldwide slide the day before, after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Nvidia added 0.6 per cent a day after its 3.4 per cent drop was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 index. Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2.2 per cent.



Such stocks led the US market to records for years, but they’ve come under pressure recently on worries that their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI. In other international markets, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. But for several, the drops were not as sharp as Monday’s caused by the slide for AI stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index, for example, fell 0.9 per cent following Monday’s 3.3 per cent drop. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Revealed: The secret backroom dealings behind $1.1bn lotto licence deal
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian budget Revealed: The secret backroom dealings behind $1.1bn lotto licence deal Kieran Rooney September 16, 2026 — 11:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A secret 40-year-extension of Victoria’s lotto licence was in the works for almost three years before it was announced, with The Lottery Corporation convincing the government it should be allowed to pay a premium in return for shutting out competitors for decades. In a new report released on Wednesday, the auditor-general raised concerns about the lack of transparency surrounding the deal and said there was uncertainty over whether taxpayers could have benefited from a bigger windfall through a competitive process. The Auditor-General reviewed the state’s decision to extend the lotto licence by 40 years. But the report did not identify any probity concerns and said the government sought to deliver value for Victorians when it chose to conduct “exclusive bilateral negotiations” with The Lottery Corporation, the existing operator, and collect $1.145 billion for the extension. TLC announced the shock 40-year deal on May 5 – the day the Victorian budget was released – through an announcement to the stock market. The government was immediately criticised for using the agreement to prop up the budget’s bottom line.



Auditor-General Andrew Greaves found the government believed that it could secure more money this way because TLC was willing to pay significantly more to extend its licence without a competitive process, and to secure a commitment that lotto taxes would not be raised without providing compensation. Related Article Updated

Victorian budget Lotto windfall boosts state budget amid warnings about election-year spending splurge A commercial adviser appointed to the process valued the licence at about $1.372 billion, which was $227 million less than finally collected, however the auditor-general cautioned that the higher figure was a “theoretical value” and not a like-for-like comparison to a price set by negotiation. The report cited internal departmental analysis that said a competitive process was “unlikely to deliver a better outcome than bilateral negotiations”, and that continuing with the current operator would minimise disruption to future tax income. Greaves did not dispute this but said it was impossible to say which method could have produced a higher payment because the price was not tested on an open market.



“We saw evidence that agencies actively assessed and negotiated proposals advanced by TLC. However, those mechanisms could not replicate the price discovery benefits of a competitive process,” he said. “As a result, while agencies sought to maximise value within a bilateral framework, it is not possible to know with certainty whether a higher premium could have been achieved under an alternative approach.” Gaming Minister Enver Erdogan said the report made clear the process to extend the licence was conducted properly. Justin McManus Wednesday’s report outlined the full timeline of events behind the deal for the first time, revealing that TLC initially approached the government in November 2023 with a proposal to pay an upfront premium in return for a 20 to 40-year extension. The government then authorised Treasury to explore reforms to the current licence, which at the time only allowed for an extension of one year.



Victorian Auditor-General Andrew Greaves. Victoria Auditor-General’s Office These discussions culminated in June 2025, almost a year before the deal was announced, when the government passed laws that paved the way for the multi-decade deal. Alongside this work, government agencies spent 2024 gauging market interest in the lottery licence and developing a negotiation strategy. A commercial adviser was appointed, and they argued TLC was likely to pay more for the licence for a range of reasons, including the fact that it was part of a national bloc of lottery corporations that already worked together. By November, the government decided to proceed with exclusive negotiations, but set a reserve price that would act as a minimum payment. If TLC could not match this floor price, they would revert to a traditional competitive process, with the intention that holding exclusive negotiations were guaranteed to deliver better value.



The auditor-general revealed that TLC was not only willing to pay this reserve price to avoid an open process, but forked out more cash to the state in return for an agreement on lottery taxes. The government promised it would compensate the company if it increased lottery taxes above current levels. Related Article Victorian Parliament Lotto extension was in the works months before laws allowed it That deal “resulted in a material increase to the premium TLC paid for the licence”, according to the report. Greaves did not find any significant integrity issues, but said the government’s approach meant the public had limited visibility over key decisions and the reasons behind them. Departmental chiefs told the auditor-general the secrecy was required for the negotiations to ensure the best value for money. Greaves said these were credible arguments, but that agencies needed to balance these objectives by making sure parliament and the public knew what the government was doing and why they were doing it.



The report recommended Treasury develop new rules that assessed how and when major commercial decisions could be disclosed to the public, which the department accepted in principle. Related Article Victorian budget Melbourne’s cooling housing market is turning into a billion-dollar budget crisis When the deal came to light in May, it sparked criticism from the state opposition, competitors and anti-gambling advocates because of its length and the fact that there was no public tender process. Speaking before the report was tabled on Tuesday, Premier Ben Carroll said he was confident that Gaming Minister Enver Erdogan had overseen the negotiation process correctly. An opposition spokesperson criticised the secretive nature of the negotiations, revealed in a report which came a month after the auditor-general exposed a previously undisclosed levy on public transport fares.

World.title: Renshaw’s maiden ODI century was great. But can he fire in Tests against South Africa when it counts?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Renshaw’s maiden ODI century was great. But can he fire in Tests against South Africa when it counts? Tom Decent Updated September 16, 2026 — 11:40am ,first published September 16, 2026 — 2:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Renshaw’s dad is trying to sell a book that he has written for cricket coaches. “He’s the biggest cricket nuffy I know,” Renshaw wrote on Instagram this week. “It covers all the principles and games that we did when I was a kid and still do now [at] training.” There is no mention on the cover – or the back – that Ian Renshaw is indeed the father of an incumbent Australian cricketer. But as far as timing goes, his son’s first international century in nearly a decade on Tuesday in Zimbabwe won’t do sales any harm.



Renshaw’s 109 from 94 balls at the Harare Sports Club, which helped Australia to a 59-run victory over Zimbabwe in the opening ODI of the series, came at No.6 against a modest attack and with the visitors wobbling at 4-107 in the 18th over. After bringing up his 50 from 55 balls, Renshaw put his foot down. An array of powerful aerial shots down the ground carried him to his maiden ODI hundred 31 balls later and Australia to 8-294. Australia’s batsman Matt Renshaw celebrates his century during the first ODI against Zimbabwe. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Nathan Ellis (5-31) then helped bowl Zimbabwe out for 235 in 45.1 overs before Renshaw’s day out took another unlikely turn as he snared the wicket of Brendan Taylor with a gentle off-spinner that was scooped to long-on. Of all the international centuries a cricketer dreams of making, one against Zimbabwe in an irrelevant ODI is nowhere near the top of the list.



But for Renshaw, ripping off an Australian helmet and raising his bat again carried plenty of symbolism. “I probably didn’t think I was going to play one-day cricket,” Renshaw said. “Batting at six, you’re probably not expecting to get a hundred. If you do, it’s probably slogging. “I was just playing my game. I know I play my best when I am nice and relaxed.” Almost a decade after announcing himself as one of Australian cricket’s brightest prospects, Renshaw is preparing for another crack at the toughest format of the game that he is yet to conquer. Matthew Renshaw at the Gabba in Brisbane after being named in the Australian Test team in 2016. Getty Images



The big question is whether he can kick on and churn out big runs as Australia’s opener in a three-Test series against South Africa, starting on October 9 in Durban. Jake Weatherald’s axing last month, after Australia’s dismal Test defeat to Bangladesh in Darwin, has handed Renshaw the keys at the top of the order against the same nation he made his international debut against 10 years ago in Adelaide. Later that summer, as a 20-year-old, Renshaw cracked 184 against Pakistan at the SCG. Australia appeared to have found its next long-term opener, a towering Queensland left-hander in the mould of Matthew Hayden. Later that year, Renshaw was dropped.



He was parachuted back into Australia’s XI in Johannesburg in 2018 for the Test immediately after the Sandpapergate scandal and has been in and out since. His past 10 Test innings - 5, 4, 22, 8, 5, 5*, 0, 2, 2 and 8 - read more like lottery numbers than the returns of a player about to open the batting for Australia in such a crucial series. Now 30, Renshaw is a far more rounded player than the youngster who was given a baggy green. His white-ball game, in particular, has come on enormously, culminating in ODI and T20 international debuts since October last year. But Test cricket remains the unfinished business.



Facing Zimbabwean spinners at both ends through the middle overs of an ODI is considerably different to seeing off a red ball in South Africa against fast bowler Marco Jansen and potentially Kagiso Rabada, pending his recovery from a hamstring injury. “It’s obviously a very different role,” Renshaw said of his opening duties. “It’s something I am trying to prepare for as well as I can. Mindset is the biggest thing. It’s about trying to get as much rhythm as you can before that Test series.” Australia had three Test representatives in their opening ODI: Renshaw, Travis Head (4) and Alex Carey (27). For the fourth innings in a row, including his three Test knocks against Bangladesh, Head chopped a ball back onto his stumps. It is becoming a bizarre trend for one of Australia’s most destructive batters. Loading



Josh Hazlewood was managed, while Cricket Australia said Cameron Green was not selected due to shoulder soreness. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket ‘Dire consequences’: BBL sell-off slammed amid fears for grassroots cricket Australia have two more ODIs against Zimbabwe and three against South Africa before a two-day warm-up match ahead of the Test series. Renshaw said he would begin facing red balls in the nets soon. But when he walks out to open the batting in Durban, he will have played one first-class match in the previous six months. David Warner’s 135 in Cape Town in 2014 remains the last Test century on South African soil by an Australian opener.



A decade after his own Test career began with such promise, you suspect Renshaw would happily trade any number of white-ball runs to be the man who breaks that drought. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Netflix’s ‘queen of screens’ hid a secret about her past. When it came to light, she froze
World.content:
Bela Bajaria, one of the most powerful people in Hollywood, on racism, being fired and why she’s embracing an aspect of her past she once concealed.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I gingerly broach the topic of Bela Bajaria’s time at Universal Television, she brushes aside my polite euphemisms and gets to the point. “Which part of [my time at] Universal?” asks Bajaria, whose role as Netflix’s global chief content officer makes her one of the most powerful people in Hollywood. “The getting fired part?” In 2011, Bajaria joined the television studio arm of NBC, then known as Universal Media Studios, which had been gutted by a previous regime. Her success in rebuilding it resulted in her promotion to president in 2015. But her success in creating and selling programs to rival platforms – also a key part of her job – became a sticking point. Bajaria started her career as an assistant at CBS in the mid-1990s. Today, she is one of the most powerful people in Hollywood. Joe Armao Among the hit series Bajaria helped bring to fruition at Universal are The Mindy Project and Brooklyn Nine-Nine for Fox, and Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt and Master of None for Netflix. “I always felt the decisions I made were best for the creator and best for the studio,” says Bajaria, in an exclusive interview with this masthead. “When you are the studio to a sister network and you sell outside to other places – and if those shows are successful – it causes tension.” Things came to a head in 2016, when Bajaria was sacked. At the time, it made no sense. After all, she’d created a slew of hit shows, treated people fairly and made what she believed to be the right decisions for the business. “Then you realise that it’s not so simple,” she says. “There are definitely tensions and personality clashes and lots of other things that happen.”



Cliches about learning from failure, she adds, “look nice stitched onto a pillow”. But they do not preclude the self-doubt that comes with being dismissed from a high-profile dream job. Twelve-hour roasted lamb shoulder served with crispy briwats, smoked eggplant, sticky lamb fat and lemony za’atar jus. Joe Armao “The reason I talk about the firing part is that some people look at me and my job now and go, ‘Oh, it’s all just great,’” Bajaria says. “But there were these big, huge lessons along the way. I definitely learned more from getting fired than I learned at any other time professionally. It gives you a sense of perspective about who you are and what you’re made of.” During her subsequent “summer of soul-searching”, Bajaria had a conversation with Ted Sarandos, now the co-chief executive of Netflix with Greg Peters. He told her not to take another job without speaking to him first. Soon, he offered her a role as head of licensing, co-productions and unscripted content. Turkish beef dumplings, braised beef shin, burnt butter with urfa pepper and smoked yoghurt. Joe Armao “I’ve worked in scripted TV for 20 years,” she told him. “You’re offering me a job, but I have no experience in any of those things.” “I just hire smart people,” Sarandos replied. “You’ll figure it out.”



It’s safe to say that Bajaria impressed her new boss: in 2023, she succeeded Sarandos as Netflix’s global chief content officer. According to the London Telegraph, she is “the woman who decides what the world is watching on TV”, while Forbes magazine labelled her “Netflix’s Queen Of Screens”. Bajaria and I are ensconced in a leather-upholstered booth at Maha, a moody, subterranean restaurant described by The Age Good Food Guide as Melbourne’s “gilded tiger of Middle Eastern fine dining”. We share several dishes including Turkish beef dumplings; roast zucchini and burnt red peppers; steamed warrigal greens with an olive oil and mustard dressing; and house flatbread with sumac butter and smoked hummus. The highlight is the slow-cooked lamb shoulder marinated in garlic sumac and cumin, so tender that it falls apart as we spoon it onto our plates. Roast zucchini and burnt red peppers, harissa and almond tarator. Joe Armao Despite an impressive drinks menu, we opt for water – in part because Bajaria is on a flying visit to Australia, to promote the first American National Football League regular season game played in this country. The match between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers drew 100,000 fans to the MCG, many of whom travelled from the United States. It was streamed live on Netflix and ESPN, and broadcast on Channel Seven. ‘When someone brought it up in an interview, I felt like some deep, dark secret was out.’ Bela Bajaria For Netflix, it marks a further dissolution of the once-solid boundaries between broadcast television and subscription video on demand. When the streaming giant launched in Australia in 2015, it trumpeted its high-end, ad-free original programming (House of Cards, Orange Is the New Black, BoJack Horseman) as its point of difference. Meanwhile, free-to-air networks played to their strengths: live sport, news and local programming. These days, it’s harder to tell the difference. Netflix now offers discounted subscriptions to viewers willing to watch ads, while investing heavily in reality shows, sport and other live events. In response, Australian broadcasters have beefed up their on-demand platforms. Two months before Netflix’s debut, Nine launched Stan, a direct rival that invests heavily in premium Australian programming. (Nine is the owner of this masthead.)



Related Article Streaming Next at Netflix: Co-CEO Greg Peters on live sport, AI and talking to your telly Globally, Netflix has more than 325 million subscribers, although household account sharing means its total number of users is significantly higher. While the company intends to increase its subscriber base, it can no longer rely on the rapid rate of growth it enjoyed in its early days – a situation made trickier by an international cost-of-living crisis. This has prompted Netflix to seek revenue from other sources, such as games, short-form video and podcasts (all of which are more amenable to daytime use, allowing Netflix to move beyond its reputation as evening-based entertainment). With all this in mind, would Netflix consider making a play for major Australian sports such as the NRL or AFL? Bajaria is not ruling it out. “I love that people in Australia love sports so much,” she says, pointing out that the immense popularity of World Baseball Classic in Japan – the only country in which Netflix has the rights to the tournament – could provide a model for other markets. “If there was [a sport] in Australia that was ‘right-sized’ in that way, we’re always going to look at it. It doesn’t have to be global.” Much has been written about Bajaria during her 30-year career. But there was one element of her past she vowed to conceal: her stint as a beauty pageant queen. Having already won Miss India LA and Miss India USA, she was crowned Miss India Worldwide in 1991. “I hid it very deeply because I thought there would always be misconceptions about my work ethic, drive, ambition and intellect,” she explains. “When someone brought it up in an interview, I felt like some deep, dark secret was out.”



She re-enacts the wide-eyed, frozen-in-fear expression that overcame her during that conversation. But as her career progressed – and she continued to defy the lazy stereotypes about pageant winners – she embraced her Miss India accomplishments. Related Article Streaming ‘It’s like Squid Game’: Why Netflix parted ways with content chief Que Minh Luu Bajaria was born in 1970 in London, a city with established South Asian communities. When she moved to LA at the age of nine, it was a huge culture shock. “There was definitely racism against Indian people in London,” she says. “But in Los Angeles at the time, there just weren’t any Indian people, so it was even weirder.” Her British accent amplified the unwanted attention, so she rid herself of it by studying popular American TV programs, from I Dream of Jeannie to Dallas. “I grew up with very Eastern, Indian values of community and village versus the hyper-individualism of LA,” she says. “And [other children in LA] had a much more casual relationship with their parents … TV really helped me learn about American culture... it also showed me the power of film and television because we watched the same shows, which connected me with the kids at school.” Competing in the Miss India contests, she now realises, allowed her “to become Indian on my own terms … I embraced my culture not just through my parents, but by meeting these Indian women from all around the world. I found my voice and learned to own my ‘Indian-ness’. By the time I entered the workplace, I’d already been out there in the world, being interviewed on stages. It ended up being an asset.”

World.title: A petrol can, a drill and six dead trees: Sydney tree vandal avoids conviction
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life A petrol can, a drill and six dead trees: Sydney tree vandal avoids conviction David Barwell September 16, 2026 — 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of poisoning six mature trees in a heritage-listed park in Sydney’s inner west has agreed to pay more than $116,000 to fund park improvements after admitting he drilled holes into the trees and poured petrol into them in a case residents said turned the site into a “tree graveyard”. The case became one of Sydney’s most closely watched tree vandalism cases, sparking community outrage and prompting calls for tougher penalties against people who illegally destroy public trees. A photo taken by a local showing a man appearing to drill into a tree at Allman Park. Facebook The settlement follows an incident on December 28, 2024, when Norman Sukkar was allegedly caught on camera using a cordless drill to bore large holes into six mature trees at Allman Park in Ashfield before pouring petrol into them. The trees, which stood along the boundary of the park, included five magenta lilly pillies and one tuckeroo, which at the time of the poisoning were mature trees standing about 11 metres tall.



Council arborists later found two trees had died, while the remaining four were in a state of “irreversible decline”, ultimately requiring all six to be removed. No permit had been issued for the clearing of the trees and no development consent was in place authorising their removal. Related Article City life Fight to save Hunters Hill trees after ‘calculated act of vandalism’ Footage of the removal was shared on social media, prompting widespread attention that inspired some resident to install “tree graveyard” signs at the site to mourn their loss. Sukkar was originally facing prosecution in the NSW Land and Environment Court after the Inner West Council commenced proceedings seeking up to $1 million in penalties. However, the council has discontinued the case after entering into an enforceable undertaking with Sukkar. Under the settlement, Sukkar has agreed to pay $100,000 to the council to fund improvements at Allman Park, including planting seven replacement trees, maintaining them for 12 months, additional garden bed planting and upgrades to drainage and pathways.



He has also accepted responsibility for the destruction of the trees and acknowledged that his actions breached planning laws, damaged the natural qualities of a heritage-listed park and undermined public confidence in the planning system. The undertaking notes that the conduct was witnessed and reported by a member of the public, helping the council pursue the enforcement action. A photo of the tree graveyard signage in Allman Park. Facebook Tree poisoning remains a persistent issue across Sydney, with councils regularly reporting attacks on public reserves and foreshore bushland. Local governments have long argued offences can be difficult to prosecute because offenders often act covertly, and substantial evidence is required. The issue was highlighted again last month when Yi Wang, director of gardening company Sydney Garden Home, pleaded guilty in the NSW Land and Environment Court to three offences under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act after illegally removing 287 trees from protected foreshore bushland at Woodford Bay Reserve in Longueville in November 2023.

World.title: Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant The creator of Top Paddock and The Kettle Black changed the way Australia thinks about cafes. Now, it wants to do the same with hotel restaurants — starting in South Brisbane. Matt Shea September 16, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Don’t know Nathan Toleman? Because he probably helped change the way you think about cafes. Toleman is founder of The Mulberry Group, the Melbourne-based hospitality powerhouse that was originally responsible for venues such as Top Paddock, The Kettle Black and Higher Ground. All have now been sold, but under Toleman’s stewardship they took the casual, bright but elegant style of all-day dining pioneered by Bills in Sydney, and step-changed it into ambitious, design-driven “breakfast restaurants”. Nathan Toleman and chef Gareth Woolcock outside High Ground. Markus Ravik “There were nice enough sandwich joints, and there were restaurants, but nothing in the middle,” Toleman says. “We were, like, ‘Why don’t we open a cafe with the elements of a restaurant at cafe price points?’ And then everyone thought, ‘Oh, there’s an opportunity’.” Now Toleman wants to do the same thing with hotel restaurants. And he’s starting in Brisbane. In October, Mulberry will open High Road Bar and Grill beneath Novotel Brisbane South Bank in South Brisbane.



Related Article Kosta’s Takeaway closes permanently in Newstead after just six months “When you look at the best hotels around the world, the first thing you want to do is go to the restaurant. Chateau Marmont [in Los Angeles], Chiltern Firehouse [in London] – the restaurants are as big a part of the experience as the hotel. There’s been almost this belief in Australia that you go to a hotel and then you go [outside] to find a good restaurant. I’m like, ‘Why don’t we change that?’” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up To be clear, there have for years been good hotel restaurants in Australia – Gowings at QT Sydney, Paper Daisy at Halcyon House in Cabarita and Raes on Wategos in Byron Bay, among many others – but overall Australian diners are yet to take this segment of the industry seriously. Within hospitality circles, hotel’s kitchens can sometimes be dismissed as being too beholden to the bureaucracy of stakeholders that come with that industry. “There’s been almost this belief in Australia that you go to a hotel, and then you go [outside] to find a good restaurant. I’m like, ‘Why don’t we change that?’” The Mulberry Group’s Nathan Toleman



“In a restaurant, some meat comes in on Monday, we do a special, it’s on the menu that night,” Toleman says. “In a hotel, you have to submit it, get the tech guy to update the point-of-sale, go to marketing. By the time you get it done, the meat’s gone. “We’re saying: if you want to be seen as a destination restaurant, you need to start acting like one.” High Road has been conceptualised with both locals and visitors to the nearby performing arts precinct in mind. The restaurant will have its own entrance, and its design is intended to capture the feel of a classic Queenslander house. Related Article Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead “It has this beautiful dappled light in the morning,” Toleman says. “So you have that Queenslander vibe where you have the house as the main restaurant, and the whole outer edge is designed to feel like the verandah of your house, so you can engage with these different experiences.”



The restaurant’s design will feature warm timbers and layered textures throughout. Expect marble-top tables, leather banquettes, an open kitchen with low-set counters, and full-height windows with timber Venetians. In the kitchen will be chef Gareth Woolcock, who has a background working in independent and hotel restaurants, both in Australia and the UK. Toleman says Woolcock’s restaurant and bar menus are yet to be finalised, but will reflect a lengthy recent history working in detail with local suppliers, and be based around a woodfired grill and oven. High Road’s design is intended to capture the feel of a classic Queenslander house. Markus Ravik For drinks, there will be an Australian-led wine list with a touch of European influence, alongside local craft beer and a cocktail menu that serves twists on the classics. It might sound like ambitious stuff for a southern restaurant group’s first play in the local market – but beyond The Mulberry Group, Toleman is also a partner in Lune Croissanterie with sister-and-brother team Kate and Cameron Reid. He spent two months in Brisbane in 2021 project managing the build of Lune South Brisbane. “I was here that whole time, experiencing the city,” he says. “And I was so impressed with the dining scene. Agnes is one of my favourite restaurants in Australia. There’s been so much focus historically on Sydney and Melbourne, but Brisbane is having this wake-up moment – we have the population, we have the produce, we have the people.”

World.title: ASX erases early gains, tracking Wall Street as oil prices, bonds lift
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX erases early gains, tracking Wall Street as oil prices, bonds lift Staff writers Updated September 16, 2026 — 11:14am ,first published September 16, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket was treading water at the end of its first hour of trade on Wednesday, erasing early gains as elevated oil prices and rising yields kept investors cautious ahead of the US Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision. Energy stocks jumped. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.7 points at 8671.80 as of 10.58am AEST, with eight of its 11 industry sectors in the green. The benchmark lost 0.9 per cent on Tuesday, hitting its lowest level since early June as the oil-price driven inflation fuelled bets for interest rate hikes in the world’s largest economy. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.31¢. Wall Street lost ground on Tuesday. Bloomberg “If the Fed follows the futures market and hikes rates, our sense is that stocks are likely to see downward pressure over the near-term,” said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. “However, we’ve found that over a longer time horizon — six to 12 months after the first rate hike — stocks typically recover and push into positive territory.” Energy stocks led the morning’s gains, with oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos up 3.1 per cent and 2.6 per cent, respectively, as Brent crude settled almost 3 per cent higher overnight as outages at a key Saudi pipeline and Libyan oil fields added to supply risks in a market already hit by disruptions from the Iran war. Refiner Ampol rose 2.4 per cent.



Traders were watching for signs of how long Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline will remain closed after drone attacks halted operations last week. Saudi Aramco is delaying oil supplies to some European customers this month, people familiar with the matter said. “The combination of higher interest rates and elevated oil prices is like asking equities to run a marathon with ankle weights strapped on,” said Darrell Cronk at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. “Higher rates increase the discount rate investors apply to future earnings, while higher energy costs drain purchasing power from consumers and pressure profit margins.” The big four banks also bounced higher after their losses on Tuesday, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.6 per cent, National Australia Bank and ANZ Bank both up 1.1 per cent and Westpac up 1.3 per cent. Meanwhile, gold miners sent the materials sector lower. Northern Star Resources dropped 1.5 per cent and Evolution Mining lost 1.7 per cent as gold was trading around $US4290 an ounce, holding a two-day decline. Traders are now pricing in a 92 per cent chance of the Fed hiking rates to battle the fuel-led inflation. Raised borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest. Iron ore and copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto both ticked higher, up 0.3 per cent and 0.1 per cent, respectively. Tech stocks were lower, with software makers Xero and WiseTech down 1.3 per cent and 1.7 per cent, and family tracking app Life 360 down 6.1 per cent after rally on Tuesday.



Reliance Worldwide jumped 5.3 per cent after Brookfield Asset Management agreed to buy the plumbing supplies business in a deal that values it at around $4.1 billion. Buying Reliance Worldwide gives Brookfield exposure to the US construction and housing market, which generates around 60 per cent of Reliance’s revenue. On Wall Street overnight, US stocks slipped after oil prices and the bond market cranked up the pressure. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.8 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Wall Street felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the US bond market, climbed to 5 per cent from 4.97 per cent late on Monday and briefly touched 5.04 per cent overnight. It’s been jumping to its highest level in years, and Monday was the first time it breached 5 per cent since 2023. Higher yields mean everyone from the US government to households to businesses must pay more in interest to borrow money, which slows the overall economy. They also make people less willing to pay high prices for stocks because they can earn more from sitting in bonds, which are considered safer investments.



“The result is a market that must work harder to generate earnings growth just as investors become less willing to pay premium valuations for that growth,” according to Darrell Cronk, president of Wells Fargo Investment Institute. The last time the 10-year yield was consistently above 5 per cent was around the turn of the millennium, and it’s been a long march back since it bottomed out below 0.50 per cent in 2020. The pace has accelerated since February, after the war with Iran sent oil prices much higher. That raised worries about high inflation potentially lasting for years, which are layering atop longstanding concerns about the US government’s massive debt level and other issues. Oil prices rose further Tuesday following several sharp swings in the morning. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.9 per cent to settle at $US108.75. It remains well above its $US72 level from early July and from before the war with Iran began in February, as doubt continues about whether the fighting will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf anytime soon through the Strait of Hormuz.



Inflation remains high enough that the widespread expectation is that the Federal Reserve will announce on Wednesday [early Thursday AEST] that it will hike the federal funds rate for the first time in three years. Related Article Opinion

Sydney Sweeney There’s a seriously bad industry behind Sweeney’s seriously bad ad Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Traders are still betting on a slight chance that the Federal Reserve could hold off on hiking interest rates, though. If it does, the market could swing because investors may see it as a sign that the Fed is less committed to getting inflation lower. Fed officials will also release forecasts for where they see interest rates heading in upcoming years, providing another opportunity to inject uncertainty into the market. On Wall Street, stocks of companies that depend on customers having enough spare cash to spend on their products fell to some of the sharper losses.



Chipotle Mexican Grill dropped 5.9 per cent. Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and Longhorn Steakhouse, sank 4.3 per cent. Dollar Tree, whose customers may have less financial cushion than others, fell 5.4 per cent. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry sank after the US Senate voted to block legislation creating a new regulatory framework for crypto, while demanding more limits on President Donald Trump’s investments. The price of Bitcoin slumped 3 per cent to $US75,725.19 at 10.20am AEST. Coinbase Global fell 10.1 per cent, and Robinhood Markets lost 3.4 per cent. Several artificial-intelligence stocks meanwhile held steadier following their worldwide slide the day before, after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Nvidia added 0.6 per cent a day after its 3.4 per cent drop was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 index. Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2.2 per cent.



Such stocks led the US market to records for years, but they’ve come under pressure recently on worries that their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI. In other international markets, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. But for several, the drops were not as sharp as Monday’s caused by the slide for AI stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index, for example, fell 0.9 per cent following Monday’s 3.3 per cent drop. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow Nick Wright September 16, 2026 — 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soon after the Dolphins squad had gathered for a 2026 preseason camp on the Gold Coast, Kristian Woolf stood in front of his players and threw down the gauntlet. Long before he was an NRL coach, Woolf fought in the Fred Brophy Boxing troupe throughout his late teens. The group is a travelling boxing tent show in Queensland that offers everyday people the chance to step in the ring. Roughly 30 years later, Woolf called on the men under his tutelage at the Dolphins to step into the ring and go toe-to-toe with him. Kristian Woolf has led the Dolphins to the a maiden finals’ berth. NRL Photos “He went head-to-head with Ray Stone I think it was,” Dolphins winger Jamayne Isaako said. “Everyone fears Ray a little bit in the game, but for him to have held his ground and give it back to him certainly showed to the playing group that’s the kind of coach you want to have.” “What he was trying to show to the players is something we want to try to show him when we suit up each week. It just shows you want to go to war with him.”



Related Article NRL 2026 Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs Halfback Isaiya Katoa added: “The boys loved it, it was probably the first and only time they’d be able to punch him. “It gained the respect of the boys straight away knowing your coach is willing to do that.” The early days of Woolf’s tenure at the helm of the Dolphins was marred by chatter of the Wayne Bennett curse. It was a regularly floated phenomenon which dictated that mentors following in Bennett’s footsteps struggled to leave a mark, and were swiftly moved on. Having served as Bennett’s assistant in 2023 (13th) and 2024 (10th), Woolf has not only defied the narrative, but taken the club forward. Last year they came ninth and this season they finished the regular season third and are through to the preliminary final next weekend at Suncorp Stadium after upsetting the Warriors in New Zealand in a 26-16 qualifying final victory.



In 2026, six Dolphins featured in State of Origin; Queensland mainstay Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow joined by Selwyn Cobbo and Thomas Flegler – making their first Maroons appearances since 2024 and 2023 respectively – and debutants Max Plath and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki. Loading Jack Bostock also debuted for NSW, while Katoa was ushered into Blues camp to cover for Mitchell Moses. So how did Woolf achieve what Anthony Seibold and Ivan Henjak (both Broncos), Steve Price (Dragons), Rick Stone (Knights) and Jason Demetriou (Rabbitohs) could not, and take a team further forward in a post-Bennett era? “He’s really calm, and I think the calmer you are as a coach, the calmer your group will be. We’ve been in so many positions in games ... understanding how to deal with those situations, a big part of that is the way Woolfy handles situations like that,” Katoa said.



“There was that saying of whenever Wayne would pass on his coaching role to his assistants they’d probably struggle, but we had all the confidence we wouldn’t be another team to go down that path. “I think the biggest part around him is understanding our players and what our players need. Every group is different, every group is really unique, and I think the way he’s dealt with that has given us a lot of confidence to back our own abilities. “One thing he does well is coach to what his team needs, rather than what his own game plan is.” A feather in Woolf’s cap, according to Dolphins veteran Felise Kaufusi, is his teaching background.



Before joining the North Queensland Cowboys as an under-20s coach, Woolf taught at Townsville’s Ignatius Park College where he led the high school to a Queensland Schoolboys Championship title. That was his first experience of getting the best out of a large group of different, and at times conflicting, personalities – both in the classroom and on the field. “For sure [you get the teacher vibe from Woolf], he’s a good communicator, but what I do like about him is he’s a straight-shooter. He’ll tell you how it is and if you need to improve on stuff you’ve done on the weekend,” Kaufusi said. Inaugural Dolphins coach Wayne Bennett. Isaako added: “I’m always one of the early risers and the first here at training, but every time I come in, Woolfy’s car is the first one I see in the carpark. I swear that guy stays here late at night dissecting through video.



“He reminds me a lot of Wayne to be honest with coaching tactics and the way he talks to the players. He reminds me a lot of the master coach, he’s a very smart coach, and the way he approaches players is certainly reflecting in the way we play together.” As the Dolphins prepare for next week’s sudden death showdown at Suncorp Stadium, with a spot in the grand final on the line, Woolf’s triumphs have freed him of the same shackles of expectations which have seemingly derailed Bennett’s successors. Such is the success Woolf has cultivated in Redcliffe, the club faces a salary cap crunch in its bid to retain their stars. From November 1, 14 players will be able to negotiate with rivals for 2028 – spearheaded by Herbie Farnworth, Cobbo, Tabuai-Fidow, Bostock and Finefeuiaki. Dolphins squad movement Unsigned beyond 2026 Brad Schneider, Brian Pouniu Off contract (end of 2027) Herbie Farnworth, Selwyn Cobbo, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, Morgan Knowles, Thomas Flegler, Connelly Lemuelu, Jack Bostock, Felise Kaufusi, Trai Fuller, LJ Nonu, Elijah Rasmussen, Sebastian Su’a, John Fineanganofo Gains (2027) George Williams Losses Jamayne Isaako (Storm), Oryn Keeley (Storm, mid-season), Daniel Saifiti (medical retirement), Ray Stone (retirement), Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers) Rookie flyer Tevita Naufahu was announced on an extension until the end of 2029 on Wednesday, and is set to replace the departing Isaako.



Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader was confident the culture which had been built would entice players to stay for less, and stressed “our intention is we’ll be able to hold on to, hopefully, all of them”. While Woolf’s contract also ends after the 2027 season, Reader declared he was their man for the long haul. “He wants to be the coach long-term here, and we want him to be a coach for long-term here. That’s something that will be taken care of quite quickly,” he said. The Dolphins will face the winner of the Roosters and Sharks semi-final to take place on Saturday.
