World.title: Man pleads not guilty over murder of two people in Auckland
World.content:
A man has pleaded not guilty over the murder of two people in the Auckland suburb of Wattle Downs.

Emergency services were called to a house on Gambare Place more than two weeks ago, and two people were found dead at the house.

Name suppression has lapsed for the victims, and they can now be named as Elaine Rudolph and Keagan Bell.

The 30-year-old accused entered not guilty pleas through his lawyer at the Auckland High Court on Wednesday, before Justice Michele Wilkinson-Smith.

The man has continued name suppression and is remanded in custody until trial next year.

More than a dozen people observed in the public gallery and when the accused first appeared in the dock, a man in the public gallery yelled "d***head".

Justice Wilkinson Smith warned the man and asked him to contain himself.

She said if there's disturbance in the public gallery, she would close the court.

World.title: Māori health and arts leader John Broughton dies
World.content:
Māori academic and playwright Emeritus Professor John Broughton CNZM (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu Ki Heretaunga) has died.

The University of Otago, where Broughton dedicated more than 40 years of his professional academic life, confirmed he passed on Tuesday.

He was a professor in the Department of Preventative and Social Medicine and associate dean Māori for the School of Dentistry.

Among his achievements was the introduction and development of hauora Māori curriculum in health professional courses, and being the inaugural director of the Ngāi Tahu Māori Health Research Unit.

In a statement the university said Broughton "was awarded a PhD in 2006 following a doctoral thesis in Māori oral health and became professor in 2012. Following his retirement in 2020, he remained dedicated to the university, contributing to the community in a variety of ways, including providing a welcome at almost every graduation ceremony."

Broughton was appointed a Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the Queen's Birthday Honours in 2016 for services to Māori health, theatre and the community.

In 2020 Broughton was awarded the status of emeritus professor for his distinguished and long service to the University. In 2025 the university awarded Broughton an honorary doctorate of science in recognition of his outstanding career and contribution to healthcare and Māori advancement.

In addition to his academic career, Broughton was an award-winning playwright whose work brought te ao Māori to stages in Aotearoa and overseas.

He also served for many decades in the New Zealand Territorial Force as a commissioned officer and was recognised with the Efficiency Decoration. And he was a dedicated member and supporter of the Otago University Rugby Football Club.

University of Otago Vice-Chancellor Grant Robertson said Broughton's immense contribution to the advancement of Māori health, dental healthcare and preventative and social medicine will forever live on in the students he taught, the research he pioneered, and the knowledge he imparted.

"The many gifts he had, he shared with intelligence and grace, enhancing our collective understanding and contributing to a better Aotearoa. The ora John planted will continue to bloom, as it was sown in every clinician who benefited from his mahi. We will miss him greatly."

World.title: Fiji declares HIV emergency as 1 in 60 Fijian adults live with HIV
World.content:
Fiji's Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu has formally declared a national HIV emergency in the country.

In a pre-recorded video press statement on Tuesday, Dr Lalabalavu said the decision was backed by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka and his Cabinet due to the "seriousness of the epidemic".

The health minister confirmed that the government's current estimates indicated that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is living with HIV.

"Five years ago, the estimate was one in 167. In 2025, we recorded 2060 new HIV diagnoses," he said.

"HIV prevalence among women attending antenatal care reached around two percent. That means one out of 50 pregnant women now has HIV. These figures tell us the response must reach further and follow through more consistently."



This week, a health researcher told RNZ Checkpoint that a "horrendously high" number of newborns were dying due to HIV-related complications in Fiji.

The NZ government's SafeTravel website is warning people traveling to Fiji to avoid activities that could increase their risk of infection.

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), Fiji has the second-fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the Asia-Pacific region behind Papua New Guinea (PNG).

An estimated 9000 Fijians were living with HIV as of March this year, and officials pointed to high-risk drug use contributing to the rapid rise.

The number of Fijians living with HIV had risen to at least 9000 as of March. RNZ Pacific

Dr Lalabalavu said every diagnosis must lead to care and every person starting treatment needed support to remain on it.

He said authorities would move quickly to introduce new interventions and scale up established services backed by evidence.

"That means expanding testing, treatment, and access to pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. It also means accelerating the introduction of a formal needle and syringe programme and long-acting injectable prevention."

He stressed that treatment was central to the government's response.

"It helps people living with HIV stay well, and when it achieves and maintains an undetectable viral load, it prevents sexual transmission."

Fiji's Sexual Reproductive Health and HIV Programme Management Unit is expected to coordinate implementation, working through divisional and sub-divisional health services, and with community partners.

Fiji experiencing fast-growing HIV epidemic Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Dr Lalabalavu said Australia, New Zealand, the Global Fund, India, and the United Nations Joint Team on HIV and AIDS, and other partners are supporting the country with its HIV response.

The Fijian government has also proposed the establishment of a parliamentary standing committee on HIV and related matters, he said.

"To anyone who has been diagnosed with HIV, a diagnosis does not take away your future. Effective treatment can help you live a long and healthy life. Keep taking your medicine as prescribed, even when you feel well.

World.title: Labour pledges to ban big companies from charging excessive prices
World.content:
Labour has promised to ban big companies from charging excessive prices, if elected.

Leader Chris Hipkins said Wednesday's policy announcement was the first in a series designed to increase competition and bring down prices.

He said a handful of big businesses were guilty of price gouging - that is, charging more than necessary for essential items.

"Right now, a company big enough to dodge competition can charge excessive prices for the basics, like food and fuel, and there's no law against it," he said.

"Labour will change that, by making it illegal for big powerful companies to rip off New Zealanders on the essentials."

Commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said 97 percent of New Zealand businesses were small, and would not be affected by the policy.

"It also only applies in markets for essentials, like food, power, fuel, transport, telecommunications banking, and insurance," she said.

Labour's policy document said the law would apply where a company had enough market power that customers could not realistically shop elsewhere, suppliers had nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggled to enter the market.

The full policy includes:

making it illegal for big companies with substantial market power to charge excessive prices for essential goods and services, or to pay unfairly low prices to suppliers

setting a legal test for price gouging: holding prices "well above what they would otherwise be in a competitive market, sustained over time"

requiring companies that gouge to pay penalties and hand back every dollar of excess profit

giving the Commerce Commission power to investigate price gouging and supporting consumer groups and suppliers to do the same.

Williams said similar rules were already in place in the United Kingdom, Europe, Canada, and Australia.

How the ban would work

Williams said the Commerce Commission would investigate dominant companies and take them to court - and consumer groups could, too.

They would have to prove price gouging was taking place - not necessarily for a single product, but across a range of essentials.

"We'd see cases being brought about that collection of goods and the prices that are being charged across it," she said.

That would likely be a class action, with a group of consumers bringing a claim against a company, Williams said.

If a company was guilty of gouging, that group would need to be paid back for being overcharged, she said.

More competition policy to come

National also had a competition policy announcement on Wednesday.

It's proposing to sever Pak'nSave from New World, contingent on whether a Commerce Commission review finds the split would leave shoppers better off.

Hipkins said National was simply announcing another review, and New Zealanders needed "decisive action", which Labour would take.

World.title: National vows to 'pursue' break up supermarket giant Foodstuffs
World.content:
National has made a supermarket break-up a key part of its election pitch, proposing to sever Pak'nSave from New World in a bid to drive down grocery prices.

The shake-up would be contingent on a six-month review by the Commerce Commission into whether the split would actually leave shoppers better off.

If the watchdog gave it the green light, National said it would legislate to force through the separation.

The significant policy was announced with little warning on Wednesday morning, and on the same day that Labour promised to ban big companies from charging excessive prices.

Foodstuffs - made up of two co-operatives - currently manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores.

National's plan would split them up, leaving the country with three nationwide supermarket chains: Pak'nSave, New World/Four Square and Woolworths.

"This is, I acknowledge, a bold and unprecedented step," finance spokesperson Nicola Willis told reporters at Parliament.

"It is the right one. It puts the Kiwi shopper first."

Willis said the proposal followed a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis - by Sense Partners - and two peer reviews which she commissioned as finance minister to explore proposals for breaking up the duopoly.

But she said rather than taking a proposal back to Cabinet this term, National would instead seek an "explicit electoral mandate" from the public given the significance of the move.

"No Kiwi shopper or store owner would thank us if we mucked this up," she said. "While it's always tempting to rush in, the stakes are very high, and work of the sort requires a prudent, careful approach from ministers."

Hipkins: "New Zealanders can't eat a review"

Labour leader Chris Hipkins dismissed National's policy as little more than "another review" and said New Zealanders deserved "more decisive" action.

"It's not a commitment. It's another review," he said. "New Zealanders can't eat a review."

Hipkins would not be drawn on whether he supported breaking up Foodstuffs, but said Labour would have more to say about supermarket competition before the election.

He also pointed out National would find it difficult to get its policy over the line with coalition partner ACT, given its leader David Seymour previously lambasted the plan, arguing it would scare away investment.

New Zealand First, in contrast, announced its own plan to break up Foodstuffs in April.

Willis said the coalition had proven an ability to compromise on various policies this term: "Obviously, this is a key priority for us, and that would be reflected in our coalition discussions."

National leader Christopher Luxon told reporters Labour had failed to put forward a proper "substantive solution" and was so far offering only "more clipboards and bureaucrats".

Willis said the shake-up could eventually save households up to $1320 a year, pushing down grocery prices about 5 percent lower than they would otherwise be.

Sense Partners' modelling estimated prices would be about 3.5 percent lower in the first year of separation, with gains growing as the new chains bedded in. By 2035, the estimated annual household benefit ranged from $200 to $1320 depending on income and family type.

"That's real money back in the pockets of New Zealanders," Willis said.

"More competition means supermarkets have to work harder for every customer, on price, specials, range and service. That is how shoppers get a better deal."

National also trumpeted a potential $12.6 billion in "consumer benefits" over 20 years. However, the underlying analysis put the overall net gain to the whole economy at just $2.9b once lost supermarket profits were counted, or even lower if Foodstuffs' costs increased.

The independent report also carried some hefty warnings, with the economists warning their analysis was "indicative rather than definitive" and flagging potential "insurmountable" legal and implementation hurdles.

Willis acknowledges "tough fight" ahead

Willis stressed that National would act carefully on the Commission's advice and not play "supermarket executive from the Cabinet table".

"There is a very high bar for this kind of intervention and National is not pursuing structural separation in any other sector," Willis said.

"However, after years of reviews and incremental reform, it's clear the status quo isn't working. It's time for change."

Willis acknowledged the difficulties ahead, saying she had already felt the "full force" of the supermarkets' well-resourced lobbyists.

"I know that I am taking on a big entity here," she said. "I've satisfied myself this is the right thing to do, but I know that it's going to be a tough fight."

National said no individual Pak'nSave, New World or Four Square owner would be forced to sell or change brands.

Instead, the two Foodstuffs brands would be split into rival nationwide groups, with separate structures and incentives to compete against each other.

The Commerce Commission's latest monitoring showed Foodstuffs and Woolworths still controlled about 82 percent of the grocery market, with little movement in the core measures of competition over the past year.

Wednesday's announcements follow repeated efforts by both the coalition and former Labour government to break the supermarket stranglehold, with little to show for it.

Willis last year put out a call for third major challenger to enter the market, sounding out potential competitors, but the industry's biggest global players declined to engage.

The government also created an "express lane" for consenting new supermarkets, but it appears no applications have yet been lodged.

World.title: Tuvalu and Taiwan 'like brothers', President Lai Ching-te says
World.content:
Tuvalu's Foreign Affairs Minister Paulson Panapa has met with Taiwan President Lai Ching-te this week.

Taiwan's Presidential Office released a translation of his remarks in which he said Taiwan and Tuvalu were "like brothers".

"This Saturday will mark the 47th anniversary of diplomatic ties between Taiwan and Tuvalu," he said.

"At present, Taiwan is implementing pioneer projects on outer islands like Vaitupu focusing on milkfish aquaculture, increased production of fruits and vegetables, and balanced nutrition and diet.

"Through our collaboration, we aspire to advance balanced development across Tuvalu's outer islands and create a better living environment for the next generation."

He also thanked the Tuvalu government for "consistently speaking up for Taiwan at international venues and supporting our international participation".

Most countries do not recognise Taiwan as separate from China.

China claims Taiwan as part of its territory, but Taipei rejects Beijing's sovereignty claim, saying only the island's people can decide their future.

In his speech, as reported by Taiwan Presidential Office, Panapa said the partnership between the two countries is very visible in the lives of Tuvaluan families.

He said Taiwan's support has helped Tuvalu build resilience against climate change, improve health and education, and expand digital connectivity.

Panapa also said Tuvalu would continue to speak in support of Taiwan's rightful place in the international community.

Taiwan maintains diplomatic ties with Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, as well as nine other nations: Eswatini, Vatican City, Belize, Guatemala, Haiti, Paraguay, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia and St Vincent & the Grenadines.

Naoero, formerly Nauru, switched its diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2024.

At the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders' meeting in Palau, New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said there were long-standing protocols that give Taiwan observer status at the Forum. He noted that Taiwan's status would change when Aotearoa hosts the annual leaders' summit next year.

New Zealand - and most of the Pacific - adheres to the One China policy, which means it does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

World.title: Global dairy price drop points to 'mixed market'
World.content:
The average price fell 1.1 percent at the Global Dairy Trade auction overnight to US$3868 (NZ$6718). It followed a 0.1 percent rise at the previous auction two weeks ago.

In a note, New Zealand Exchange head of dairy insights Cristina Alvarado said the result pointed to a "more mixed market".

Milk powders held "relatively steady", with whole milk powder dropping 0.8 percent to US$3565 (NZ$6191).

However, milkfats saw a "more pronounced correction", with butter prices down 5.7 percent, consistent with the increase in Fonterra's butter offer quantities.

"Milk powders showed relative resilience, particularly SMP (skim milk powder), while milkfat prices corrected as additional butter availability met softer buying pressure."

There was a signicificant difference between prices at physical auctions and earlier pricing.

Alvarado said cheddar provided a "significant counterweight to the broader weakness", with the index rising 16.5 percent and all contracts recording price increases.

There was a notable shift in which regions were buying. North Asian purchasing dropped from 46 percent to 37 percent, while Southeast Asia/Oceania and the Middle East increased their shares.

North Asia remained the largest buyer of whole milk powder, although its share fell 51 percent to 40 percent, while Southeast Asia/Oceania was the leading skim milk powder buyer, purchasing 60 percent of the product offered.

Alvarado said current product availability remained "relatively strong".

"The impact of drought and heatwaves on Northern Hemisphere milk production has yet to be reflected in published production data. The extent of any resulting supply impact therefore remains uncertain.

"At the same time, the potential for an El Niño event in New Zealand has yet to materialise, while higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran have increased cost pressures.

World.title: Pacific nations show promise at inaugural Women's Handball Championship
World.content:
The tournament director at the first-ever Oceania Women's Handball Championship believes Fiji, Cook Islands and Kiribati are on the right path in the sport.

David Ireland, who is also president of New Zealand Handball, made the comments following the Fijians' performance at the event, which concluded on Monday.

Fiji finished fifth after defeating the Cook Islands 17-15 in the play-off, with the team playing in their first international event.

They also beat Kiribati 37-16 in their last pool game, after having lost 41-10 to Tahiti (3rd place) and 49-8 to Australia (eventual winners) in their other two pool matches.

Cook Islands lost 24-9 to New Zealand, 33-13 to New Caledonia before beating Kiribati 25-6.

Kiribati also lost 40-9 to New Zealand and 43-10 to New Caledonia in their other pool games.

Ireland said the three teams displayed some exciting skills.

"I think Fiji have been the absolute revelation," he said.

"They've played really well. They're clearly getting a lot of work into their infrastructure and working through, and have really come on in the last year or so."

IHF Nations Trophy Oceania Women 2026 tournament director David Ireland. @2026 Masanori Udagawa / photowellington.com

Ireland described the Cook Islands as a very well organised team.

"They've always been one of the traditional, regular nations that takes part, and they've got some really strong players and a good structure around what they do."

He said for Kiriabti it was about development for the team.

"They came here and they don't have a coach. A lot of them have never played indoor handball before, and this is their first taste of it, but they've got some really strong athletes, like amazing the power they've got in some of in their shots.

"[It's] exciting and it's just the sheer enjoyment seeing them of them playing."

"That's what this tournament is all about - the Oceanian nations coming together and just really celebrating the joy that is handball."

Action from the New Caledonia vs Tahiti match. @2026 Masanori Udagawa / photowellington.com

French connections

Ireland said Tahiti and New Caledonia were strong regional teams with a lot of French influence.

New Caledonia lost 18-28 to Australia in the final, after they had defeated New Zealand 28-13 in the semi-final.

They also defeated New Zealand 23-15 in pool play, Kiribati 40-9 and Cook Islands 24-9.

Tahiti claimed third position following their 26-22 victory over New Zealand in the play-off, with a close 31-30 loss to New Caledonia in the semi's.

The team lost 27-17 to Australia in pool play but claimed a win over Fiji.

Ireland said the clash between the two French territories was intense and down to the wire in the end.

"It's exceeded all our expectations. Had an absolutely epic game between New Caledonia and Tahiti in the semifinals.

"New Caledonia and Tahiti are the traditional powerhouses because they've got the French heritage. So, Handball is very strong in France, and so a lot of theTahitian and New Caledonia people will grow up playing handball, and they went toe-to-toe right down to the final final second, where New Caledonia won.

"It was all tied up. There were some penalties, really exciting, and that was really intense, and really really good quality handball."

Aussies champs

He said the other semi-final between Australia and New Zealand, also proved to a tough contest but the Aussies had the upper hand.

Australia, the first Oceania champion, now represents the region to the Asian Championship in December, as part of the pathway for the world championships.

"Australia have looked looked really strong. They are one of the the top nations in Oceania for handball, and they are all gearing up towards the 2032 Olympics.

"The New Zealand team, they haven't been together that long. They've done really well.

"They came through pool play, a couple of really good good wins for them in pool play, but were beaten by New Caledonia, so had to play Australia, who finished top in their pool.

"It was quite quite a big gap, and look a lot of our girls are quite young, so great experience for them."

Ireland said the Oceania event was one of the regional events that the International Handball Federation (IHF) had come up with to help the developing nations.

These are nations around the world that are outside of the top-tier nations, mostly in Europe.

"So they actually improve and have a competition for themselves, sort of a second-tier nations concept," he said.

"The winner of this tournament will be funded by the International Handball Federation to go and compete at the Asian Handball Championships for Women, which takes place I think in December.

"That is our pathway, and then the top five nations from that competition will go on to the World Championships next year. For the other regions they have different pathways, but it's all about trying to get the developing nations to qualify to take part in the World Championships."

Australia finished the tournament undefeated.

New Caledonia's Jenny Bazit was the top scorer of the competition, with 31 goals, three more than New Zealand's Kianna Dawson, with the podium completed by Kiribati's Veronika Batiri, with 18 goals.

Ireland said New Zealand and Oceania Handball are now working on the Oceania tournaments for the under-18s and under-20s men's categories in December to be held in Auckland from 10 to 14 December.

Samoa and Tonga have also been invited to be part of that youth event.

Fiji proud

Fiji's head coach Samuela Cava said he was proud of the team's performance, especially as they were playing together for the first time.

He said winning two matches of out four matches and finishing fifth was a great achievement.

Four players in the squad were members of the Fiji U18 team at the World Championship in Romania in August.

"This was the first international tournament of most of our girls, so this was a huge learning experience for us," he said.

"We played two very tough and well-developed teams in our pool, in Australia and Tahiti.

"We made a lot of mistakes in those matches, but we learned quickly from them. I'm just incredibly proud of the ladies.

"They are a young team, but they showed the real Fijian hearts and fought until the very end. To finish fifth overall is a huge milestone for us, especially as the first ever Fiji women's national team to compete at this level.

"I'm so proud of their performance and the character they showed."

Fiji coach Samuela Cava at the Akau Tangi Sports Centre in Wellington. RNZ Pacific / Iliesa Tora

Cava said the sport is still making its headway in the country, with six clubs now competing on aregular basis.

Most of the players have come out of volleyball and netball and Handball Fiji is currently working on developing its youth base.

An U18 and U20 team are in training in Suva for December's youth championship in Auckland.

"Our focus now shifts straight to the development pathway," Cava said.

"At the moment, our junior and youth men's team are in preparation mode for the Oceania Handball Championship.

"For the Fiji Handball Federation, we are in a learning phase, and we are keen to learn more about the sport at international level. Our executives are working hard behind the scenes to develop the sport across Fiji.

"This includes the organizing the official IHF coaching and refereeing course, and most importantly, running more domestic competition back home to grow the player base."

World.title: Messi offered farewell by Argentina after international retirement
World.content:
Lionel Messi has been invited by Argentina to make a farewell appearance in ​a home friendly in October following his international retirement.

Messi, who led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title, announced his retirement from international matches earlier this month.

The 39-year-old has not confirmed whether he will join the team for the friendly in October.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

"We invited the ​best player in ‌the world to play, the icon of our selection, our captain Lionel Andres Messi, to have a deserved farewell … here in Argentina," Argentine Football Association president Claudio ⁠Tapia said on social media.

Argentina will play ‌three home friendlies during FIFA 's international window in September and October, which will be its first matches since the World Cup.

The Argentines will take on Benin in Buenos Aires's Monumental Stadium on October 7, AEST, ​where ‌Messi has been invited to ⁠play his farewell match.

Argentina ‌will also face Bolivia ‌in Córdoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires during the FIFA international window.

Three Argentine players — Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina and Thiago Almada — were recently handed bans by FIFA for a scuffle after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey in July.

Paredes received a 10-match ban.

Reuters

World.title: PGA Tour not considering return program for LIV Golf players
World.content:
The PGA Tour is not considering a returning-member program that would allow players from LIV Golf to return to the US-based circuit the way Brooks Koepka did in January.

Speaking one week after LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection ‌in New Jersey, PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp said accountability and discipline were essential elements for any sports league.

"In terms of where we are ‌today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one ⁠you saw in January," he said.

"Everyone at the PGA Tour, myself included, has been focused on what is best for the organisation."

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Rolapp added: "The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place."

LIV Golf's bankruptcy filing has left the playing futures of some of the breakaway circuit's biggest names in doubt.

Major ‌champions Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, two of the sport's more popular players, were listed as the top unsecured creditors, with each ⁠owed more than $US5 million.

Five-time major champion Koepka ‌took advantage of a limited-time ‌returning member program in January to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV ‌Golf last December.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the former world number one facing a five-year forfeiture of potential ‌equity in the PGA Tour's Player ⁠Equity Program, representing an estimated $US50-85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

LIV Golf hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

Reuters

World.title: Sturt versus Norwood stirs up 1978 controversy ahead of SANFL final
World.content:
Football Park was barely four years old when Sturt and Norwood last met in a famous grand final that included a brief tussle between players and officials in the Sturt dug-out.

The Redlegs came away with a one-point win in 1978 despite Sturt being favoured, but with both teams meeting again for this weekend's SANFL Grand Final, there are several controversies that remain front of mind for some.

First and foremost, there was the winning goal.

After kicking 5:9 to Norwood's 1:5 in the first quarter, Sturt was in front and living up to expectations, having only lost one game for the entire season.

But, 29 points down in the last quarter, the Redlegs mounted a comeback, briefly taking the lead before Sturt kicked another goal.

"Then there was a rough contest in Norwood's forward pocket, and [Redleg] Phil Gallagher took it out of the ruck, quickly slammed it on his boot, and it went straight to Sturt fullback Colin Casey," said SANFL senior media producer Zac Millbank.

"He kicked it straight back out of the area and then Phil Gallagher went to mark Casey's kick, but he actually dropped it."

Field umpire Des Foster blew his whistle and gave what commentators at the time assumed to be a weak free kick to Gallagher.

Foster later said that he actually called it a mark but admitted it was the wrong call, explaining that his field of vision had been obscured by players at the key moment when the ball came down.

In front of more than 50,000 spectators and a live television audience, Gallagher went back and kicked a goal, putting Norwood in front.

Sturt's Lucas Slade and Norwood's Alex Wright will compete for the SANFL flag on Sunday. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

There were about three minutes left, however, and Sturt made several more 50-metre entries but only managed a point.

Mr Millbank pointed out that Sturt had kicked 14 goals and 25 points that day, so the upset loss could not be blamed on "the Des Foster blunder".

"Fourteen goals and 26 points is just horrendous kicking and some of the shots were very simple ones," he said.

Regardless, the moment went down in history as one of the most contentious free kicks or marks ever played at Football Park, the former stadium that was home to SA football between 1974 and 2013.

Mr Millbank said there had been a lot of commentary on the SANFL's social media pages about the 48-year-old moment since Sunday's match-up was confirmed, proving the incident was very much "still on people's minds".

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and Sturt captain Tom Lewis are playing for the cup on Sunday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt captain Tom Lewis said he was reminded about the 1978 final by a pedestrian walking past his house on Monday morning.

"He reminded me at about 7am how disappointed he was at that grand final and asked us to right a few wrongs," he said.

"Both clubs have such a history; it does bring a lot of excitement, a lot of pressure.

"I'm thoroughly looking forward to it, and the boys are. Everyone's amped up; I know Norwood are as well, so hopefully we get a good turnout."

A dug-out scuffle

Another memorable moment occurred in the third quarter in 1978 when Norwood player John Wynne overran the ball on the boundary and ended up inside the enemy's camp, much to his own apparent amusement.

A skirmish ensued, with more players and officials from the Redlegs getting involved, until umpires quelled the situation and broke the parties apart — even as strong words continued to fly.

"Legend has it that master [Sturt] coach Jack Oatey was a bit ruffled after that incident," Mr Millbank said.

"I don't know how true it is, but there's a bit of thought that Wynne did it deliberately to try and stir him up a bit, put them off their game."

Norwood took the 1978 premiership after a long period of SANFL dominance for Sturt, in which they had won five flags in a row from 1966 to 1970, and then in 1974 and 1976 as well.

The fact they had only dropped one game for the entire season — a feat Sturt repeated in 2025 before winning the premiership — had made them the "raging favourites".

For this year's grand final, however, the shoe is on the other foot, and Norwood are the warm favourites going into the game.

Norwood beat Sturt by 19 points during the second semi-final earlier this month. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

Having won the minor premiership and winning the second semi-final against Sturt two weeks ago, the team has only played one match in three weeks.

Coach Jade Sheedy said that after the team's main training session, they had another strong session on Saturday, "which put the boys through their paces and tried to replicate as much as we can to get them ready for a grand final," he said.

"Our preparation has been good … players are fresh."

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said it was always a big game when Sturt and Norwood met, "so to be able to play in a grand final against them is a bigger deal".

"You can certainly feel the anticipation living in the eastern suburbs and knowing that rivalry, the history, the '78 grand final was obviously huge," he said.

"I've heard a lot about that even though it was 48 years ago now. That famous Gallagher mark, my former number 11, so I know a lot about the history."

Digging deep for a repeat

Sturt, which finished third on the ladder, has played three finals to get to the big dance, and will defend their 2025 premiership with a slightly different list to Sunday's preliminary due to injuries.

This includes midfielder Jared Dakin, who injured his hamstring in the opening quarter against Woodville-West Torrens; key defender Casey Voss, who dislocated his shoulder in the game; and ruckman Amos Doyle, who was a late withdrawal due to a neck injury.

The Superjesus will play a set before the SANFL Grand Final at Adelaide Oval on Sunday. (@they.muse)

Coach Marty Mattner said Doyle had been progressing and may still play on Sunday, depending on Wednesday's training, and there was still a window open for Voss, although his inclusion is considered unlikely.

"The positive is that everyone who hasn't been playing in the league side is fit and ready to go," he said.

"Realistically there’s probably seven or eight in that [reserves] group who have played league footy this year."

The 2026 SANFL Grand Final, which will feature Adelaide rockers The Superjesus in pre-game entertainment, will commence at Adelaide Oval from 2:30pm Sunday.

World.title: Rush to put Zverev in Alcaraz-Sinner tier premature despite twin titles
World.content:
When the latest edition of the ATP singles rankings dropped earlier this week, a 24-year streak came to an end.

After being bounced in the first round of the US Open, Novak Djokovic dropped out of the top-10 for the first time since 2018.

Djokovic's exit marks the first time since October 2002 that neither he nor Rafael Nadal nor Roger Federer is inside the top-10.

For tennis fans who wondered when the 'Big 3' era in the men's game would end, the end is now.

Novak Djokovic's first-round exit at the US Open caused him to drop outside the top-10 for the first time since 2018. (Getty Images: Mike Stobe)

With the Djokovic-Federer-Nadal triumvirate dominating the men's game for so long, the question of who their successors would be has been a popular one around tennis.

Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have emulated Federer and Nadal's rivalry from the mid-2000s, exchanging grand slam titles while playing some spellbinding epics along the way, but would any other men's players on tour join them as Djokovic joined Federer and Nadal?

Alexander Zverev appears to be the third member of the party, having claimed two of the four available grand slam titles this year.

But questions remain as to whether Zverev's candidacy to join the very top tier of men's tennis is legitimate.

Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

Since first achieving a top-10 ranking in May 2017 as a 20-year-old, Zverev has been one of the most consistent performers on the men's tour.

Zverev has spent 414 weeks as a top-10 ranked player throughout his career, currently 15th all-time. He ranks second among active players in this metric, behind only Djokovic, with 959 weeks, just behind Federer's 968.

At the time of writing, Zverev has spent 102 consecutive weeks ranked inside the top 10 since his most recent streak began in September 2023.

Those numbers are not the problem when it comes to Zverev's bid to be considered the best player in the world.

It is this one.

Career wins against top-10 ranked opponents Wins % Novak Djokovic 69 66 Roger Federer 64 62 Rafael Nadal 55 67 Carlos Alcaraz 16 70 Jannik Sinner 14 50 Alexander Zverev 5 22

Despite being a constant presence in the top-10 rankings over the best part of the last decade, Zverev has consistently struggled to beat the other players ranked in the same vicinity.

The German owns an unenviable 5-18 (21.7 per cent) win-loss record against fellow top-10 opponents in grand slam matches. He has won 59 of his 146 matches against top-10 opponents overall, roughly a 40 per cent conversion rate.

Zverev's record pales in comparison to Alcaraz and Sinner, as well as Djokovic, Federer and Nadal.

Alcaraz has an astounding 16-7 record against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with his 69.6 per cent conversion rate by far the best among the elite cohort, while Sinner has gone 14-14 in such matches.

Zverev has been beaten by Sinner (pictured) in two of his six grand slam final appearances. (Getty Images/Frey)

Nadal, Djokovic and Federer all won over 60 per cent of their matches against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with Djokovic's 69 wins leading the way.

This record against the very best players helped make Zverev a perennial grand slam semifinalist and finalist before he broke through with his first title at Roland-Garros earlier this year.

While Zverev now has two grand slam titles to his name, the calibre of opponents he has overcome suggests he hasn't really gone up a tier.

The German claimed the French Open title without facing a single top-10-ranked opponent, with the runner-up Flavio Cobolli the top-ranked player at No.14.

US Open finalist Ben Shelton is the only top-10 ranked opponent Zverev has beaten en route to his two grand slam titles this year. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

Overall, the average ranking of the players Zverev beat en-route to his first grand slam title is 57.7, with his fourth-round opponent, world No.106, Jesper de Jong the lowest-ranked.

Zverev had a slightly tougher run to the US Open title, but still faced just one top-10-ranked opponent in finalist Ben Shelton (eighth).

On average, Zverev's US Open opponents ranked 45th overall, with his first-round opponent, Lorenzo Sonego, the lowest-ranked at No.89.

Zverev's victories offer hope for the rest of the non-Alcaraz and Sinner division on the men's tour, including players such as Australia's Alex de Minaur.

De Minaur, like Zverev, has struggled against top-10 opponents at grand slams, winning just two of 14 matches.

Zverev's breakthroughs offer hope for the likes of Australia's Alex de Minaur (pictured). (AP: Christinne Muschi)

Despite reaching a career-high ranking of No.5 this year, de Minaur has yet to win a grand slam quarterfinal.

The Australian has a 0-7 record in quarters, with six of those losses coming over the last three seasons.

De Minaur has looked downtrodden after his recent grand slam exits, but will hope that like Zverev, he too can capitalise on the bracket breaking just right for him at some point down the line.

For now, Zverev looks to have graduated above the class featuring the likes of Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Felix Auger-Aliassime, de Minaur and others.

But for him to truly climb into the upper echelon of men's tennis, it is time he starts taking down the big names when it matters most.

World.title: Renshaw scores first ODI century as Aussies defeat Zimbabwe
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has scored his first ODI century, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

Australia chose to bat first, and the surprise decision from captain Mitchell Marsh was vindicated as ​the tourists scored 8-294 from ‌their 50 overs, setting Zimbabwe an imposing target at Harare Sports Club.

In reply, Zimbabwe was dismissed for 235 in 45.1 overs, showing good fight but always behind ‌the required run rate.

Renshaw, who last scored an international ton in ⁠a Test against Pakistan in 2017, made 109.

He featured ‌in some key partnerships, while Cooper ​Connolly made 51.

Renshaw put on 72 runs with Alex Carey for the fifth wicket and 75 with Ollie Peake for the sixth wicket, leaving Zimbabwe with a ​required ‌run rate of 5.90.

The 20-year-old left-arm quick Newman Nyamhuri finished with 5-62, only the second Zimbabwe bowler to take five wickets in ⁠an ODI against Australia.

Zimbabwe lost four ‌wickets quickly before Craig Ervine ‌and Sikandar steadied the innings with a 98-run partnership that offered the hosts hope ‌of victory on a surface that traditionally gets better for batting as the day wears on.

Ellis had taken two ‌wickets ​in his first spell and when he was reintroduced, took three balls to clean bowl Ervine for 59 and put the brakes on Zimbabwe.

Sikandar was dispensed by Spencer Johnson for 57 to leave Zimbabwe ⁠still significantly adrift.

Ellis finished with 5-31 in 9.1 overs, also cleaning up the tail.

The second ODI ‌will be played on ‌Friday in Harare, ​after which Australia moves to South Africa.

Reuters

World.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
World.content:
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.

A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".

It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.

The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.

"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.

"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."

SafeWork SA says it lodged the proceedings against Christian Brothers College earlier this month. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".

According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.

"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.

The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.

World.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.

A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".

Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.

"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.

Former England captain Ben Stokes will join the Adelaide Strikers for BBL16. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde-ICC)

"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.

"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.

"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."

The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.

In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.

Steve Smith has played 40 matches for the Sydney Sixers, including 6 in BBL15. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.

"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.

"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."

Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.

Mitch March playing for the Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred in the UK. (Getty Images: Annabel Lee-Ellis)

"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.

"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.

CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

World.title: Dockers will not be 'ambushed' by 'galvanised' Swans, Longmuir vows
World.content:
Many see it as a golden opportunity for Fremantle to reach just their second AFL grand final, but Justin Longmuir insists there is no chance the Dockers will underestimate a Sydney side missing a host of star players in Friday night's preliminary final at the SCG.

Fremantle is set to enter the game as warm favourite, despite being away from home against a team which thrashed reigning premier Brisbane by 53 points in their qualifying final, with the Swans hard hit by suspension and injury.

When Sydney stood down Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice in the wake of the off-field scandal at a Melbourne hotel, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said they had "effectively torpedoed" their season.

Remarkably since then, they have defied expectations, beating North Melbourne just days later before the stunning upset of the Lions.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

That was despite losing Callum Mills during the game, with the captain joining the long list of absentees, ruled out for the season with a knee injury.

Longmuir has urged his side to put its full focus on the Sydney players who are taking the field, rather than those ruled out.

"Already done that. They dropped 141 points on Brisbane who were the flag favourites, it's a wake-up call," he said.

Errol Gulden and the Swans are undermanned but coming off a dominant qualifying final win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They didn't seem to miss those guys, so we just play what's in front of us.

"Clearly they haven't lost any of their scoring power, and all I can go on is what I see from the last two games, and playing like a really galvanised team, playing with great spirit, great physicality.

"It looks like whatever has happened has galvanised them, and they're playing a really tough brand of footy.

"We're definitely not going up there and getting ambushed by what they're trying to do. We've seen [it] in the last couple of weeks and we've seen it work really well.

"We've got to make sure that we don't just think it's going to happen for us, we've got to make sure we impose our footy."

Longmuir calls for no fear

The Dockers rebounded from their qualifying final loss to Hawthorn with a 14-point semifinal victory over Geelong, with Longmuir pleased with how his players took the contest on against the Cats.

Luke Jackson was instrumental in Fremantle's semifinal win and shapes as a big factor against Sydney. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He urged his side to not to be afraid of making mistakes on the big stage, and to always be prepared to move on to the next contest.

"If we're going to make mistakes, let's make sure we make mistakes playing our way and playing with the right mindset, because usually those mistakes you can move on from a little bit quicker," he said.

Dockers show they have the steel to be AFL's best Fremantle booked a spot in the AFL preliminary finals with a stirring win over Geelong, breathing life into the club's premiership dream.

"At times we didn't make those mistakes the right way against Hawthorn and we stood still after, because we didn't move on from them.

"It's been a message for a long time because we play such an imperfect game, players who have played their best games would've been full of mistakes. It's just the nature and the scrappiness of our game, so let's make them with the right mindset."

The Dockers are set to fly to Sydney on Wednesday, with the two clubs naming their teams on Thursday ahead of the clash.

Tech.title: The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.

The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.

Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.

Image: Canon

The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.

Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.

Image: Canon

Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.

In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

Tech.title: AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular in every poll
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Poll data released Tuesday by the New York Times and Siena University confirms what we’ve already been seeing, and what politicians are responding to — AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular. Asked if they support or oppose the construction of data centers to power AI tech, 61 percent of the 1,503 likely voters surveyed in early September (ahead of the recent AI safety slowdown discussion) said they were opposed, with only 14 percent saying they strongly support. The split was about even among 2024 Donald Trump voters, at 49 percent support to 45 percent oppose, while people who had voted for Kamala Harris or who didn’t vote leaned oppose, at 74 percent and 67 percent, respectively.

56 percent of voters surveyed who said they were opposed to data centers said they supported limits, while 38 percent instead preferred a total ban. The list of reasons for opposition is also revealing, with the environment/water usage most common at 32 percent, impact on local communities at 21 percent, general distrust or dislike of AI at 18 percent, followed by regulation concerns and the economy at 10 and 9 percent.

An NBC News poll in March showed AI polling lower than ICE, and a Gallup poll in May revealed seven in ten Americans opposed local construction of AI data centers.

Still, the data released today ranked AI and data centers low on the list of issues that voters saw as most important in deciding their midterm vote. Across the board, AI and data centers registered at less than one percent for most demographics, with exceptions for younger voters like the 18-29 group, where three percent picked that one instead of the most popular responses like the economy, foreign policy, inflation, and opposition to Trump/Republicans. Voters in either party still overwhelmingly picked their own party as the one they trusted to handle the issue, while overall the 554 respondents had 40 percent favoring Democrats, 42 percent favoring Republicans, and 18 percent saying they didn’t know or refused.

It’s been more than two years since the last major Windows event, so Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month to outline the future of Windows and Surface devices. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be in attendance, alongside Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri. Microsoft’s event invite. Image: Microsoft

Tech.title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
Tech.content:
Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.

Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.

In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.

“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”

In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.

Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”

Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.

Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”

Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”

“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”

Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”

But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.

With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

Tech.title: Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.

One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.

All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!

Previous Next







1 / 5

The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.

Previous Next









1 / 6

This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.

While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”

PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.

I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

Tech.title: One of the best 3D printers for beginners is almost $100 off
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If the high price tag of premium 3D printers have kept you from exploring the hobby, this deal is a great entry point. Elegoo has its Centauri Carbon 2 Combo on sale for $369, almost $100 off its usual price of $449. This capable 3D printer can handle four filament rolls at once, with a fully enclosed printing area, auto-leveling bed, and big touchscreen for easy project management. It’s altogether very capable 3D printer for beginners, or just anyone who doesn’t want to spend a lot of time tinkering with settings just to print occasional trinkets and brackets.

The Centauri Carbon 2 is fast and capable right out of the box, though first-time setup is a little involved (I found it tough to get the upper shield and filament hub to fit together, for example). But I really like its fully-enclosed build area, which results in consistent prints, and the auto-leveling bed checks that everything is locked in the right place before each print. It’s worth noting that the filament rolls are stored externally, so if you’re in a particularly humid environment and don’t print often, you may want to remove them between uses.
